**Explain the approach**

Get all unique values in a JavaScript array & remove duplicates — Remove array values that appear more than once

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If we want to keep only values that are not duplicated, we can use the `Array.prototype.filter()` method. Elements that appear more than once have to appear in **at least two different indexes**, so we can use `Array.prototype.indexOf()` and `Array.prototype.lastIndexOf()` to check for this. If we expect the array to have many duplicate values, creating a `Set` from it first may improve performance.

```js
const removeNonUnique = arr =>
  [...new Set(arr)].filter(i => arr.indexOf(i) === arr.lastIndexOf(i));

removeNonUnique([1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5]); // [1, 3, 5]
```

We can also do the opposite, and remove all values that appear only once. In this case the two indices have to be the same. Notice that using a `Set` for this operation will drop duplicates from the result.

```js
const removeUnique = arr =>
  [...new Set(arr)].filter(i => arr.indexOf(i) !== arr.lastIndexOf(i));

removeUnique([1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5]); // [2, 4]
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/unique-values-in-array-remove-duplicates.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you keep only the values that appear exactly once in an array, dropping every value that has duplicates?
back:
A value appears exactly once when its first and last positions are the same: keep it if `arr.indexOf(x) === arr.lastIndexOf(x)`. Flip the test to `!==` to get only the values that repeat.

```js
const removeNonUnique = arr =>
  [...new Set(arr)].filter(i => arr.indexOf(i) === arr.lastIndexOf(i));

removeNonUnique([1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5]); // [1, 3, 5]

const removeUnique = arr =>
  [...new Set(arr)].filter(i => arr.indexOf(i) !== arr.lastIndexOf(i));

removeUnique([1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5]); // [2, 4]
```

Filtering the deduplicated `Set` (not `arr`) means each repeated value is listed once in `removeUnique`'s result. Each `indexOf` scans the array, so this is O(n²); for large arrays, count occurrences in a `Map` first.

front: How do you split an object into an array of its keys and a parallel array of its values (e.g. labels and data for a chart)?
back:
`[Object.keys(obj), Object.values(obj)]`. Both use the same property order, so `keys[i]` always pairs with `values[i]`.

```js
const unzipObject = obj => [Object.keys(obj), Object.values(obj)];

const countsByStatus = { open: 3, closed: 5, pending: 1 };
const [labels, data] = unzipObject(countsByStatus);
labels; // ['open', 'closed', 'pending']
data;   // [3, 5, 1]
```

The order is insertion order, except that integer-like keys (`'1'`, `'2'`) always come first in ascending order. If you need the pairs together, use `Object.entries(obj)`, which gives `[['open', 3], ...]`.

How can I zip and unzip arrays in JavaScript? — Unzip arrays

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The inverse of zipping is unzipping, which converts the array of arrays back into separate arrays. We can use `Math.max()` and the spread operator (`...`) to get the **longest subarray** in the array and `Array.from()` to create an array of appropriate length.

Then, using `Array.prototype.reduce()` and `Array.prototype.forEach()`, we can **map grouped values to individual arrays**, by pushing each value to the **array at the same index**.

```js
const unzip = arr =>
  arr.reduce(
    (acc, val) => (val.forEach((v, i) => acc[i].push(v)), acc),
    Array.from({
      length: Math.max(...arr.map(x => x.length))
    }).map(x => [])
  );

unzip([['a', 1, true], ['b', 2, false]]); // [['a', 'b'], [1, 2], [true, false]]
unzip([['a', 1, true], ['b', 2]]); // [['a', 'b'], [1, 2], [true]]
```

How can I add a key-value pair to a JavaScript object? — Square bracket notation

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: When must you use square brackets (`obj[key] = value`) instead of dot notation to add a property to a JavaScript object?
back:
Use brackets when the property name is only known at runtime (held in a variable, built from a string) or is not a valid identifier, such as `'created-at'`. For a fixed, valid name, `obj.key = value` and `obj['key'] = value` do exactly the same thing.

```js
const filters = {};
const field = 'status';         // e.g. the value of a <select>
filters[field] = 'active';      // key comes from the variable
filters['created-at'] = '2024'; // not a valid identifier
filters.field = 'oops';         // adds a key literally named "field"
// { status: 'active', 'created-at': '2024', field: 'oops' }
```

Pitfall: `obj.field` never reads a variable called `field`. In an object literal, use a computed key instead: `{ [field]: 'active' }`.

---

One solution:

```js

```

Bracket notation evaluates the expression inside `[]` and uses the result as the key. `filters.field = value` would add a key named `field` instead.

To return a new object rather than mutate the argument (the usual choice for React state), use a computed key: `return { ...filters, [field]: value };`

front: What does `Object.defineProperty()` let you control when adding a property, and what happens to the flags you leave out?
back:
It sets the property's full descriptor: a `value` (or a `get`/`set` pair) plus the flags `writable`, `enumerable` and `configurable`. Every flag you omit defaults to `false`, so the new property is read-only, hidden from `Object.keys()` and `JSON.stringify()`, and cannot be deleted.

```js
const user = { name: 'Ada' };
Object.defineProperty(user, 'id', { value: 7 });

Object.keys(user);    // ['name']  (not enumerable)
JSON.stringify(user); // '{"name":"Ada"}'
user.id = 8;          // ignored; TypeError in strict mode
user.id;              // 7
```

Plain assignment (`user.id = 7`) sets all three flags to `true`, which is what you want almost always. Reach for `defineProperty` (or `Object.defineProperties()` for several at once) only when you need a read-only, hidden, or getter-backed property.

---

One solution:


Descriptor flags you omit default to `false`. Leaving out `writable` makes the property read-only; you must opt in to `enumerable: true` or `Object.keys()` and `JSON.stringify()` will skip it. `configurable` also stays `false`, so the property cannot be deleted or redefined later.

previous.back:
In the ActiveRecord pattern, models can have relationships with other models. These relationships can be **one-to-one**, **one-to-many**, or **many-to-many**. One-to-one and one-to-many relationships are the most common and are relatively easy to implement, while many-to-many relationships are a little trickier to deal with.

We'll largely do away with these conventions and, instead simplify relationships to _single_ and _multiple_. A single relationship means that a model instance references a **single instance** of another model, while a multiple relationship means that a model instance references **multiple instances** of another model.

front: How do you format a numeric id as a fixed-width hex string such as `0x0000002a`?
back:
Convert to base 16 with `toString(16)`, then left-pad to 8 characters with `padStart(8, '0')`:

```js
const hexId = id => `0x${id.toString(16).padStart(8, '0')}`;

hexId(42);  // '0x0000002a'
hexId(255); // '0x000000ff'
```

Eight hex digits cover every id below 2^32 (about 4.3 billion). `padStart` never shortens a string, so a larger id simply comes out longer. Don't add `.slice(0, 8)`: it would silently cut large ids down to their first 8 digits, so two different records could print the same id. This is only for display; keep comparing ids as numbers.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/complex-object-autoloading-console.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

```js

____

```
back:
One solution:

```js
const id = `0x${record.id.toString(16).padStart(8, '0')}`;
```

`Number.prototype.toString(16)` gives `'2a'`; `padStart(8, '0')` adds zeros on the left until the string is 8 characters long. Don't add `.slice(0, 8)`: it would cut ids of 2^32 and above down to their first 8 digits, so different records could print identical ids.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — Index methods

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you add `first` and `last` getters to an `Array` subclass, and which built-in array method reads the last element directly?
back:
Define `get` accessors that return `this[0]` and the last element. The built-in for the last element is `Array.prototype.at(-1)` (ES2022); negative indexes count from the end.

```js
class RecordSet extends Array {
  get first() { return this[0]; }
  get last()  { return this.at(-1); } // same as this[this.length - 1]
}

const posts = RecordSet.from([{ id: 1 }, { id: 2 }, { id: 3 }]);
posts.first.id;        // 1
posts.last.id;         // 3
new RecordSet().last;  // undefined (no error on an empty set)
```

Getters are read without parentheses (`posts.last`, not `posts.last()`). On any plain array you can skip the subclass and just write `arr.at(-1)`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/complex-object-collections-in-memory.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```js
return this.at(-1);
```

`at(-1)` counts from the end of the array. The older equivalent is `return this[this.length - 1];`. Both return `undefined` for an empty array instead of throwing.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/complex-object-collections-in-memory.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — Record querying

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Querying records is the most crucial part of this implementation. After all, it's the main reason we're doing this. We can create a `RecordSet` as a **subclass** of `Array` class to handle this responsibility. It provides a way to query records based on their attributes.

> [!NOTE]
>
> While the name may suggest that the `RecordSet` is a subclass of `Set`, I've found that arrays are much simpler to work with. Thus, I decided to subclass `Array` instead, but the original name stuck, reminding me of its `Set` origins.

Leveraging the power of array methods, we need only implement a handful of alias methods to make querying records a breeze. Fan favorites such as `Array.prototype.filter()`, `Array.prototype.find()`, `Array.prototype.map()`, `Array.prototype.reduce()`, and `Array.prototype.sort()` are already available to us!

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/complex-object-collections-in-memory.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Why subclass `Array` to build a `RecordSet` of query results, and what type does `filter()` return when called on a `RecordSet`?

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — The core classes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
At the core of this project are two main classes: `Model`, `RecordSet`. In future articles, we'll explore some more of the features that can be added to these classes, but for now, let's focus on the basics.

The `Model` is the **base class** for all models. Its job is to provide a way to define attributes and relationships. Model instances (or **records**) are, for the intents of this implementation, considered immutable. The `RecordSet` is a **collection of records**, which can be queried and filtered.

> [!NOTE]
>
> In this article, I use the terms _instance_ and _record_ **interchangeably**. They both refer to a single model instance in memory. Do not confuse the term "record" with a database record, the JavaScript `Record` type or the class of the same name implemented by various libraries.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/complex-object-collections-in-memory.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: In an in-memory ActiveRecord-style layer, what is the job of the `Model` base class, and what is the job of the `RecordSet` class?
back:
`Model` is the base class every model (such as `Post` or `Author`) extends. It defines attributes and relationships, stores each model's instances, and provides static entry points like `all`, `find` and `where`. `RecordSet` is the collection type: an array of records with chainable query helpers (`where`, `pluck`, `first`, `last`).

```js
Post.find(1);                       // Model: one record by id
Post.where({ status: 'published' }) // Model -> RecordSet
  .pluck('title');                  // RecordSet method
```

In this design, records are loaded once and treated as read-only. "Record" here means one model instance in memory, not a database row or TypeScript's `Record<K, V>` type.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/complex-object-collections-in-memory.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — The `where` method

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How can a `where(query)` helper accept exact values, lists of allowed values, and predicate functions in the same query object?

back:
One solution:

```js
return Object.keys(query).every(key => {
```

`Object.keys(query)` lists the conditions, and `every` returns `true` only when all of them pass, so `where({ status: 'draft', authorId: 1 })` means status AND author. An empty query matches every record, because `every` on an empty array returns `true`.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — Models & instances

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
As we've already mentioned, all model records are **immutable** and loaded into memory. This means that each model's records are known ahead of time, so each model class can have a `static` property to store all of its instances.

Unfortunately, if we are to create a core `Model` class and define a `static` property on it, it would be **shared across all subclasses**. This isn't what we want.

After rummaging through various websites, I came across [**static initialization blocks**](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Classes/Static_initialization_blocks), a relatively new addition to JavaScript. It allows us to run some code when the class is defined, but before any instances are created.

You may be thinking _but how does this help us?_ If we had a global storage for all model instances, we could use a static initialization block to create an array for each subclass. This way, each model class would have its own array of instances.

---

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

I'm using [**ESM** (ECMAScript Modules)](https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html) for this project, so I can use `import` and `export` statements. previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — More record querying

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Having set up the two core classes and loaded some data into memory, we should finally be able to query the records. Except, we don't have any way to query them yet.

This is yet another responsibility for the `Model` class. Leveraging the resolution of `this` in the context of `static` methods, we can essentially create query methods on all subclasses, referencing themselves.

Ok, that last bit was somewhat confusing. Let me explain. If we define a `static` method on `Model` and it references `this`, it will resolve to the **subclass that called the method**. Neat, right? This way, we can find the right set of instances in the `instances` array.

> [!TIP]
>
> Confused? Don't worry, the `this` keyword is a tricky thing to master. I suggest reading [this article](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/this) to get a better understanding of it.

---

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — Querying in the model

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How can every model support `Post.where({...})` as a shortcut for `Post.all.where({...})`, with the method written only once?

back:
One solution:

```js
return this.all.where(query);
```

In a static method called as `Post.where(...)`, `this` is `Post`, so `this.all` reads `Post`'s records rather than every model's. The query logic stays in `RecordSet.where`; the model method is only a shortcut.

**Explain the approach**

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — Preparing the storage

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How can a static `prepare(model)` method give each model class its own storage array inside one shared registry?

back:
One solution:

```js
Model.instances[name] ??= [];
```

Equivalent older form: `if (!Model.instances[name]) Model.instances[name] = [];`. Either way, a second `prepare` call keeps the existing array instead of wiping the stored records.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — The idea

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
What I wanted to accomplish with this project is to have a way to load a fairly large amount of plain objects, which are related to each other. Instead of JavaScript's nesting, referencing and moving around things, I wanted something simple and elegant.

ActiveRecord was my initial inspiration, but the implementation has delved a little bit away from it. Instead of relying on a database, my need was to do this on the fly, using **memory**. I also didn't have a need to update the data in the objects. What I was essentially after was a way to load a **snapshot of data** into memory, populate a bunch of models and then query them.

---

**Explain the approach**

Modeling complex JavaScript object collections in memory — Partial records

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: On a collection of records, what do `pluck('title')` and `select('id', 'title')` return, and how are both built from `map()`?

back:
One solution:

```js
return RecordSet.from(super.map(record => record[attribute]));
```

`map` turns each record into one value; `record[attribute]` uses bracket notation because the attribute name is in a variable. `super.map` reaches the original `Array.prototype.map`, and `RecordSet.from` keeps the result chainable.

```plaintext
src/
├── core/
│   ├── model.js
│   └── recordSet.js
└── models/
    └── post.js
```

We'll come to expand upon this setup in future posts, but for now, this is all we need. The `core` directory contains the core classes, while the `models` directory contains the model classes.

front: In a small in-memory model project, what belongs in `src/core/` and what belongs in `src/models/`?
back:
`src/core/` holds the generic, reusable building blocks (`Model`, `RecordSet`) that know nothing about your domain. `src/models/` holds the domain classes (`Post`, `Author`) that extend them.

```plaintext
src/
├── core/
│   ├── model.js
│   └── recordSet.js
└── models/
    └── post.js
```

The dependency goes one way: models import from core, and core never imports a specific model. That keeps the core reusable and avoids circular imports.

```js
Post.all.map(post => post.title)
```

front: How does a test-data factory's `build(...traits)` merge the base data with named traits, and which value wins when two of them set the same field?

back:
One solution:

```js
...desiredTraits.map((trait) => traits[trait])
```

`map` turns trait names into trait objects, and spread passes each one as a separate argument to `Object.assign`. Later sources overwrite earlier ones, so the last trait wins on conflicts. Starting from `{}` keeps `base` itself unchanged.

front: How can a factory's `build()` accept one-off overrides (plain objects, or functions computed from the data so far) as well as named traits?

back:
One solution:

```js
Object.assign(data, arg(data));
```

The function receives the current `data`, so it can derive fields from earlier arguments (here the overridden `name`). Its return value is an object of new fields, merged over `data`. Because arguments are applied in order, put the function after the overrides it depends on.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Modeling complex JavaScript object factories — Fixtures & Factories

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In the world of testing, we often need to create **mock data** to test our code. This is often done with **fixtures**, static pieces of data that we can use to test our code. However, fixtures can be cumbersome to maintain, especially as our objects grow complex. They also often break or get outdated, making seemingly unrelated tests fail.

This is where **factories** come in. Factories are **dynamic** pieces of code that can generate **mock data** for our tests. They can be as simple or as complex as we need them to be, and they can be updated easily when our objects change. As far as I can tell, they are based on the **Factory pattern** from the [Gang of Four book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_Patterns).

For this particular implementation, I'm going to loosely base my factories on the [Factory Bot](https://thoughtbot.github.io/factory_bot/) gem for Ruby. The reason is that I'm rather familiar with this library and I like using it, so that's where I'm drawing my inspiration from.

---

front: What's wrong with this registry guard, where `factoryMap` is a `Map`: `if (!Factory.factoryMap[factoryName]) Factory.factoryMap.set(factoryName, {...})`?

back:
One solution:

```js
if (!Factory.factoryMap.has(factoryName))
```

Map entries are only reachable through `has`, `get`, `set` and `delete`. Writing `if (!Factory.factoryMap[factoryName])` reads a normal property of the `Map` object, which is always `undefined`, so the check would always pass and overwrite existing factories.

front: How do static `serialize()` and `serializeArray()` shortcuts on a `Serializer` base class let callers skip writing `new PostSerializer(post).serialize()`?

back:
One solution:


Modeling complex JavaScript object serialization — Serialization

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you're not familiar, **serialization** is the conversion of an object into a format that can be stored or transmitted. In our case, we want to convert our `Post` and `Author` objects into a format that can be sent to the client. This format is usually **JSON**.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/complex-object-serialization.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What is serialization in a web API, and what does `JSON.stringify` do with a `Date`, an `undefined` field, a `Map`, and a class instance?
back:
Serialization turns an in-memory object into a format that can be stored or sent, usually a JSON string for an API response. `JSON.stringify` handles several common types in surprising ways:

```js
JSON.stringify({
  created: new Date('2025-01-02'), // ISO string via Date#toJSON
  note: undefined,                  // key dropped
  tags: new Map([['a', 1]]),        // {} - Map entries are lost
  list: [undefined, 1],             // [null,1] inside arrays
  post: new Post('Hi'),             // own enumerable fields only
});
// '{"created":"2025-01-02T00:00:00.000Z","tags":{},"list":[null,1],"post":{"title":"Hi"}}'
```

Functions are dropped too, and prototype getters are skipped. That's why APIs usually build response objects explicitly (a serializer) instead of stringifying models directly.

front: How do you convert a plain object into a `Map`, and what type are the keys afterwards?
back:
Pass its entries to the `Map` constructor: `new Map(Object.entries(obj))`. The constructor accepts any iterable of `[key, value]` pairs. The keys stay strings, because object keys were already strings.

How can I deep freeze an object in JavaScript? — `Object.freeze()` vs `Object.seal()`

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: What is the difference between `Object.freeze()` and `Object.seal()`?
back:
Both stop properties from being added or deleted. `freeze` also makes existing properties read-only; `seal` still lets you change the values of existing properties. Only `freeze` makes an object immutable.

```js
const frozen = Object.freeze({ username: 'johnsmith' });
const sealed = Object.seal({ username: 'johnsmith' });

frozen.name = 'John';       // ignored (TypeError in strict mode)
sealed.name = 'John';       // ignored (TypeError in strict mode)
delete sealed.username;     // ignored
sealed.username = 'jsmith'; // allowed
frozen.username = 'jsmith'; // ignored
// sealed = { username: 'jsmith' }, frozen = { username: 'johnsmith' }
```

| | Add | Update | Delete |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `freeze` | No | No | No |
| `seal` | No | Yes | No |

Both are shallow: nested objects stay mutable (`Object.freeze({ user: {} }).user.name = 'x'` works). Use a recursive deep freeze if nested data must be locked too.

---

One solution:

```js
Object.seal
```

`Object.seal` marks existing properties non-configurable and the object non-extensible, but leaves them writable. `Object.freeze` would also make `theme` read-only, so the first assignment would be ignored too. Both are shallow: nested objects are not affected.

How can I deep freeze an object in JavaScript? — Checking if an object is deep frozen

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Checking if an object is frozen is simple, using `Object.isFrozen()`. However, to check if an object is deeply frozen, you will have to perform a **recursive check** on all its properties. This is very similar to how you would go about deep freezing the object in the first place, but instead of `Array.prototype.forEach()`, you can use `Array.prototype.every()` to check if all properties are deeply frozen.

```js
const isDeepFrozen = obj =>
  Object.isFrozen(obj) &&
  Object.keys(obj).every(
    prop => typeof obj[prop] !== 'object' || isDeepFrozen(obj[prop])
  );

const x = Object.freeze({ a: 1 });
const y = Object.freeze({ b: { c: 2 } });
isDeepFrozen(x); // true
isDeepFrozen(y); // false
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/deep-freeze-object.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: `Object.isFrozen()` only checks the top level. How do you check whether an object is frozen all the way down?
back:
Recurse: the object must be frozen, and every property value that is an object must itself be deeply frozen. Use `every` so the check stops at the first failure, and skip `null` (because `typeof null === 'object'`).

```js
const isDeepFrozen = obj =>
  Object.isFrozen(obj) &&
  Object.keys(obj).every(prop =>
    obj[prop] === null ||
    typeof obj[prop] !== 'object' ||
    isDeepFrozen(obj[prop])
  );

isDeepFrozen(Object.freeze({ a: 1 }));        // true
isDeepFrozen(Object.freeze({ b: { c: 2 } })); // false: b isn't frozen
isDeepFrozen(Object.freeze({ n: null }));     // true
```

Without the `null` check, `Object.keys(null)` throws a TypeError as soon as any property is `null`, which is common in API data.

front: Why does `Object.freeze()` fail to protect the contents of a `Set` or `Map`?
back:
`Object.freeze` only affects an object's own properties. A `Set`'s or `Map`'s items live in internal storage and are changed through methods (`add`, `set`, `delete`, `clear`), which freezing does not disable.

```js
const tags = Object.freeze(new Set(['js']));
tags.add('css'); // works
tags.size;       // 2
```

To guard one, shadow the mutating methods on the instance (for example `tags.add = undefined`) and then freeze it, or expose only read functions. Neither is bulletproof, since `Set.prototype.add.call(tags, 'x')` still works. The same applies to other built-ins with internal state, such as `Date`.

Assign default values for a JavaScript object's properties

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you have worked with classes for any length of time, you have probably encountered the need to **assign default values to object properties**. This is usually handled by the constructor function, but what if you want to assign default values to an object that is not a class instance?

Luckily, we can use `Object.assign()` for this task. Using this method, we can create a new **empty object** and **copy the original object** to maintain the key order. We can then use the spread operator (`...`) and `Array.prototype.reverse()` to **combine the default values from left to right**. If multiple default values are provided for the same property, the first one will take precedence.

Finally, we can use the original object again to **overwrite properties that originally had a value**. This way, we can assign default values to all properties in an object that are `undefined`.

```js
const defaults = (obj, ...defs) =>
  Object.assign({}, obj, ...defs.reverse(), obj);

defaults({ a: 1 }, { b: 2 }, { b: 6 }, { a: 3 }); // { a: 1, b: 2 }
```

> [!TIP]
>
> If you find yourself needing to assign the same default values to multiple objects, you can create a **factory function** that generates a new function with the default values already set. This way, you can reuse the same defaults across different objects and optimize your code.

---

**Explain the approach**

How can I define an enum in JavaScript?

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: JavaScript has no `enum` keyword. How do you define a fixed set of named constants that can't be changed at runtime?
back:
Use a frozen object: `Object.freeze({ ... })`. The names are the keys, and freezing stops code from adding, changing or removing members.

```js
const Status = Object.freeze({
  Draft: 'draft',
  Published: 'published',
  Archived: 'archived',
});

post.status === Status.Published;              // readable comparisons
Object.values(Status).includes(input.status);  // validate form/API input
Status.Draft = 'x';                            // ignored (TypeError in strict mode)
```

String values are easier to debug and store than `0, 1, 2`, and they read clearly in JSON and database rows. Pitfall: a typo such as `Status.Publsihed` is just `undefined`, with no error. TypeScript catches it: add `as const` to the object, or use a union type like `'draft' | 'published'`.

```js
  Object.keys(obj).find(key => fn(obj[key], key, obj));

  fred: { age: 40, active: false },
  pebbles: { age: 1, active: true },
};

findKey(users, u => u.age > 100); // undefined (no match)
```

Passing `(value, key, obj)` mirrors array callbacks, so the test can use the key too. Order follows the object's key order: integer-like keys first, then other strings in insertion order.

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Recent versions of JavaScript also added `Array.prototype.findLast()` which can be used to find the last matching key.

```js
const findLastKey = (obj, fn) =>
  Object.keys(obj).findLast(key => fn(obj[key], key, obj));

findLastKey(
  {
    barney: { age: 36, active: true },
    fred: { age: 40, active: false },
    pebbles: { age: 1, active: true }
  },
  x => x['active']
); // 'pebbles'
```

For older JavaScript versions, you'll have to use `Array.prototype.reverse()` to reverse the order of the keys and then use `Array.prototype.find()` to find the last matching key.

> [!WARNING]
>
> JavaScript object keys are not ordered, nor is the order guaranteed to match the insertion order. If you need to rely on the order of the keys, you should most likely be using a `Map`, instead.

---

front: How do you find the last key in an object whose value matches a condition?
back:
Use `Object.keys(obj).findLast(...)` (ES2023, in all current browsers and Node 18+). It searches from the end and returns the first match it meets.

```js

  Object.keys(obj).findLast(key => fn(obj[key], key, obj));

findLastKey(
  {
    barney: { age: 36, active: true },
    fred: { age: 40, active: false },
    pebbles: { age: 1, active: true },
  },
  x => x.active
); // 'pebbles'
```

"Last" depends on key order, which is well defined: integer-like keys (`'1'`, `'42'`) come first in ascending order, then other string keys in insertion order. So `{ b: 1, 2: 'x' }` iterates `'2'` before `'b'`. If you need exact insertion order for any key, use a `Map`.

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you safely read a nested value from an object when the path is given as an array of keys, returning `null` if any step is missing?
back:
Reduce over the keys, stepping one level deeper each time with optional chaining: `keys.reduce((cur, k) => cur?.[k] ?? null, obj)`. If a level is missing, `?.` yields `undefined` and `??` turns it into `null` instead of throwing.

```js
const deepGet = (obj, keys) =>
  keys.reduce((cur, key) => cur?.[key] ?? null, obj);

const data = { foo: { foz: [1, 2, 3], bar: { baz: ['a', 'b', 'c'] } } };

deepGet(data, ['foo', 'foz', 2]);               // 3
deepGet(data, ['foo', 'bar', 'baz', 8, 'foz']); // null
deepGet(data, 'foo.foz.2'.split('.'));          // 3 (string path)
```

If the path is fixed in your code, just write `data.foo?.foz?.[2]`; the helper is for paths that arrive as data (for example a table column config). Note that `0`, `''` and `false` are returned as-is, because `??` only replaces `null` and `undefined`.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

What are the differences between Maps and objects in JavaScript? — Key types

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: What types can be used as keys in a plain object versus a `Map`, and what happens to a number used as an object key?
back:
Plain object keys are strings or symbols; anything else, including numbers, is converted to a string. A `Map` accepts any value as a key (numbers, objects, functions) and keeps its type.

```js
const obj = {};
obj[1] = 'x';
Object.keys(obj); // ['1'] (a string)

const people = [{ id: 1, name: 'John' }, { id: 2, name: 'Jane' }];
const visits = new Map(people.map(p => [p, 0])); // objects as keys
visits.get(people[0]);           // 0
visits.get({ id: 1, name: 'John' }); // undefined
```

Object keys in a `Map` are matched by reference, not by content, so a look-alike object won't find the entry. Keying by the object itself is handy for attaching data to things you don't own (DOM nodes, records) without mutating them; use a `WeakMap` if the entries shouldn't keep those objects alive.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/map-vs-object.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```js
people.map(person => [person, `${person.name} ${person.surname}`])
```

The `Map` constructor takes `[key, value]` pairs, and the key can be any value, including an object. A plain object couldn't do this: the key would become the string `'[object Object]'`. Lookups use the same object reference, so a copy of `people[0]` won't match.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

What are the differences between Maps and objects in JavaScript? — Other differences

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Apart from the two main differences mentioned already, there are some other, less noticeable, ones. These include the following:

- Object size requires manual computation. Maps, on the other hand, have a built-in `size` property that can be used to track the number of key-value pairs.
- You can check for a given key's presence in an object using the `in` operator or `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty()`. `Map.prototype.has()` accomplishes the same thing for Maps.
- Clearing an object requires manual operation and might be non-trivial in some cases. Maps solve this problem via the use of `Map.prototype.clear()`.
- Objects inherit some keys from the prototype, whereas maps do not.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/map-vs-object.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Apart from key types and iteration, what practical differences between a `Map` and a plain object matter day to day?
back:
A `Map` has a built-in `size`, `has(key)` and `clear()`, and no inherited keys. A plain object needs `Object.keys(obj).length`, `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` and manual clearing, and it inherits keys such as `toString`. Plain objects serialize to JSON; Maps don't.

```js
'toString' in {};                 // true (inherited!)
Object.hasOwn({}, 'toString');    // false
new Map().has('toString');        // false

JSON.stringify({ a: 1 });         // '{"a":1}'
JSON.stringify(new Map([['a', 1]])); // '{}'
```

Rule of thumb: use a plain object for fixed-shape records (API data, config), and a `Map` for dynamic lookups with frequent adds and removes or non-string keys.

---

**Explain the approach**

Check if two JavaScript objects have the same properties — One-sided comparison

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
First off, let's create a function that compares two objects to determine if **the first one contains equivalent property values to the second one**. This essentially means checking if the keys of the first object are a **superset** of the keys of the second object, and if the values of the first object are equal to the values of the second object.

Comparing objects this way requires **iterating over the keys of the second object**, using `Object.keys()`, and checking if each key exists in the first object using `Array.prototype.every()`, `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty()`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/match-object-properties.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: To check whether `obj` contains all of `source`'s properties (a partial match), why do you loop over `source`'s keys rather than `obj`'s?
back:
Because the question is "does `obj` have everything in `source`?" Every key of `source` must exist in `obj` with an equal value, while extra keys on `obj` are allowed. Looping over `obj`'s keys would wrongly fail on those extras.

```js
const matches = (obj, source) =>
  Object.keys(source).every(
    key => Object.hasOwn(obj, key) && obj[key] === source[key]
  );

const user = { id: 1, role: 'admin', active: true };
matches(user, { role: 'admin' });           // true: extra keys are fine
matches({ role: 'admin' }, user);           // false: id and active are missing
```

This one-sided check is what test helpers like Jest's `toMatchObject` do. `Object.hasOwn` makes sure the key is the object's own property, not something inherited.

---

Check if two JavaScript objects have the same properties — Comparison by value

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: Using `===` to compare values, how do you write `matches(obj, source)` so it returns `true` when `obj` has every key of `source` with the same value?
back:
Check every key of `source`: it must be an own property of `obj` and the values must be strictly equal.

```js
const matches = (obj, source) =>
  Object.keys(source).every(
    key => Object.hasOwn(obj, key) && obj[key] === source[key]
  );

matches({ age: 25, hair: 'long', beard: true }, { hair: 'long', beard: true }); // true
matches({ hair: 'long', beard: true }, { age: 25, hair: 'long', beard: true }); // false
matches({ tags: ['a'] }, { tags: ['a'] });                                      // false!
```

`===` compares objects and arrays by reference, so two arrays with the same contents are not equal. For nested data, pass a custom comparison or use a deep-equality helper. `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)` is the modern, safer form of `obj.hasOwnProperty(key)`, which breaks on objects without a prototype.

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:

```js
      fn(obj[key], source[key], key, obj, source)

  { greeting: 'hello' },
  { greeting: 'hi' },
  (a, b) => isGreeting(a) && isGreeting(b)
); // true
```

**Explain the approach**

How do I compare two objects in JavaScript? — Equality comparison

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Even though two different objects can have the **same properties with equal values**, they are not considered equal when compared using either the loose or strict equality operators (`==` or `===`). This is because arrays and objects in JavaScript are **compared by reference**. This is unlike primitive values which are compared by value.

```js
const a = { name: 'John', age: 26 };
const b = { name: 'John', age: 26 };

a === b; // false
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/object-comparison.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Two separately created objects have identical properties, like `{ name: 'John', age: 26 }`. What do `a === b` and `a == b` return, and why?
back:
Both return `false`. Objects (including arrays) are compared **by reference**: `==` and `===` ask "is this the very same object in memory?", not "do these have the same contents?". Primitives like strings and numbers are compared by value.

```js
const a = { name: 'John', age: 26 };
const b = { name: 'John', age: 26 };
const c = a;

a === b; // false: two different objects
a === c; // true: same reference
```

In real code this bites when you check whether form state "changed" (`if (draft === original)`) or look up an object in an array with `includes`. To compare contents, compare the specific fields you care about or use a deep-equality helper (for example Node's `util.isDeepStrictEqual`, or a library's `isEqual`).

---

**Explain the approach**

How do I compare two objects in JavaScript? — JSON.stringify

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: Why is `JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b)` an unreliable way to check whether two objects are equal?
back:
Because different objects can serialize to the same string, and equal objects can serialize to different strings. `JSON.stringify` drops `undefined` values and functions, turns `NaN` into `null`, and keeps the order in which keys were added.

```js
const equals = (a, b) => JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b);

equals({ name: 'John' }, { name: 'John', age: undefined }); // true, but should be false
equals({ a: 1, b: 2 }, { b: 2, a: 1 });                     // false, but should be true
equals({ n: NaN }, { n: null });                            // true
```

It can be fine for a quick check on simple API data whose keys are built in the same order. For real equality checks, use a deep-equal helper (Node's `util.isDeepStrictEqual`, or a library's `isEqual`).

**Explain the approach**

Check if a JavaScript object has a given value or key — Check if an object has a given key

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Checking if an object has a given key is equally as easy, using `Object.keys()` instead of `Object.values()`. Then, you can use `Array.prototype.includes()` to check if the target key is included in the keys array.

```js
const hasKey = (obj, key) => Object.keys(obj).includes(key);

const obj = { a: 100, b: 200 };
hasKey(obj, 'a'); // true
hasKey(obj, 'c'); // false
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/object-has-value-or-key.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you check whether an object has a given key, say whether `user` has an `email` property? Name the modern built-in and say how it differs from the `in` operator.
back:
Use `Object.hasOwn(obj, key)`, which checks for an **own** property (one on the object itself, not inherited). `key in obj` also returns `true` for inherited properties.

```js
const user = { id: 1, email: undefined };

Object.hasOwn(user, 'email');        // true (the key exists even though its value is undefined)
Object.hasOwn(user, 'toString');     // false
'toString' in user;                  // true (inherited from Object.prototype)
Object.keys(user).includes('email'); // true, but builds an array first
```

Checking the value (`user.email !== undefined`) is not the same thing: a key can exist and still hold `undefined`. `Object.hasOwn` (ES2022) is the safer replacement for `obj.hasOwnProperty(key)`, which breaks on objects created with `Object.create(null)`.

front: How can you check whether any property of an object holds a given value, for example whether a `statusByUser` map contains `'banned'`?
back:
Get the values with `Object.values(obj)` and check them with `includes(value)`.

```js
const hasValue = (obj, value) => Object.values(obj).includes(value);

const statusByUser = { ada: 'active', bob: 'banned' };
hasValue(statusByUser, 'banned');  // true
hasValue(statusByUser, 'pending'); // false
```

**Explain the approach**

Is JavaScript pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: JavaScript is pass-by-value, yet a function that does `obj.count++` changes the caller's object. How do both of these facts hold, and what happens if the function reassigns `obj = {}` instead?
back:
For objects, the value that gets copied into the parameter is a **reference** (a pointer to the object). Caller and function then hold two copies of the same pointer. Mutating through either copy changes the one shared object. Reassigning the parameter only changes the function's own copy, so the caller never sees it.

```js
const cart = { count: 1 };

const addOne = obj => { obj.count++; };         // mutates the shared object
const replace = obj => { obj = { count: 99 }; }; // rebinds the local copy only

addOne(cart);
cart.count;  // 2
replace(cart);
cart.count;  // 2 (unchanged)
```

In true pass-by-reference (like C#'s `ref`), `replace` would change the caller's variable. JavaScript has no way to do that. In practice, if a function receives an object from your state (props, form data, API results), mutating it changes it everywhere. Copy it first (`{ ...obj }` or `structuredClone(obj)`) when you need changes to stay local.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/pass-by-reference-or-pass-by-value.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```js
cart.count; // 2
```

The parameter `obj` receives a copy of the reference to `cart`. `obj.count++` changes the shared object, so the count becomes 2. `obj = { count: 99 }` only points the local parameter at a new object, and the caller's `cart` still refers to the original. JavaScript passes a reference by value; it never passes the variable itself.

---

**Explain the approach**

JavaScript property enumerability

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: What does it mean for an object property to be non-enumerable, and which common operations skip such a property?
back:
A non-enumerable property still exists and can be read directly, but it is skipped by `for...in`, `Object.keys/values/entries`, `JSON.stringify`, and object spread `{ ...obj }`. You create one with `Object.defineProperty(obj, key, { enumerable: false })`.

```js
const person = { name: 'John', ssn: '123-45-6789' };
Object.defineProperty(person, 'ssn', { enumerable: false });

person.ssn;                            // '123-45-6789' (still readable)
Object.hasOwn(person, 'ssn');          // true
person.propertyIsEnumerable('ssn');    // false
Object.keys(person);                   // ['name']
JSON.stringify(person);                // '{"name":"John"}'
Object.getOwnPropertyNames(person);    // ['name', 'ssn']
({ ...person }).ssn;                   // undefined
```

Properties you create with literals or assignment are enumerable, and that includes Symbol-keyed ones. Symbol keys are skipped by `Object.keys` and `for...in` because they are Symbols, not because they are non-enumerable (spread does copy them). Built-in methods like `toString` are non-enumerable, which is why `for...in` does not list them. This hides a property from loops; it does not make it private.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/property-enumerability.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front:
Fill in the line that makes `ssn` a non-enumerable property, so it stays readable but is skipped by `Object.keys` and spread.

```js
const person = { name: 'John', ssn: '123-45-6789' };

____

person.ssn;            // '123-45-6789'
Object.keys(person);   // ['name']
({ ...person }).ssn;   // undefined
```
back:
One solution:

```js
Object.defineProperty(person, 'ssn', { enumerable: false });
```

When you redefine an existing property, `defineProperty` changes only the attributes you pass, so `ssn` keeps its value and stays writable. When it *creates* a new property, any attribute you leave out defaults to `false` (not enumerable, not writable, not configurable).

How do I remove a property from a JavaScript object? — Use object destructuring

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Using the spread syntax, (`...`), you can destructure and assign the object with specific properties omitted to a new object. This trick comes in handy especially if you want to remove a subset of properties instead of just one and has the added benefit of not mutating the original object.

```js
const pet = {
  species: 'dog',
  age: 3,
  name: 'celeste',
  gender: 'female'
};

const { gender, ...newPet } = pet;
Object.keys(pet); // ['species', 'age', 'name', 'gender]
Object.keys(newPet); // ['species', 'age', 'name']
```

**Explain the approach**

How do I remove a property from a JavaScript object? — Set the property to undefined

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: What is the difference between `obj.key = undefined` and `delete obj.key`, and when does that difference show up?
back:
Setting the property to `undefined` keeps the key; only its value becomes `undefined`. `delete` removes the key entirely. Both mutate the original object.

```js
const pet = { name: 'Celeste', gender: 'female' };

pet.gender = undefined;
Object.keys(pet);            // ['name', 'gender']
'gender' in pet;             // true
JSON.stringify(pet);         // '{"name":"Celeste"}'

delete pet.gender;
Object.keys(pet);            // ['name']
'gender' in pet;             // false
```

The difference shows up in anything that enumerates keys: `Object.keys`, `for...in`, `in`/`Object.hasOwn`, and spreading into another object (`{ ...defaults, ...pet }` overwrites a default with `undefined`). `JSON.stringify` drops `undefined` values, so both look the same in a JSON body. To remove a field without mutating, use rest destructuring: `const { gender, ...rest } = pet`.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

How can I clone an object in JavaScript? — Deep cloning using `structuredClone()`

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
<baseline-support featureId="structured-clone">
</baseline-support>

Apparently, cloning is a fairly common and important problem. So much so that JavaScript introduced the `structuredClone()` global function, which can be used to **deep clone objects**. Instead of implementing a complicated recursive function, we can simply use this function to clone the object.

```js
const a = { x: 1, y: { y1: 'a' }, z: new Set([1, 2]) };
const b = structuredClone(a); // a !== b, a.y !== b.y, a.z !== b.z
```

[Further reading](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/deep-clone-structured-clone)

This technique can be used for both **arrays and objects**, requires minimal code and is the recommended way of cloning objects in JavaScript, as it's the most **performant and reliable**.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The `structuredClone()` function is a fairly recent addition to the language. Even so, it's supported by all modern browsers and Node.js since **v17.0.0**.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/shallow-deep-clone-object.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `structuredClone(obj)` give you that `{ ...obj }` does not, and what kinds of values can it not clone?
back:
`structuredClone` makes a **deep** copy: nested objects, arrays, `Date`, `Map`, `Set` and so on are copied too, so changing the copy never touches the original. Spread copies only the top level.

```js
const order = { id: 1, items: [{ sku: 'A1' }], placed: new Date() };

const shallow = { ...order };
const deep = structuredClone(order);

shallow.items === order.items; // true  (shared)
deep.items === order.items;    // false (copied)
deep.placed instanceof Date;   // true
```

It is built into all modern browsers and Node 17+, and it handles circular references.

Limits: it **throws** on functions and DOM nodes. Class instances come back as plain objects that have lost their prototype and methods. Getters are copied as plain values. For plain API/state data (the common case) it is the right default; for class instances, write your own copy method.

---

Write a one-line `shallowClone(obj)` that returns a new object with the same top-level properties.

```js
____

copy.theme = 'light';  // settings.theme is still 'dark'
copy.tags.push('b');   // settings.tags is now ['a', 'b'] (shared)
```

```js
Object.entries(obj).map(([k, v]) => [k, deepClone(v)])
```

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

What is the difference between static and instance methods?

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Static methods belong to a class and don't act on its instances. This means that they can't be called on instances of the class. Instead, they're called on the class itself. They are often utility functions, such as functions to create or clone objects.

Instance methods belong to the class prototype, which is inherited by all instances of the class. As such, they act on class instances and can be called on them.

```jsx
const arr = [1, 2, 3];  // An Array instance

Array.isArray(arr);     // Static method of Array
arr.push(4);            // Instance method of Array
```

In the context of ES6 classes, the `static` keyword is used to define static methods for a class. Conversely, methods not defined as `static` are instance methods.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/static-instance-methods.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

```js
if (seen.has(value)) return;
```

Returning `undefined` from a replacer omits that property from the output. The first time an object is visited it is added to `seen`, and later visits (the cycle) are skipped. Note that any object referenced twice loses its second copy, even if it is not circular.

Understanding the "this" keyword in JavaScript — Function context

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: A regular `function f() { return this; }` is called on its own as `f()`, not as a method. What is `this` in sloppy mode, and what is it in strict mode?

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Understanding the "this" keyword in JavaScript — Global context

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In the global execution context, `this` refers to the global object.

```js
console.log(this === window); // true
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does top-level `this` (outside any function) refer to in a classic browser script, in an ES module, and in a Node CommonJS file?
back:
It depends on the kind of file. In a classic `<script>` it is the global object (`window`). In an ES module it is `undefined`. In a Node CommonJS file it is `module.exports` (initially `{}`).

```js
// classic browser script
this === window;          // true

// ES module (<script type="module"> or an .mjs file)
this;                     // undefined

// Node CommonJS (.cjs, or .js without "type": "module")
this === module.exports;  // true
```

Do not rely on top-level `this` to reach globals. Use `globalThis`, which refers to the global object in every environment (browser, Node, workers).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Understanding the "this" keyword in JavaScript — Arrow function context

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: Where does an arrow function get its `this` from, and why does `bar: () => this.name` misbehave as an object method?
back:
An arrow function has no `this` of its own: it uses the `this` of the scope where the arrow was **written**, and calling it as a method does not change that. As an object property, that surrounding scope is the module or script, not the object.

```js
const user = {
  name: 'Ada',
  regular() { return this.name; },        // this = user (the caller)
  arrow: () => this?.name,                // this = outer scope, not user
  later() {
    return [1].map(() => this.name);      // arrow inherits later()'s this
  },
};

user.regular(); // 'Ada'
user.arrow();   // undefined in a module (never 'Ada')
user.later();   // ['Ada']
```

Rule of thumb: use method shorthand (`regular() {}`) for object and class methods. Use arrows *inside* methods for callbacks (`map`, `setTimeout`, `then`), where keeping the outer `this` is exactly what you want.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```js
() => { this.seconds++; }
```

An arrow function has no `this` of its own. It uses the `this` of `start()`, which is `timer` because `start` was called as `timer.start()`. A regular `function () { this.seconds++ }` would get whatever `this` `setInterval` passes (`window` in browsers, a Timeout object in Node), so `timer.seconds` would never change.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Understanding the "this" keyword in JavaScript — Object context

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: When you call `user.greet()`, what is `this` inside `greet`? Does that still hold if `greet` is inherited from a prototype, or if you store it first (`const g = user.greet; g()`)?
back:
`this` is the object before the dot **at call time**. That holds even when the method is inherited from a prototype. But it is lost when the function is called without an object: `g()` gets `undefined` in strict code.

```js
const proto = { greet() { return `Hi ${this.name}`; } };
const user = Object.create(proto);   // user inherits greet
user.name = 'Ada';

user.greet();          // 'Hi Ada' (this = user, not proto)

const g = user.greet;
g();                   // TypeError in strict code (this is undefined)
```

With `new`, `this` is the object being constructed (`class C { constructor() { this.x = 10; } }`). The detached case is common in real code: passing `user.greet` as a callback (`button.onclick = user.greet`, `promise.then(user.greet)`) loses `this`. Pass `() => user.greet()` or `user.greet.bind(user)` instead.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```js
user.whoAmI(); // 'Ada'
```

`this` is set by the call site (`user.whoAmI()`), not by where the method is defined. The method is found on `proto` through the prototype chain, but `this` is `user`, and `user` has its own `name`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Understanding the "this" keyword in JavaScript — Binding `this`

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: What do `fn.call(obj, ...)`, `fn.apply(obj, [...])` and `fn.bind(obj)` each do with `this`, and how do they differ?
back:
All three set `this` to `obj`. `call` and `apply` **invoke the function immediately**: `call` takes the arguments one by one, `apply` takes them as an array. `bind` **returns a new function** whose `this` is permanently `obj`, to be called later.

```js
function greet(greeting, punct) {
  return `${greeting}, ${this.name}${punct}`;
}
const ada = { name: 'Ada' };

greet.call(ada, 'Hi', '!');      // 'Hi, Ada!'
greet.apply(ada, ['Hey', '?']);  // 'Hey, Ada?'
const yo = greet.bind(ada, 'Yo'); // can also preset leading arguments
yo('.');                          // 'Yo, Ada.'
```

Use `bind` when handing a method to something else to call later (an event listener, `setTimeout`, a callback prop). A bound function's `this` cannot be changed again, not even with `call`. `apply` is rarer today because spread does the same: `greet.call(ada, ...args)`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```js
const onTick = clock.tick.bind(clock);
```

`bind` returns a new function whose `this` is fixed to `clock`. Plain `const onTick = clock.tick` would lose `this` (class bodies are strict, so `this` would be `undefined`) and throw. `const onTick = () => clock.tick();` also works.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Understanding the "this" keyword in JavaScript — What is `this`?

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In JavaScript, the `this` keyword refers to the object that is currently executing the code. The short version of what `this` evaluates to is as follows:

- By default, `this` refers to the global object.
- In a function, when not in strict mode, `this` refers to the global object.
- In a function, when in strict mode, `this` is `undefined`.
- In an arrow function, `this` retains the value of the enclosing lexical context's `this`.
- In an object method, `this` refers to the object the method was called on.
- In a constructor call, `this` is bound to the new object being constructed.
- In an event handler, `this` is bound to the element on which the listener is placed.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What decides the value of `this` inside a JavaScript function? List the main cases.
back:
For regular functions, `this` is decided by **how the function is called**, not where it is defined. Arrow functions are the exception: they take `this` from the surrounding code.

- `obj.method()`: `this` is `obj` (the object before the dot).
- `new Fn()` / `new Class()`: the newly created object.
- `fn.call(x)`, `fn.apply(x)`, `fn.bind(x)`: `x`, set explicitly.
- Plain call `fn()`: `undefined` in strict code (modules, classes), the global object in sloppy scripts.
- DOM listener written as a `function`: the element the listener is attached to.
- Arrow function: whatever `this` was where the arrow was written. `call`/`bind` cannot change it.

```js
const user = { name: 'Ada', hi() { return this?.name; } };
user.hi();          // 'Ada'
const hi = user.hi;
hi();               // undefined (plain call in strict code)
hi.call({ name: 'Bo' }); // 'Bo'
```

Most `this` bugs are a method passed around as a callback and then called plainly.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/this.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

**Explain the approach**

Understanding the "this" keyword in JavaScript — Event handler context

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: Inside a click listener added with `el.addEventListener('click', handler)`, what is `this` when `handler` is a regular `function`, what is it when `handler` is an arrow function, and what is the safer way to get the element?

back:
One solution:

```js
const el = event.currentTarget;
```

`event.currentTarget` is always the element whose listener is running, whatever style the function is written in. `event.target` is the innermost element actually clicked (for example an icon inside the button), which may not be the button.

**Explain the approach**

Transform the keys of a JavaScript object — Transform object keys using a function

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How can a generic `transform(obj, fn, acc)` helper fold over an object's keys, for example to invert `{ a: 1, b: 2, c: 1 }` into `{ 1: ['a', 'c'], 2: ['b'] }`?

back:
One solution:

```js
Object.keys(obj).reduce((a, k) => fn(a, obj[k], k, obj), acc);
```

`reduce` threads the accumulator through every key. Here the callback groups keys by their value, and `??=` creates the array the first time a value is seen.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Transform the keys of a JavaScript object — Symbolize object keys

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: If you convert an object's keys to Symbols (`{ [Symbol('id')]: 10 }`), how do those keys behave with `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify` and property lookup?
back:
Symbol keys are unique and hidden from ordinary string-key tools. `Object.keys`, `for...in` and `JSON.stringify` skip them, and you can only read one back with the exact same Symbol value. `Symbol('id')` creates a new Symbol every time.

```js
const symbolizeKeys = obj =>
  Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(obj).map(([k, v]) => [Symbol(k), v]));

const s = symbolizeKeys({ id: 10, name: 'apple' });
// { [Symbol(id)]: 10, [Symbol(name)]: 'apple' }
Object.keys(s);                          // []
JSON.stringify(s);                       // '{}'
s[Symbol('id')];                         // undefined (a different Symbol)
Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(s).length;  // 2
```

Symbols are useful for keys that must never collide with user data, such as library metadata attached to an object. Converting a whole data object this way is rarely useful in CRUD code: the data can no longer be serialized or looked up by name.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/transform-object-keys.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```js
(acc, key) => ({ ...acc, [Symbol(key)]: obj[key] }),
```

The computed key `[Symbol(key)]` creates a brand-new Symbol for each key. The result is invisible to `Object.keys` and `JSON.stringify`, and a value can only be read with the same Symbol instance, which you can get back with `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/transform-object-keys.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Transform the keys of a JavaScript object — Map object keys

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you rename every key of an object with a function, for example turning an API row `{ first_name: 'Ada' }` into `{ firstName: 'Ada' }`?

back:
One solution:

```js
Object.entries(obj).map(([k, v]) => [fn(v, k, obj), v])
```

`Object.entries` gives `[key, value]` pairs, `map` swaps in the new key, and `Object.fromEntries` builds the object. The original `Object.keys(obj).reduce(...)` version does the same thing. If two keys map to the same new key, the last one wins.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Unwind a JavaScript object

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you "unwind" an object with an array field, e.g. `{ orderId: 1, items: ['pen', 'ink'] }`, into one object per array element: `[{ orderId: 1, items: 'pen' }, { orderId: 1, items: 'ink' }]`?

back:
One solution:

```js
return obj[key].map(val => ({ ...rest, [key]: val }));
```

`rest` holds every field except the array one. Each element becomes its own object with those shared fields spread in and the computed key `[key]` set to that element.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Uppercase or lowercase object keys in JavaScript — Lowercase object keys

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you make a copy of an object with every key lowercased, for example to normalize HTTP header names like `'Content-Type'` before looking them up?

back:
One solution:

```js
Object.entries(obj).map(([k, v]) => [k.toLowerCase(), v])
```

Build new `[key, value]` pairs and let `Object.fromEntries` assemble the object. The `reduce` version (`acc[k.toLowerCase()] = obj[k]`) is equivalent. Keys that differ only by case collide, and the last one wins.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Uppercase or lowercase object keys in JavaScript — Uppercase object keys

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: Write a helper that uppercases every key of an object. What happens if the input has two keys that differ only in case, such as `id` and `ID`?

back:
One solution:

```js
acc[k.toUpperCase()] = obj[k];
```

Each step writes one property onto the accumulator object and returns it for the next key. If two input keys uppercase to the same string (`id` and `ID`), the later one silently overwrites the earlier.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

What does 'use strict' do and what are some of the key benefits to using it? — No `this` boxing

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: In strict mode `this` is not "boxed". What does that mean for `f()` and for `f.call(5)`, compared with sloppy mode?
back:
Strict mode passes `this` through exactly as given. `f()` gets `undefined` and `f.call(5)` gets the primitive `5`. Sloppy mode "boxes" it: `undefined`/`null` become the global object, and primitives are wrapped in objects (`new Number(5)`).

```js
function sloppy() { return this; }
sloppy() === globalThis;   // true
typeof sloppy.call(5);     // 'object' (a Number wrapper)

function strict() { 'use strict'; return this; }
strict();                  // undefined
strict.call(5);            // 5
```

The practical win: a method called without its object (`const f = obj.method; f()`) fails fast with a `TypeError`, instead of silently reading or writing properties on the global object. Modules and classes are strict by default, so this is how modern code behaves.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/use-strict.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

What does 'use strict' do and what are some of the key benefits to using it? — Simplified `eval`

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Strict mode makes `eval` more transparent by preventing the introduction of new variables in the surrounding scope. In strict mode, `eval` creates variables only for the code being evaluated.

```js
'use strict';
let x = 1;
eval('let x = 3; console.log(x);'); // LOGS: 3
console.log(x); // LOGS: 1
```

---

**Explain the approach**

What does 'use strict' do and what are some of the key benefits to using it? — Simplified `arguments`

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: In a sloppy-mode function, assigning to a parameter (`x = 5`) also changes `arguments[0]`. What does strict mode change about `arguments`?
back:
In strict mode, `arguments` is not linked to the named parameters. It keeps the values the function was called with, however you reassign the parameters. Accessing `arguments.callee` also throws a `TypeError`.

```js
function sloppy(x) { x = 5; return arguments[0]; }
sloppy(10); // 5 (linked)

function strict(x) { 'use strict'; x = 5; return arguments[0]; }
strict(10); // 10 (not linked)
```

In modern code you rarely need `arguments` at all. Use rest parameters (`(...args) => ...`), which give a real array and also work in arrow functions (arrows have no `arguments` of their own).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/use-strict.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```js
f(10); // 10
```

In strict mode, `arguments` is a snapshot of the call's arguments and is not linked to the named parameters, so reassigning `x` does not change `arguments[0]`. In sloppy mode the two are linked and it would return `5`.

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

What does 'use strict' do and what are some of the key benefits to using it? — Other changes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Strict mode implements a few more, less commonly-mentioned changes. These include:

- `with` is prohibited, resulting in an error if used
- `Function.prototype.arguments` and `Function.prototype.caller` are non-deletable properties which throw when set or retrieved
- `implements`, `interface`, `let`, `package`, `private`, `protected`, `public`, `static`, and `yield` are reserved keywords
- Function statements are only allowed at the top level of a script of function

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/use-strict.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Which silent mistakes does strict mode turn into errors (for example, assigning to an undeclared variable), and which code is strict automatically?
back:
Strict mode throws where sloppy mode would silently misbehave. Code in ES modules and `class` bodies is strict automatically; elsewhere you opt in with `'use strict'`.

- Assigning to an undeclared variable (`totl = 5`) throws `ReferenceError` instead of creating a global.
- Writing to a read-only property (a frozen object, or a string's `length`) or deleting an undeletable one throws `TypeError` instead of doing nothing.
- `with`, duplicate parameter names (`function f(a, a)`) and legacy octal literals (`010`) are syntax errors.
- Words like `let`, `static`, `yield`, `implements`, `interface`, `private` and `public` are reserved.
- Reading `arguments.callee` or a strict function's `caller`/`arguments` throws.

```js
'use strict';
const cfg = Object.freeze({ debug: false });
cfg.debug = true; // TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property
```

Function declarations inside blocks (`if (x) { function f() {} }`) *are* allowed in strict mode; they are block-scoped.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/use-strict.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

Complete `keysAreValid(obj, allowed)` so that it returns `true` only if every key of `obj` appears in the `allowed` array (extra allowed keys are fine).

```js
const keysAreValid = (obj, allowed) =>

keysAreValid({ name: 'Pen', price: 2 }, ['name', 'price', 'stock']);       // true
```

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

6 JavaScript Regular Expression features you can use today — Non-capturing groups

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: In a JavaScript regex, how do you group alternatives like `JavaScript|Python` without capturing them, and why would you want to?
back:
Use a non-capturing group, `(?:...)`. It groups the alternatives (or a quantified part) like normal parentheses, but adds nothing to the match array, so your capture numbers only count the parts you actually want to read.

```js
const str = 'JavaScript is a programming language';

const m = /(?:JavaScript|Python) is a (.+)/.exec(str);
m[1];     // 'programming language'
m.length; // 2 (full match + one capture)

// With plain ( ) the language is captured too, and the description moves to m[2]
/(JavaScript|Python) is a (.+)/.exec(str).length; // 3
```

Why it matters: adding plain parentheses just for grouping silently shifts every later `m[n]` and `\n` backreference. Use `(?:...)` whenever you don't need the value.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/6-regexp-tricks.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

**Explain the approach**

6 JavaScript Regular Expression features you can use today — Capturing group backreferences

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How can a JavaScript regex require the *same text* that an earlier group matched, e.g. to find a word typed twice (`'the the'`) or a matching pair of quotes?
back:
Use a backreference: `\1`, `\2`, … repeat the exact text captured by that numbered group, and `\k<name>` repeats a named group. It matches the captured *text*, not the pattern again.

```js
const text = 'Please review the the pull request';
text.match(/\b(\w+) \1\b/)[0]; // 'the the'

// Opening quote must match the closing one
`She said "hi" and 'bye'`.match(/(['"]).*?\1/g); // ['"hi"', "'bye'"]

// Same with a named group
/(?<q>['"]).*?\k<q>/.test('"x"'); // true
```

Pitfall: `\1` inside the pattern is a backreference, but in a `replace()` replacement string you write `$1` (or `$<name>`) instead.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/6-regexp-tricks.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).
