How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you read a text file synchronously in Node.js into an array of lines, and when is the synchronous version acceptable?

back:
One solution:

```js
readFileSync(path, 'utf8').trimEnd().split(/\r?\n/);
```

The `'utf8'` encoding makes `readFileSync` return a string instead of a `Buffer`. Most text files end with a newline, so a plain `split('\n')` returns an extra `''` at the end; `trimEnd()` removes it. The regex `/\r?\n/` splits on both `\n` and `\r\n`.

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you read a text file into an array of lines in Node.js without blocking the event loop?

back:
One solution:

```js
const lines = await readFileLines('todo.txt');
```

An `async` function always returns a Promise. `await` pauses until it settles and gives you the resolved value. Without `await`, `lines` would be a Promise and `lines.length` would be `undefined`. Top-level `await` works in ES modules; elsewhere use `readFileLines('todo.txt').then(lines => ...)`.

front: What does Node's `fs.readFile()` give you when you don't pass an encoding, and how do you get a string instead?
back:
It gives you a `Buffer`, which holds the raw bytes. Pass an encoding such as `'utf8'` to get a string, or call `buffer.toString('utf8')` afterwards.

```js
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

readFileSync('notes.txt');          // <Buffer 6c 69 6e 65 31 0a ...>
readFileSync('notes.txt', 'utf8');  // 'line1\nline2\n'

await readFile('notes.txt');         // <Buffer ...>
await readFile('notes.txt', 'utf8'); // 'line1\nline2\n'
```

Node has three styles: `readFileSync` (blocks and returns the data), `readFile` from `node:fs` (takes a callback), and `readFile` from `node:fs/promises` (returns a Promise). Prefer the promise version with `await` in server code. Keep the Buffer (no encoding) for binary files such as images.

---

```js
console.log(buf);   // <Buffer 6c 69 6e 65 31 0a ...>

____
console.log(text);  // 'line1\nline2\n'
```


Passing an encoding makes `readFile` decode the bytes for you. Converting the Buffer you already have also works: `const text = buf.toString('utf8');`. Without an encoding you get raw bytes, which is what you want for images or other binary files.

```js
delete require.cache[require.resolve(modulePath)];
```

front: How do you write a `rearg(fn, indexes)` helper that calls `fn` with its arguments reordered, and what is usually a better fix for a confusing argument order?
back:
Return a function that builds a new argument list by picking `args[i]` for each index in `indexes`, then spreads it into `fn`.

```js
const rearg = (fn, indexes) => (...args) =>
  fn(...indexes.map(i => args[i]));

const rearged = rearg((a, b, c) => [a, b, c], [2, 0, 1]);
rearged('b', 'c', 'a'); // ['a', 'b', 'c']
```

`indexes[0]` says which incoming argument becomes the first parameter, and so on. In application code, a function with many positional arguments is usually better redesigned to take one options object, such as `createUser({ name, email, role })`, so the order stops mattering.

**Explain the approach**

Change the order of arguments in a JavaScript function — Flip function arguments

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
A very common need is to **make the first argument the last**. This is particularly useful when [currying a function](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/currying) or when you need to [partially apply a function](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/partially-apply-function).

You can easily achieve this by using a [**higher-order function**](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/higher-order-functions) that takes a function as an argument and returns a new function that flips the arguments before calling the original function. In order to do so, you can use **argument destructuring** and a **closure** with variadic arguments.

```js
const flip = fn => (first, ...rest) => fn(...rest, first);

const parseInteger = flip(Number.parseInt);
parseInteger(8, '10'); // 8 (10 in base 8)

const parseIntegerBase16 = parseInteger.bind(null, 16);
parseIntegerBase16('10'); // 16 (10 in base 16)
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> `Number.parseInt()` is a very clear example of how JavaScript's APIs might be ill-optimized for **currying and functional programming**. It takes the base as the second argument, which is not very convenient when partially applying the function. Flipping the arguments makes it easier to use in a curried context.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/reorder-function-arguments.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you write a `flip(fn)` helper that moves a function's first argument to the end, and why is that useful with `Number.parseInt`?
back:
Take the first argument separately and pass it last: `(first, ...rest) => fn(...rest, first)`. It lets you preset an argument that the original function expects at the end.

```js
const flip = fn => (first, ...rest) => fn(...rest, first);

const parseInteger = flip(Number.parseInt);
parseInteger(8, '10');  // 8   (parseInt('10', 8))

const parseHex = parseInteger.bind(null, 16);
parseHex('ff');         // 255
```

`parseInt(string, radix)` takes the radix (the number base) second, so you can't preset it with `bind`, which only fixes leading arguments. After `flip`, the radix comes first and `bind(null, 16)` creates a reusable hex parser.

---

Create a JavaScript promise that resolves after a given amount of time

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you create a promise that resolves with a given value after a delay of N milliseconds?

back:
One solution:

```js
setTimeout(() => resolve(value), delay);
```

The Promise executor runs immediately and schedules a timer. When the timer fires, `resolve(value)` settles the promise, and any `.then` or `await` waiting on it continues. Writing `setTimeout(resolve(value), delay)` would be a bug: it calls `resolve` right away.

```js
ps.reduce((p, next) => p.then(next), Promise.resolve());
```

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Introduction to Semantic Versioning (SemVer) — Releases and pre-releases

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The **first version** of a software package is typically denoted as `1.0.0`. This is because the initial release of a software package is considered to be a major version, and the first version of a major version is always `1.0.0`. Versions starting with `0.x.x` are considered to be pre-release versions and are not intended for production use.

Additionally, SemVer allows for **pre-release versions** to be appended to the version number. These are denoted by a hyphen followed by a series of alphanumeric identifiers, such as `1.0.0-alpha.1` or `1.0.0-beta.2`. Pre-release versions are typically used to indicate that the software is still under active development and may not be ready for production use.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/semantic-versioning.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: In semantic versioning (SemVer), what do `0.x.y` versions and pre-release tags such as `1.0.0-beta.2` mean?
back:
A `0.x.y` version means the package is in initial development: its public API is not yet considered stable, and anything may change between releases. A tag after a hyphen, such as `-alpha.1` or `-beta.2`, marks a pre-release: a test build of an upcoming version that is not yet final.

```text
0.4.2          initial development, API may still change
1.0.0          first stable public API
1.0.0-beta.2   pre-release of 1.0.0; sorts before 1.0.0
2.0.0-rc.1     release candidate for 2.0.0
```

Pre-releases sort before the final version (`1.0.0-beta.2 < 1.0.0`). npm ranges ignore them unless you ask explicitly: `^1.0.0` will not install `1.1.0-beta.1`. Many packages start at `0.1.0` rather than `1.0.0`. Release `1.0.0` when others depend on your API.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/semantic-versioning.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Introduction to Semantic Versioning (SemVer) — Specifying which version to use

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
When installing a package, you can specify which version to use by appending the version number to the package name, as follows:

```shell
npm install my-package@1.0.0
```

If you don't specify a version, npm will install the **latest version** of the package. You can also use the `^` or `~` symbols to specify a range of versions. For example, `^1.0.0` will install the latest version of the package that is compatible with `1.0.0`. Similarly, `~1.0.0` will install the latest version of the package that is compatible with `1.0.0` and has the same major version. Here's a quick summary of the different ways to specify a version:

- Exact version: `1.0.4`
- Patch releases: `1.0` or `1.0.x` or `~1.0.4`
- Minor releases: `1` or `1.x` or `^1.0.4`

Note that you can also change the version of each dependency by editing the `package.json` file directly. Just remember to run `npm install` after making any changes to the `package.json` file.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/semantic-versioning.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: In `package.json`, which versions do the ranges `^1.2.3` and `~1.2.3` allow, and what does `npm install pkg@1.2.3` do?
back:
`^1.2.3` allows any compatible version with the same major number (`>=1.2.3 <2.0.0`), so minor and patch updates are allowed. `~1.2.3` allows only patch updates (`>=1.2.3 <1.3.0`). `npm install pkg@1.2.3` installs exactly that version.

```shell
npm install express         # installs the latest version, saves "^x.y.z"
npm install express@4.21.2  # installs 4.21.2 (saved as "^4.21.2" by default)
npm install --save-exact express@4.21.2   # saves "4.21.2" exactly
```

| Range | Allows |
| ----- | ------ |
| `1.2.3` | exactly 1.2.3 |
| `~1.2.3` | `>=1.2.3 <1.3.0` (patches only) |
| `1.2.x` | `>=1.2.0 <1.3.0` |
| `^1.2.3` | `>=1.2.3 <2.0.0` |
| `1.x` | `>=1.0.0 <2.0.0` |
| `^0.2.3` | only `<0.3.0` (for 0.x, caret is stricter) |

The range only decides what a fresh resolve may pick. `package-lock.json` pins the exact versions actually installed, and `npm ci` installs exactly those.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Using Test-Driven Development to refactor a JavaScript project — Refactoring goals

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The main goals of this refactoring are threefold: reduce **complexity**, make the code **less error-prone**, and make the code **more maintainable**. As a health metric, we'll be aiming to keep **readability** at about the same level. We'll also be leaning quite heavily on the test suite to ensure that we don't break anything.

As I was originally looking to reduce the bundle size, I went with an approach akin to <dnf title="Code golf is a type of recreational computer programming competition in which participants strive to achieve the shortest possible source code that solves a certain problem.">code golf</dnf>, but not quite. I first took a long hard look at what may be redundant or could be simplified, and then I tried to simplify and shorten pieces of logic that seemed like they were doing too much.

_Why code golf?_ Because it's a really fun thing to do. It's been quite a long time since I last did it, and I felt like making something this small even tinier was a fun place to dust off those skills.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/tdd-codebase-refactoring.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Before refactoring working code that has a test suite, what goals should you set, and what job do the tests do during the refactor?
back:
Aim to reduce complexity, make the code less error-prone and easier to maintain, while keeping behavior identical and readability at least as good. The tests are the safety net: they pin down current behavior, so you run them after every small change and any failure means that step changed what the code does.

```shell
npx vitest --watch   # keep tests re-running on every save while you refactor
```

Refactoring means changing structure, not behavior. Don't change a test to make it pass mid-refactor unless you meant to change behavior. Shorter code is not a goal in itself: squeezing code into as few characters as possible ("code golf") is fun, but it often hurts readability.

back:
One solution:

```js
export const namedGroup = name => wrapSegments(`(?<${name}>`, ')');
```

Unlike the other two groups, the prefix depends on a value (the group name), so `namedGroup` is a function that builds the prefix and then calls `wrapSegments`. That's why it is called twice: `namedGroup('year')` returns a builder, and the builder takes the expressions. `(?<year>...)` is a named capture group, which you read back as `match.groups.year`.

back:
One solution:

```js
return new RegExp(sanitize(expression));
```

In a regex, characters like `$`, `.` and `(` have special meanings, so `new RegExp('$9.99')` does not match the text `'$9.99'`. Escaping them first makes the string match literally. front: After a refactor, how do you judge whether it was worth it?
back:
It was worth it if the tests still pass unchanged (behavior is the same), the code is smaller or has fewer concepts to understand, and a teammate can read it at least as easily as before. Measurable wins, such as a smaller bundle or faster build, are a bonus.

```text
Tests:        all green, none edited      -> behavior kept
Code:         fewer helpers, one pattern  -> less to learn
Readability:  about the same              -> acceptable
Bundle:       6.04 kB -> 4.08 kB          -> bonus
```

If the new code is shorter but harder to follow, it usually wasn't worth it. Code is read far more often than it is written.

front: How can adding an optional `mapFn` parameter to a generic helper like `toSegments` let you delete a special-case function?
back:
If the special case differs from the generic helper only by transforming each input first, add that transformation as a parameter with an identity default (`x => x`). Normal callers don't notice, and the special case becomes one more preset call.

```js
export const toSegments =
  (prefix = '', suffix = '', separator = '', mapFn = x => x) =>
  (...expressions) =>
    new RegExp(`${prefix}${expressions
      .map(e => toSegment(mapFn(e)).source)
      .join(separator)}${suffix}`);

const toCharacterSet = expression =>
  Array.isArray(expression) && expression.length === 2
    ? toSegments('', '', '-')(...expression)   // ['a', 'z'] -> a-z
    : toSegments()(expression);

export const anythingFrom = toSegments('[', ']', '', toCharacterSet);
anythingFrom(['a', 'z'], '_'); // /[a-z_]/
```

Pitfall: inside `[...]`, `|` is not "or", it is a literal pipe character. The original used `'|'` as the separator here, which made `[a-z|_]` also match `|`.

previous.back:
Like I said, I started by taking a long hard look at the code. Where could one spot complexity that wasn't really necessary? What patterns could be extracted into abstractions?

> [!NOTE]

front: How do you find what to refactor in code that already works and has tests?
back:
Read it looking for two things: complexity that isn't needed, and repeated patterns that could become one abstraction. Then change one thing at a time and run the tests after each step.

```text
Unneeded complexity         -> helpers that only forward arguments (inline them)
                            -> classes that only wrap a built-in (use the built-in)
Repeated patterns           -> functions with the same body but different values
                               (extract a higher-order function)
Wasted work                 -> two .map() calls in a row (merge into one)
```

Small steps keep each change easy to review and easy to undo. If a test fails, you know exactly which step caused it. Commit after each green step.

One solution:

```js
const remaining = wait - (Date.now() - lastTime);
```

`Date.now() - lastTime` is the time since `fn` last ran. If a full `wait` has passed, `remaining` is zero or negative and `fn` runs now. Otherwise one trailing call is scheduled for exactly when the window ends, and `clearTimeout` makes sure only the latest call's arguments are used.

How can I check if a value implements a stream in Node.js? — Check if value is a stream

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In the most general case, we can check if a value is a stream by checking if it is an **object** and has a `pipe` property that is a function.

```js
import { createReadStream } from 'fs';

const isStream = val =>
  val !== null && typeof val === 'object' && typeof val.pipe === 'function';

isStream(createReadStream('test.txt')); // true
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/typecheck-nodejs-streams.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How can you check whether a value is a Node.js stream, and what are the limits of that check?
back:
Check that it is a non-null object with a `pipe` method. This is duck typing: judging a value by the methods it has rather than by its class.

```js
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs';

const isStream = val =>
  val !== null && typeof val === 'object' && typeof val.pipe === 'function';

isStream(createReadStream('todo.txt')); // true
isStream({ pipe() {} });                // true, a false positive
isStream(new ReadableStream());         // false (web streams use pipeTo)
```

Limits: any object with a `pipe` method passes. Web streams, such as a `fetch()` response body, are a different API and fail the check. For a stricter check of Node streams, use `val instanceof Stream`, with `Stream` imported from `node:stream`.

---

**Explain the approach**

Check if two numbers are approximately equal in JavaScript

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
We've all seen the classic **floating point arithmetic** problem in JavaScript, usually demonstrated as `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` returning `false`. This is due to the **limited precision** of floating point numbers, and is a common problem in many programming languages.

In many cases, not limited to precision issues, you might want to check if two numbers are approximately equal to each other. Generally speaking, the straightforward way to do this is to use `Math.abs()` to compare the **absolute difference** of the two numbers to a certain `epsilon` value.

```js
const approximatelyEqual = (v1, v2, epsilon = 0.001) =>
  Math.abs(v1 - v2) < epsilon;

approximatelyEqual(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3); // true
approximatelyEqual(Math.PI / 2.0, 1.5708); // true
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/approximately-equal.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Why is `0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3` false in JavaScript, and how should you compare two decimal results instead?
back:
Numbers are stored as binary floating point, which cannot represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly. Their sum comes out as `0.30000000000000004`. Instead of `===`, check whether the difference is smaller than a tolerance (an *epsilon*) that fits your data.

```js
0.1 + 0.2;          // 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3;  // false

const approximatelyEqual = (v1, v2, epsilon = 0.001) =>
  Math.abs(v1 - v2) < epsilon;

approximatelyEqual(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3);        // true
approximatelyEqual(Math.PI / 2, 1.5708);   // true
```

Choose the epsilon for the scale of your values. `Number.EPSILON` (about 2.2e-16) is only a sensible tolerance for numbers around 1; for large values it is far too strict. For money, avoid the problem altogether: store integer cents (`1999`, not `19.99`) and divide only when displaying.

**Explain the approach**

Clamp or map a number to a range in JavaScript — Map a number to a range

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Mapping a number to a range is a simple **linear transformation**. Provided the original and the target range, you can map between the limits of the two ranges.

```js
const mapNumRange = (num, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax) =>
  ((num - inMin) * (outMax - outMin)) / (inMax - inMin) + outMin;

mapNumRange(5, 0, 10, 0, 100); // 50
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/clamp-or-map-number-to-range.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you linearly map a value from one range to another, for example a score of 0–10 to a progress-bar width of 0–100%?
back:
Find how far the value is through the input range (a fraction from 0 to 1), then scale that fraction to the output range and add the output minimum.

```js
const mapNumRange = (num, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax) =>
  ((num - inMin) * (outMax - outMin)) / (inMax - inMin) + outMin;

mapNumRange(5, 0, 10, 0, 100);     // 50
mapNumRange(75, 0, 100, 0, 1);     // 0.75
mapNumRange(512, 0, 1024, 0, 360); // 180
```

`(num - inMin) / (inMax - inMin)` is the fraction; multiplying by `(outMax - outMin)` stretches it to the new range. This is called linear interpolation.

Pitfall: it does not clamp. `mapNumRange(15, 0, 10, 0, 100)` returns `150`, so clamp the input or the result when a value can fall outside the range.

---

**Explain the approach**

Clamp or map a number to a range in JavaScript — Clamp a number

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In order to clamp a number, you can use `Math.max()` and `Math.min()` to find the **closest value** within the specified range.

```js
const clampNumber = (num, a, b) =>
  Math.max(Math.min(num, Math.max(a, b)), Math.min(a, b));

clampNumber(2, 3, 5); // 3
clampNumber(1, -1, -5); // -1
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/clamp-or-map-number-to-range.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you clamp a number into a range, for example forcing a quantity input to stay between 1 and 99, using `Math.min` and `Math.max`?
back:
Cap it from above with `Math.min(num, max)`, then from below with `Math.max(..., min)`: `Math.max(min, Math.min(num, max))`.

```js
const clamp = (num, min, max) => Math.max(min, Math.min(num, max));

clamp(150, 1, 99); // 99
clamp(-3, 1, 99);  // 1
clamp(42, 1, 99);  // 42

// Version that accepts the bounds in either order:
const clampNumber = (num, a, b) =>
  Math.max(Math.min(num, Math.max(a, b)), Math.min(a, b));
clampNumber(1, -1, -5); // -1
```

Pitfall: `NaN` passes straight through (`clamp(NaN, 1, 99)` is `NaN`), and an empty form field converted with `Number('')` becomes `0`. Validate the input as a finite number before clamping it.

---

**Explain the approach**

Clamp or map a number to a range in JavaScript — Convert a number to a safe integer

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
A special case of clamping a number is converting it to a **safe integer**. You can use the `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` and `Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER` constants to find the closest safe value. Additionally, use `Math.round()` to convert to an integer.

```js
const toSafeInteger = num =>
  Math.round(
    Math.max(Math.min(num, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER), Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER)
  );

toSafeInteger('3.2'); // 3
toSafeInteger(Infinity); // 9007199254740991
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/clamp-or-map-number-to-range.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What is a "safe integer" in JavaScript, and how would you clamp any value into the safe-integer range and round it?
back:
A safe integer is one that a JavaScript number can represent exactly, and whose neighbours it can also tell apart. The range is -(2^53 - 1) to 2^53 - 1, available as `Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER` and `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. To convert a value, clamp it between those constants and round it.

```js
const toSafeInteger = num =>
  Math.round(
    Math.max(Math.min(num, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER), Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER)
  );

toSafeInteger('3.2');     // 3 (Math.min converts the string)
toSafeInteger(Infinity);  // 9007199254740991
toSafeInteger('abc');     // NaN

Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2;          // 9007199254740992 (off by one!)
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53);        // false
```

Real-world pitfall: 64-bit database IDs (such as a PostgreSQL `bigint` or a Twitter/X ID) can exceed this range. Parsed as numbers, they silently change. Keep them as strings, or use `BigInt`.

---

The **modulo operator** (`%`) returns the **remainder of a division operation**. Given that, we can check if a number is even or odd by dividing it by `2` and checking the remainder. If the remainder is `0`, the number is even, otherwise it's odd.

```js
const isEven = num => num % 2 === 0;
const isOdd = num => num % 2 === 1;

isEven(3); // false
isOdd(3); // true
```

front: Why is `num % 2 === 1` a buggy odd-number check, and how should you write `isEven` and `isOdd`?
back:
In JavaScript, the result of `%` takes the sign of the left operand, so `-3 % 2` is `-1`, not `1`. The check therefore calls every negative odd number "not odd". Compare with `0` instead: `num % 2 === 0` for even, `num % 2 !== 0` for odd.

```js
const isEven = num => num % 2 === 0;
const isOdd = num => num % 2 !== 0;

isEven(4);   // true
isOdd(3);    // true
isOdd(-3);   // true
-3 % 2;      // -1 (why `=== 1` fails)
```

`%` is a remainder operator, not a mathematical modulo. Decimals also slip through: `isOdd(2.5)` is `true` because `2.5 % 2` is `0.5`. If the input might not be an integer, check `Number.isInteger(num)` first.

front: `num & 1` can also tell whether a number is odd. Why is `num % 2` still usually the better choice?
back:
`%` works on any number and reads clearly. Bitwise operators first convert the value to a 32-bit integer, cutting off decimals and high bits, so `& 1` can give confident but wrong answers for non-integers.

```js
7 & 1;     // 1 (odd)
-3 & 1;    // 1 (odd; bitwise handles negatives)
2.5 & 1;   // 0 ("even": the .5 was silently dropped)
2.5 % 2;   // 0.5 (not even, but `!== 0` would call it odd)
```

Bitwise tricks save nothing measurable in everyday code and make readers stop and think. Write `num % 2 === 0` for "even", and check `Number.isInteger` first if decimals are possible.

Validate a number in JavaScript

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: A form field gives you a string such as `'42'`, `' 3.5 '`, `''` or `'10px'`. How do you check that it is a valid, finite number?
back:
Reject blank strings, convert with `Number()` (not `parseFloat`), and check the result with `Number.isFinite`.

```js
const isNumeric = str => str.trim() !== '' && Number.isFinite(Number(str));

isNumeric('42');       // true
isNumeric(' 3.5 ');    // true (surrounding spaces are ignored)
isNumeric('');         // false (Number('') would be 0!)
isNumeric('10px');     // false (parseFloat('10px') would be 10)
isNumeric('Infinity'); // false
isNumeric('1e3');      // true (scientific notation is valid)
```

Each piece closes a trap. `parseFloat` stops at the first invalid character, so it accepts `'10px'`. `Number('')` and `Number('  ')` are `0`, which is why blanks are rejected first. `Number.isFinite` rejects `NaN` and `Infinity`, and unlike the global `isFinite` it does not convert its argument. For `<input type="number">`, you can read `input.valueAsNumber`, which is `NaN` when the field is empty or invalid.

---

One solution:


Number validation is probably one of the hardest things to do even for intermediate developers. However, it's a necessary evil, especially when working with **user input**. It's even more so in JavaScript, due to the language's quirks and the fact that it's loosely typed.

While, a simple check that `parseFloat()` produces a sensible **numeric value** might seem enough, it's a little more involved than that. You also need to check for `NaN`, using `Number.isNaN()`, and for `Infinity`, using `Number.isFinite()`.

And, as if that wasn't already enough, you also need to check if the **coercion** of the value to a number is correct, using `Number()` and the loose equality operator (`==`). Putting everything together, you get a pretty robust number validation function.

```js
const validateNumber = n => {
  const num = parseFloat(n);
  return !Number.isNaN(num) && Number.isFinite(num) && Number(n) == n;
}

validateNumber('10'); // true
validateNumber('a'); // false
```

JavaScript's numeric separators explained

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: What does `1_000_000` mean in JavaScript source code, and where do numeric separators *not* work?
back:
It is the number one million. The underscores are **numeric separators**: purely visual digit grouping in number literals (ES2021), ignored by the engine.

```js
const msPerYear = 31_536_000_000;   // clearly ~31.5 billion
const priceInCents = 42_00;         // 4200, grouped to hint "42.00"
const mask = 0b1111_0000;           // works in binary/hex too

Number('1_000');    // NaN
parseInt('1_000');  // 1
```

Separators only work in literals written in code. Strings, including form input and JSON, are not parsed with them, so `Number('1_000')` is `NaN`. Syntax rules: no separator at the start or end, none next to the decimal point, never two in a row (`1__000`), and none after a leading `0`.


The underscores are ignored by the engine, so the value is identical. They only work in number literals written in code, not in strings: `Number('31_536_000_000')` is `NaN`.

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Logical operators

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: Do `&&` and `||` always return `true` or `false`? Predict `'' || 'Guest'` and `user && user.name`.
back:
No. They return one of their **operands**. `a || b` returns `a` if it is truthy, otherwise `b`. `a && b` returns `a` if it is falsy, otherwise `b`. `!` is the only one that always returns a boolean.

```js
'' || 'Guest';           // 'Guest'
'Ada' || 'Guest';        // 'Ada'
null && null.name;       // null (stops early, no crash)
({ name: 'Ada' }) && 'ok'; // 'ok'
!'Ada';                  // false
```

Both short-circuit: the right side is not evaluated when the left side already decides the result. That is why `user && user.name` is safe, although `user?.name` is the modern way. Watch out: `||` treats `0` and `''` as "missing", so `count || 10` replaces a real `0`; use `??` for defaults. In React, `{items.length && <List />}` renders a literal `0` when the list is empty.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```js
label; // 'Anonymous'
```

`user && user.name` returns `user.name` (because `user` is truthy), which is `''`. Then `'' || 'Anonymous'` returns the right side, since `''` is falsy. With `??` instead of `||`, the result would be `''`, because `??` only falls back on `null` or `undefined`.

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Nullish coalescing operator

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: A form's `quantity` can legitimately be `0`. Why default it with `quantity ?? 1` instead of `quantity || 1`?
back:
`??` (nullish coalescing) falls back only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`, so a real `0` is kept. `||` falls back for any falsy value (`0`, `''`, `false`, `NaN`), so `0 || 1` silently becomes `1`.

```js
const quantity = 0;
quantity ?? 1; // 0  (0 is a real value)
quantity || 1; // 1  (0 is falsy, so it is replaced)

null ?? 1;      // 1
undefined ?? 1; // 1
'' ?? 'n/a';    // ''
```

Use `??` for "missing value" defaults and `||` only when every falsy value should count as missing. You cannot mix `??` with `||` or `&&` without parentheses: `a || b ?? c` is a SyntaxError.

---


`??` returns the right-hand side only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`. With `||` instead, `apiOffset || 10` would turn a valid `0` into `10`, because `||` treats every falsy value as missing.

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Comma operator

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The comma operator (`,`) evaluates each of its operands (from left to right) and returns the value of the last operand.

```js
const a = (1, 2, 3);      // a is 3
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `const a = (1, 2, 3)` set `a` to, and where does the comma operator actually show up in real code?
back:
`a` is `3`: the comma operator evaluates each operand left to right and returns the value of the last one. In practice you mostly see it in a `for` loop that updates two variables at once.

```js
const a = (1, 2, 3); // 3

for (let i = 0, j = 4; i < j; i++, j--) {
  console.log(i, j); // 0 4, then 1 3
}
```

The commas in `let x = 1, y = 2`, in function arguments, and in array/object literals are separators, not this operator. Outside loops, avoid it: `(doThing(), value)` is hard to read, so write two statements instead.

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Nullish assignment operator

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: What does `settings.theme ??= 'light'` do, and how is it different from `settings.theme ||= 'light'`?
back:
`??=` assigns `'light'` only if `settings.theme` is currently `null` or `undefined`; otherwise it leaves the value alone. `||=` also overwrites falsy values such as `''`, `0` and `false`.

```js
const a = { theme: '' };
a.theme ??= 'light'; // stays '' (not null/undefined)

const b = { theme: '' };
b.theme ||= 'light'; // becomes 'light' ('' is falsy)

const c = {};
c.theme ??= 'light'; // 'light' (was undefined)
```

`x ??= y` means `x ?? (x = y)`: when `x` already has a value, no assignment happens at all. Use it to fill in missing options without clobbering values the user chose on purpose.

previous.back:
One solution:

```js

```

The nullish assignment operator (`??=`) assigns the right-hand operand to the left-hand operand only if the left-hand operand is `null` or `undefined`.

```js
let a = null;
let b = 5;
a ??= b;  // a is now 5 (a was null)
let c = 0;
c ??= b;  // c is still 0 (c was not null or undefined)
```

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Math operators

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Math operators are pretty much exactly what you'd expect. They perform basic arithmetic operations:

- `+`: addition (binary) or casting to number (unary)
- `-`: subtraction (binary) or negation (unary)
- `*`: multiplication
- `/`: division
- `%`: modulo (remainder of integer division)
- `**`: exponentiation (equivalent to `Math.pow()`)

```js
const a = 5;
const b = 2;

const sum = a + b;          // 7
const difference = a - b;   // 3
const product = a * b;      // 10
const quotient = a / b;     // 2.5
const remainder = a % b;    // 1
const exponent = a ** b;    // 25
const negation = -a;        // -5
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: In JavaScript, what are `5 / 2`, `-5 % 2`, `2 ** 3`, and `'5' + 2`, and why do they surprise people?
back:
`5 / 2` is `2.5`, `-5 % 2` is `-1`, `2 ** 3` is `8`, and `'5' + 2` is `'52'`. JavaScript has one number type, so `/` never does integer division. `%` is a remainder whose sign follows the left operand, not a true modulo. And `+` joins strings as soon as either side is a string.

```js
5 / 2;              // 2.5
Math.trunc(5 / 2);  // 2  (integer division)
-5 % 2;             // -1 (not 1)
5.5 % 2;            // 1.5 (% works on decimals too)
2 ** 3;             // 8
'5' + 2;            // '52' (string concatenation)
'5' - 2;            // 3  (- always converts to numbers)
+'42';              // 42 (unary + converts to a number)
```

Form inputs always give strings, so convert with `Number(value)` before doing arithmetic.

---

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Ternary operator

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The ternary operator (`?`) is a shorthand for an `if...else` statement. It takes three operands:

- A condition to evaluate
- The value to return if the condition is `true`
- The value to return if the condition is `false`

```js
const age = 18;
const canVote = age >= 18 ? 'Yes' : 'No'; // 'Yes'
```

[Further reading](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/ternary-operator)

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you pick between two values inside an expression, such as a template literal or JSX, where an `if` statement is not allowed?
back:
Use the conditional (ternary) operator `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`. Unlike `if`, it is an expression that produces a value, so it works in `const` initializers, template literals, function arguments and JSX.

```jsx
const age = 18;
const canVote = age >= 18 ? 'Yes' : 'No'; // 'Yes'

const label = `${count} ${count === 1 ? 'item' : 'items'}`;

<button>{isSaving ? 'Saving…' : 'Save'}</button>
```

The operator is `? :` used together, and both branches are required. Nested ternaries get unreadable quickly, so for three or more cases use `if`/`else` or a lookup object.

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Equality comparison operators

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
JavaScript equality comes in two flavors:

- `==` (loose equality) & `!=` (loose inequality)
- `===` (strict equality) & `!==` (strict inequality)

```js
// Loose equality
10 == '10'; // true
10 != '10'; // false

// Strict equality
10 === '10'; // false
10 !== '10'; // true
```

[Further reading](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/equality)

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Why is `10 == '10'` true but `10 === '10'` false, and which should you use to compare an `<input>` value with a number?
back:
`==` (loose equality) converts both sides to a common type before comparing, so `'10'` becomes `10`. `===` (strict equality) never converts: a number and a string are always unequal. Use `===`, and convert the input yourself with `Number()` first, since `input.value` is always a string.

```js
10 == '10';          // true  (string converted to number)
10 === '10';         // false (different types)
Number('10') === 10; // true  (explicit conversion)

0 == '';             // true  (surprise: '' converts to 0)
null == undefined;   // true
NaN === NaN;         // false: use Number.isNaN(x)
```

`!=` and `!==` follow the same rules. The one common deliberate use of `==` is `x == null`, which matches both `null` and `undefined`.

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Comparison operators

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Comparison operators compare two values, much like in math:

- `>`: greater than
- `<`: less than
- `>=`: greater than or equal to
- `<=`: less than or equal to

```js
const a = 5;
const b = 10;
a > b;  // false
a < b;  // true
a >= b; // false
a <= b; // true
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What do `'10' < '9'` and `'10' < 9` return in JavaScript, and why do they differ?
back:
`'10' < '9'` is `true` and `'10' < 9` is `false`. When both sides are strings, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare them character by character (so `'1'` sorts before `'9'`). When one side is a number, the string is converted to a number first.

```js
'10' < '9';   // true  (text comparison: '1' < '9')
'10' < 9;     // false (numeric: 10 < 9)
5 >= 5;       // true
'abc' < 5;    // false ('abc' becomes NaN)
NaN >= 1;     // false (every comparison with NaN is false)
```

Values from form inputs and query strings are strings, so convert them with `Number()` before comparing, or `'10' < '9'`-style bugs appear in validation and sorting.

---

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Increment & decrement operators

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The increment (`++`) and decrement (`--`) operators are shorthand for adding or subtracting 1 from a variable. They can be used in two ways:

- **Prefix**: `++a` or `--a` (increments/decrements the variable before using it)
- **Postfix**: `a++` or `a--` (increments/decrements the variable after using it)

```js
let a = 5;
let b = 5;
let c = ++a;  // a is now 6, c is 6
let d = b++;  // b is now 6, d is 5
let e = --a;  // a is now 5, e is 5
let f = b--;  // b is now 5, f is 6
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What do `++` and `--` do to a variable, and why does `const count = 0; count++;` throw?
back:
`++` adds 1 to a variable and `--` subtracts 1, and both write the new value back into the variable. Because they reassign, they need a `let` variable (or an object property); on a `const` they throw a TypeError.

```js
let a = 5;
a++;   // a is 6 (same as a += 1)
a--;   // a is 5

const count = 0;
count++; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

let s = '5';
s++;     // s is 6, a number (the string is converted)
```

Prefix (`++a`) and postfix (`a++`) both change the variable; they only differ in the value the expression returns. Many style guides prefer `a += 1` for clarity.

---

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Arrow function operator

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
While not technically an operator, it's often confused with one. The arrow function syntax (`=>`) is a shorthand for writing function expressions. It allows you to create anonymous functions in a more concise way.

```js
const add = (a, b) => a + b; // Arrow function
add(2, 3); // 5
```

[Further reading](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/arrow-functions)

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: When does an arrow function return a value without `return`, and why does `() => { id: 1 }` return `undefined`?
back:
An arrow function with an expression body (no braces) returns that expression automatically. With braces it is a block body and needs an explicit `return`. `{ id: 1 }` after `=>` is read as a block containing a label, so nothing is returned; wrap an object literal in parentheses.

```js
const add = (a, b) => a + b;            // returns a + b
const add2 = (a, b) => { return a + b; }; // block body needs return

const bad = () => { id: 1 };    // bad() is undefined
const good = () => ({ id: 1 }); // good() is { id: 1 }

users.map(u => ({ id: u.id, name: u.name }));
```

Arrow functions also have no `this` of their own; they use the `this` of the surrounding code, which is why they work well as callbacks.

---

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Spread operator

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you add an item to an array, or change one field of an object, without mutating the original (e.g. for React state)?

previous.back:
One solution:

```js
const newArr = [...arr, 4, 5];    // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
```

The spread operator (`...`) is used to expand an iterable (like an array or object) into its individual elements. It can be used in function calls, array literals, and object literals.

```js
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
const newArr = [...arr, 4, 5];    // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

const obj = { a: 1, b: 2 };
const newObj = { ...obj, c: 3 };  // { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }
```

[Further reading](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/spread-rest-syntax)

---

```js
console.log(user.role); // 'viewer'
```
back:
One solution:

```js

```

Object spread copies `user`'s properties into a new object, and the later `role` key overrides the copied one. Writing `{ role: 'admin', ...user }` would keep `'viewer'`, because the spread comes last and wins.

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Double negation operator

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The double NOT (`!!`) is not technically an operator, but provides a way to convert a value to its boolean equivalent. It negates the value twice, effectively converting it to a boolean.

```js
const str = 'Hello';
const isNotEmpty = !!str; // true

const num = 0;
const isNotZero = !!num; // false
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `!!value` return for `'Hello'`, `0`, `''`, `[]` and `'0'`, and what is a more readable way to write it?
back:
`!!value` converts a value to its boolean: `true`, `false`, `false`, `true`, `true`. The first `!` converts and negates, the second negates back. `Boolean(value)` does exactly the same and reads more clearly.

```js
!!'Hello'; // true
!!0;       // false
!!'';      // false
!![];      // true (every object, even an empty array, is truthy)
!!'0';     // true (non-empty string)
Boolean('Hello'); // true, same as !!
```

The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`; everything else is truthy. So to check "has items", test `list.length > 0`, not `!!list`.

---

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Math assignment operators

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
A similar, set of operators combines assignment (`=`) with the math operators. These are shorthand for the longer forms:

- `+=`: addition assignment
- `-=`: subtraction assignment
- `*=`: multiplication assignment
- `/=`: division assignment
- `%=`: modulo assignment
- `**=`: exponentiation assignment

```js
let a = 5;
let b = 2;
a += b;     // a = a + b; a is now 7
a -= b;     // a = a - b; a is now 5
a *= b;     // a = a * b; a is now 10
a /= b;     // a = a / b; a is now 5
a %= b;     // a = a % b; a is now 1
a **= b;    // a = a ** b; a is now 25
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `total += price` do, and what goes wrong when `price` comes straight from a form input?
back:
`total += price` is shorthand for `total = total + price`. If `price` is a string (as every `input.value` is), `+` concatenates instead of adding, so starting from `total = 0`, `total += '5'` gives the string `'05'`.

```js
let total = 0;
total += '5';          // '05' (string!)

let sum = 0;
sum += Number('5');    // 5

let a = 5;
a -= 2;   // 3
a *= 4;   // 12
a /= 3;   // 4
a %= 3;   // 1
a **= 2;  // 1  (1 ** 2)
```

Every math operator has a compound form: `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`, `**=`. Only `+=` has the string trap; the others convert to numbers. Convert inputs with `Number()` before accumulating.

---

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Optional chaining operator

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The optional chaining operator (`?.`) allows you to safely access deeply nested properties of an object without having to check if each property in the chain exists. If any property in the chain is `null` or `undefined`, it returns `undefined` instead of throwing an error.

```js
const obj = { a: { b: { c: 1 } } };
const value = obj?.a?.b?.c;   // 1
const value2 = obj?.a?.b?.d;  // undefined (no error thrown)
```

[Further reading](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/nullish-coalescing-optional-chaining#optional-chaining)

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: An API response may have no `user.address`. How do you read `user.address.city` without a TypeError, and what do you get when it is missing?
back:
Write `user?.address?.city`. Optional chaining (`?.`) stops and returns `undefined` when the value to its left is `null` or `undefined`, instead of throwing "Cannot read properties of undefined". Pair it with `??` to show a fallback.

```js
const user = { name: 'Ana' };            // no address
user.address.city;                        // TypeError
user?.address?.city;                      // undefined
user?.address?.city ?? 'Unknown';         // 'Unknown'

user.getAvatar?.();   // call only if the method exists
user.tags?.[0];       // index only if tags exists
```

It only protects the spot where you write it: `user.address?.city.length` still throws if `city` is missing. Use it for data that is genuinely optional; sprinkling it everywhere hides real bugs. You also cannot assign through it (`user?.name = 'x'` is a SyntaxError).

The optional chaining operator (`?.`) allows you to safely access deeply nested properties of an object without having to check if each property in the chain exists. If any property in the chain is `null` or `undefined`, it returns `undefined` instead of throwing an error.

```js
const obj = { a: { b: { c: 1 } } };
const value = obj?.a?.b?.c;   // 1
const value2 = obj?.a?.b?.d;  // undefined (no error thrown)
```

front: When must you use bracket notation `obj[key]` instead of dot notation `obj.key`?
back:
Use brackets when the property name is in a variable or computed at runtime, or when it is not a valid identifier (contains `-` or spaces, or starts with a digit). Dot notation only works with a fixed, identifier-like name written in the code.

```js
const user = { name: 'Ana', 'first-name': 'Ana' };
user.name;            // 'Ana'
user['first-name'];   // 'Ana' (user.first-name would be user.first minus name)

const field = 'name';
user[field];          // 'Ana'
user.field;           // undefined (looks for a key literally called "field")

// Generic form handler
setValues({ ...values, [e.target.name]: e.target.value });
```

Both forms work on any object, and methods are called the same way: `user.toString()` or `user['toString']()`.

**Explain the approach**

JavaScript Operator Cheatsheet — Logical assignment operators

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Logical assignment operators combine logical operations with assignment. They are shorthand for the longer forms:

- `&&=`: logical AND assignment (assigns the value if the left operand is truthy)
- `||=`: logical OR assignment (assigns the value if the left operand is falsy)

```js
let a = true;
let b = false;
let c = true;

a &&= b;  // a is now false (b is assigned to a)
b ||= c;  // b is now true  (c is assigned to b)
```

[Further reading](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/logical-operations)

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/operator-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: When does `a ||= b` assign, when does `a &&= b` assign, and how does `??=` differ from both?
back:
`a ||= b` assigns `b` only when `a` is falsy; `a &&= b` assigns `b` only when `a` is truthy; `a ??= b` assigns only when `a` is `null` or `undefined`. In every case, if the condition fails, nothing is assigned.

```js
const form = { name: '', email: '  ana@example.com ', phone: 0 };

form.name ||= 'Anonymous';            // '' is falsy -> 'Anonymous'
form.email &&= form.email.trim();     // has a value -> 'ana@example.com'
form.phone ??= null;                  // 0 is not nullish -> stays 0
```

`a ||= b` means `a || (a = b)`, not `a = a || b`, so an existing value is never re-written. Choose `??=` when `0`, `''` or `false` are valid values, and `||=` when any falsy value should be replaced.

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

What is the difference between prefix and postfix operators?

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The increment operator (`++`) adds `1` to its operand and returns a value. Similarly, the decrement operator (`--`) subtracts `1` from its operand and returns a value. Both of these operators can be used either prefix (`++i`, `--i`) or postfix (`i++`, `i--`).

If used prefix, the value is incremented/decremented, and the value of the expression is the updated value.

```js
let i = 0;    // i = 0
let j = ++i;  // i = 1, j = 1
let k = --i;  // i = 0, k = 0
```

If used postfix, the value is incremented/decremented, and the value of the expression is the original value.

```js
let i = 0;    // i = 0
let j = i++;  // i = 1, j = 0
let k = i--;  // i = 0, k = 1
```

---

**Explain the approach**

Generate a random boolean value in JavaScript

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
JavaScript doesn't have a built-in function to generate a random boolean value, but you can easily create one using `Math.random()`. All you need to do is check if the result of `Math.random()` is greater than or equal to `0.5`.

As `Math.random()` generates a random number between 0 and 1, the **probability** of the result being greater than or equal to `0.5` is 50%, which makes for an **even distribution** of `true` and `false` values.

```js
const randomBoolean = () => Math.random() >= 0.5;

randomBoolean(); // true
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/random-boolean.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you generate a random `true` or `false` with 50/50 odds in JavaScript?
back:
Use `Math.random() < 0.5`. `Math.random()` returns a decimal from 0 (inclusive) up to but not including 1, so half the range is below `0.5`.

```js
const randomBoolean = () => Math.random() < 0.5;

randomBoolean(); // true or false, each about 50% of the time
```

`Math.random()` is fine for UI things like shuffling a demo list or A/B picks in tests, but it is not cryptographically secure. For tokens or anything security-related use `crypto.getRandomValues()` or `crypto.randomUUID()`.

---

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Subsequently, generating a **random integer** is very similar, except for an additional step at the end. You need to use `Math.floor()` to **round the result down** to the nearest integer.

```js
const randomIntegerInRange = (min, max) =>
  Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min;

```

front: How do you get a random integer from `min` to `max` inclusive, and why does the formula need `+ 1`?
back:
Use `Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min`. There are `max - min + 1` possible integers (0 to 5 is six values). `Math.random() * 6` gives a decimal in [0, 6), and `Math.floor` turns that into 0 to 5 with equal odds; adding `min` shifts the range.

```js
const randomIntegerInRange = (min, max) =>
  Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min;

randomIntegerInRange(0, 5); // e.g. 2 (any of 0-5)
randomIntegerInRange(1, 6); // a dice roll
```

Without `+ 1`, `max` can never appear. Using `Math.round` instead of `Math.floor` is a common bug: the two end values come up only half as often as the others. The formula assumes `min` and `max` are integers.

**Explain the approach**

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The simplest use case you'll come across is to generate a **random number in a specified range**. All you need to do is multiply the result of `Math.random()` by the **difference** between the maximum and minimum values, and then add the minimum value.

```js
const randomNumberInRange = (min, max) => Math.random() * (max - min) + min;

randomNumberInRange(2, 10); // 6.0211363285087005
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/random-number-or-integer-in-range.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you generate a random decimal number between `min` and `max` with `Math.random()`, and can the result equal `max`?
back:
Use `Math.random() * (max - min) + min`. The result can equal `min` but is always less than `max`, because `Math.random()` returns a value in [0, 1): 0 inclusive, 1 exclusive.

```js
const randomNumberInRange = (min, max) =>
  Math.random() * (max - min) + min;

randomNumberInRange(2, 10); // e.g. 6.0211363285087005 (2 <= n < 10)
```

Multiplying stretches [0, 1) to the width of the range, and adding `min` shifts it to start at `min`. For whole numbers, use the `Math.floor(... * (max - min + 1)) + min` version instead.

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you add N minutes to a JavaScript `Date` without changing the original, and why multiply by `60_000`?

back:
One solution:

```js
d.setTime(d.getTime() + n * 60_000);
```

`getTime()` returns the timestamp in milliseconds and a minute is `60 * 1000` ms. `setTime()` mutates the date it is called on, which is why the function works on the copy `d` instead of the argument.

How can I add minutes, hours or days to a JavaScript date? — Add hours to date

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How do you add N hours to a `Date`, and on a daylight-saving (DST) day, how does "+24 hours" differ from "same time tomorrow"?

back:
One solution:

```js
d.setTime(d.getTime() + n * 3_600_000);
```

One hour is `1000 * 60 * 60 = 3_600_000` ms. Adding milliseconds to the timestamp moves the instant by exactly N hours; across a DST switch the local clock time will shift by an hour, which is correct for a duration.

**Explain the approach**

How do I compare two dates in JavaScript? — Date equality comparison

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Comparing two dates using the [equality operators (`==` or `===`)](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/js/s/equality) is ineffective, as it compares the objects **by reference**. Luckily, `Date.prototype.toISOString()` returns a string representation of the date in a **standardized format**, which can be used to compare two dates.

```js
const isSameDate = (dateA, dateB) =>
  dateA.toISOString() === dateB.toISOString();

isSameDate(new Date('2020-10-20'), new Date('2020-10-20')); // true
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/date-comparison.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Why is `new Date(2020, 9, 20) === new Date(2020, 9, 20)` false, and how do you check that two `Date` objects represent the same moment?
back:
`===` on objects compares **references**: two separate `Date` objects are never `===`, even with identical values. Compare their timestamps instead: `a.getTime() === b.getTime()`.

```js
const isSameDate = (dateA, dateB) => dateA.getTime() === dateB.getTime();

const a = new Date(2020, 9, 20);
const b = new Date(2020, 9, 20);
a === b;            // false (different objects)
```

front: Why does `dateA > dateB` correctly compare two `Date` objects, when `dateA === dateB` does not?
back:
Relational operators (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`) convert both objects to primitives first, and a `Date` converts to its millisecond timestamp via `valueOf()`. So `>` compares numbers. `===` does no conversion and compares object identity.

```js
const isAfterDate = (dateA, dateB) => dateA > dateB;

isAfterDate(new Date(2020, 9, 21), new Date(2020, 9, 20)); // true
new Date(2020, 9, 21).valueOf(); // a number like 1603263600000 (depends on time zone)
```

Real-world use: "is this coupon expired?" → `new Date() > coupon.expiresAt`. Make sure both sides are `Date` objects, not strings: comparing two ISO strings with `>` compares text, which only works when both use the same format and offset.

How to calculate date difference in JavaScript — Date difference in months

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Months and years are easier to calculate with other `Date` methods, instead of subtraction. In such cases, we prefer to use `Date.prototype.getFullYear()` and `Date.prototype.getMonth()` to calculate the difference between the two dates.

```js
const dateDifferenceInMonths = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  Math.max(
    (dateFinal.getFullYear() - dateInitial.getFullYear()) * 12 +
      dateFinal.getMonth() -
      dateInitial.getMonth(),
    0
  );

dateDifferenceInMonths(
  new Date('2017-12-13'),
  new Date('2018-04-29')
); // 4
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/date-difference.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you count the calendar months between two dates with `getFullYear()`/`getMonth()`, and what does that formula ignore?
back:
Months have different lengths, so don't divide milliseconds. Instead: `(yearB - yearA) * 12 + (monthB - monthA)`. This counts month boundaries crossed and **ignores the day of the month**: Jan 31 → Feb 1 counts as 1 month, Jan 1 → Jan 31 as 0.

```js
const dateDifferenceInMonths = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  Math.max(
    (dateFinal.getFullYear() - dateInitial.getFullYear()) * 12 +
      dateFinal.getMonth() - dateInitial.getMonth(),
    0
  );

dateDifferenceInMonths(new Date(2017, 11, 13), new Date(2018, 3, 29)); // 4 (Dec → Apr)
```

`Math.max(…, 0)` clamps a reversed range to 0. If you need "full months elapsed", subtract 1 when `dateFinal.getDate() < dateInitial.getDate()`. Avoid `new Date('2018-04-01')` here: date-only strings parse as UTC and can land in March in US time zones.

How to calculate date difference in JavaScript — Date difference in weeks

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Calculating the date difference in weeks is still possible with simple date subtraction. We need only divide the difference in milliseconds by the number of milliseconds in a week (`1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 7`).

```js
const dateDifferenceInWeeks = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  (dateFinal - dateInitial) / 604_800_000;

dateDifferenceInWeeks(
  new Date('2023-01-01'),
  new Date('2023-01-08')
); // 1
```

front: How do you compute the difference between two dates in weeks, and why might the result come out fractional?
back:
Subtract the dates (which gives milliseconds) and divide by the milliseconds in a week: `(b - a) / 604_800_000` (`1000 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 7`).

```js
const dateDifferenceInWeeks = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  (dateFinal - dateInitial) / 604_800_000;

dateDifferenceInWeeks(new Date(2023, 0, 1), new Date(2023, 0, 8)); // 1
dateDifferenceInWeeks(new Date(2023, 0, 1), new Date(2023, 0, 11)); // 1.4285714285714286
```

The result is fractional whenever the span isn't whole weeks, and a span that crosses a DST change in local time is an hour short or long (e.g. 0.994…). Wrap it in `Math.floor()` for "full weeks" or `Math.round()` for "about N weeks".

front: What does subtracting one `Date` from another return in JavaScript, and how do you turn it into seconds?
back:
`dateB - dateA` returns a **number of milliseconds**: the `-` operator converts each `Date` to its timestamp. Divide by `1000` for seconds.

```js
const dateDifferenceInSeconds = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  (dateFinal - dateInitial) / 1_000;

  new Date(2020, 11, 24, 0, 0, 15),
  new Date(2020, 11, 24, 0, 0, 17)
); // 2
```

front: How do you compute the hours between two `Date`s, and when is "the same clock time on the next day" not 24 hours apart?
back:
Subtract the dates and divide by the milliseconds in an hour: `(b - a) / 3_600_000`. The result is real elapsed time, so across a daylight-saving change, 10:25 today to 10:25 tomorrow is **23 or 25 hours**, not 24.

```js
const dateDifferenceInHours = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  (dateFinal - dateInitial) / 3_600_000;

// US time zones (DST began Mar 14 2021):
dateDifferenceInHours(new Date(2021, 2, 13, 10, 25), new Date(2021, 2, 14, 10, 25)); // 23
```

That is usually correct for billing or shift length ("how long was this open?"), but surprising if you expected calendar math.

front: Why can `(end - start) / 86_400_000` return `29.958…` instead of `30` for two local dates, and how do you count whole days reliably?
back:
Because a local "day" is not always 24 hours: when the range crosses a daylight-saving change, one day is 23 (or 25) hours long, so the millisecond difference is an hour off. Round the result, or convert both dates to UTC calendar dates before subtracting.

```js
const dateDifferenceInDays = (dateInitial, dateFinal) =>
  Math.round((dateFinal - dateInitial) / 86_400_000);

// US time zones, DST starts Mar 10 2024:
(new Date(2024, 2, 31) - new Date(2024, 2, 1)) / 86_400_000; // 29.958333333333332
dateDifferenceInDays(new Date(2024, 2, 1), new Date(2024, 2, 31)); // 30

// Time-zone-proof alternative: compare calendar dates in UTC
const utcDay = d => Date.UTC(d.getFullYear(), d.getMonth(), d.getDate());
(utcDay(new Date(2024, 2, 31)) - utcDay(new Date(2024, 2, 1))) / 86_400_000; // 30
```

`Math.round` is fine when both dates are midnights; for arbitrary times use the `utcDay` version.

**Explain the approach**

Determine if a JavaScript date is a weekday or weekend

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
I've often found myself needing to check if a given **date is a weekday or weekend**. As I'm not particularly fond of using libraries for such simple tasks, I've come up with a couple of simple helper functions to do the job.

```js
const isWeekday = date => date.getDay() % 6 !== 0;
const isWeekend = date => date.getDay() % 6 === 0;

isWeekday(new Date('2024-01-05')); // true
isWeekend(new Date('2024-01-05')); // false

isWeekday(new Date('2024-01-06')); // false
isWeekend(new Date('2024-01-06')); // true
```

The entire premise of these snippets is quite simple. We use `Date.prototype.getDay()` to get the **day of the week**, which is a number between `0` and `6`, where `0` is Sunday and `6` is Saturday. We then use the modulo operator (`%`) to check if the day is a multiple of `6`, which is the case for both Saturday and Sunday. If the remainder is `0`, we know the date is a weekend. If the remainder is not `0`, we know the date is a weekday.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/date-is-weekday-or-weekend.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How does `date.getDay() % 6 === 0` detect a weekend, and why can `isWeekend(new Date('2024-01-06'))` wrongly return `false` in the US?
back:
`getDay()` returns 0 (Sunday) to 6 (Saturday). Only 0 and 6 give a remainder of 0 when divided by 6, so `% 6 === 0` means weekend and `!== 0` means weekday.

```js
const isWeekday = date => date.getDay() % 6 !== 0;
const isWeekend = date => date.getDay() % 6 === 0;

isWeekday(new Date(2024, 0, 5)); // true  (Fri, Jan 5 local)
isWeekend(new Date(2024, 0, 6)); // true  (Sat, Jan 6 local)
```

The catch: `new Date('2024-01-06')` is a date-only ISO string, which JavaScript parses as **UTC midnight**. In US time zones that is still Friday evening locally, and `getDay()` reads local time, so it returns 5. Build local dates with `new Date(2024, 0, 6)` (month is 0-based), or use `getUTCDay()` if you really mean UTC. `% 6` is clever; `day === 0 || day === 6` is clearer.

**Explain the approach**

Convert between a JavaScript Date object and a Unix timestamp

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Unix timestamps are a **number representing the number of seconds** since the Unix epoch (_January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC_). JavaScript `Date` objects are a **number representing the number of milliseconds** since the Unix epoch.

This means that you can convert between `Date` objects and Unix timestamps by dividing or multiplying by `1000`.

```js
const toTimestamp = date => Math.floor(date.getTime() / 1000);
const fromTimestamp = timestamp => new Date(timestamp * 1000);

toTimestamp(new Date('2024-01-04')); // 1704326400
fromTimestamp(1704326400); // 2024-01-04T00:00:00.000Z
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/date-to-unix-timestamp.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: An API sends `created_at: 1704326400` (a Unix timestamp). How do you convert between Unix timestamps and JavaScript `Date` objects?
back:
A Unix timestamp counts **seconds** since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC; a `Date` stores **milliseconds** since the same moment. So multiply by 1000 to build a `Date`, and divide by 1000 (and floor) to get a timestamp.

```js
const toTimestamp = date => Math.floor(date.getTime() / 1000);
const fromTimestamp = timestamp => new Date(timestamp * 1000);

toTimestamp(new Date('2024-01-04T00:00:00Z')); // 1704326400
fromTimestamp(1704326400).toISOString();       // '2024-01-04T00:00:00.000Z'
Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);                 // "now" as a Unix timestamp
```

Classic bug: `new Date(1704326400)` without `* 1000` gives a date in January 1970. Timestamps are time-zone independent; the zone only matters when you display the date.

**Explain the approach**

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Finding the day of the year (in the range `1-366`) from a `Date` object is fairly straightforward. We can use the `Date` constructor and `Date.prototype.getFullYear()` to get the **first day of the year** as a `Date` object.

Then, we can subtract the first day of the year from the given `date` and divide with the milliseconds in each day to get the result. Finally, we can use `Math.floor()` to appropriately round the resulting day count to an integer.

```js
const dayOfYear = date =>
  Math.floor((date - new Date(date.getFullYear(), 0, 0)) / 86_400_000);

dayOfYear(new Date('2024-09-28')); // 272
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/day-week-month-quarter-of-year.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you compute the day of the year (1–366) for a `Date`, and why can `Math.floor((date - new Date(y, 0, 0)) / 86_400_000)` be off by one?
back:
Subtract "day 0" (Dec 31 of the previous year) from the date and divide by the milliseconds in a day, but do it on **UTC calendar dates** so every day is exactly 24 hours. With local dates, the spring daylight-saving change makes the span one hour short, and `Math.floor` then drops a whole day.

```js
const dayOfYear = date =>
  (Date.UTC(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth(), date.getDate()) -
    Date.UTC(date.getFullYear(), 0, 0)) / 86_400_000;

dayOfYear(new Date(2024, 8, 28)); // 272
dayOfYear(new Date(2024, 0, 1));  // 1
dayOfYear(new Date(2024, 11, 31)); // 366 (leap year)
```

`Date.UTC(y, 0, 0)` uses day 0 of January, which rolls back to Dec 31. The naive local version returns 271 for Sep 28 2024 in US time zones.

front: How do you get the quarter of the year (1–4) from a `Date` in one expression?
back:

front: Why does `new Date(2024, 8, 28).getMonth()` return `8` for a date in September, and how do you get the human month number?
back:

front: How do you get the first day of the month for a given `Date`, and what is the matching trick for the last day?
back:
Build a new local date from the same year and month with day `1`: `new Date(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth(), 1)`. For the last day, ask for day `0` of the *next* month, which rolls back to the final day of this one.

```js
const firstDateOfMonth = (date = new Date()) =>
  new Date(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth(), 1);
const lastDateOfMonth = (date = new Date()) =>
  new Date(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth() + 1, 0);

lastDateOfMonth(new Date(2024, 1, 10)).getDate();       // 29 (Feb 2024)
```

Both return a `Date` at local midnight, handy for "this month" filters in a report. `getMonth() + 1` on December gives 12, which the constructor rolls into January of the next year.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Check if a value is a valid JavaScript date

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
JavaScript provides a `Date` object that represents a single moment in time. It can be created using **various formats**, such as a string, an array of values, or individual values for the year, month, day, etc. However, not all values can be used to create a valid `Date` object.

So, how can you check if a **value or set of values** can be used to create a valid `Date` object? The simplest way is to use the `Date()` constructor with any value we want to check. Then, using `Date.prototype.valueOf()` and `Number.isNaN()`, we can determine if a valid `Date` object can be created.

In order to create a robust method, we can use the spread operator (`...`) to pass the values to the `Date()` constructor. This way, we can check if a valid `Date` object can be created from **any number of values** (e.g. a single string, a set of numeric values etc.).

```js
const isDateValid = (...val) => !Number.isNaN(new Date(...val).valueOf());

isDateValid('December 17, 1995 03:24:00'); // true
isDateValid('1995-12-17T03:24:00'); // true
isDateValid('1995-12-17 T03:24:00'); // false
isDateValid('Duck'); // false
isDateValid(1995, 11, 17); // true
isDateValid(1995, 11, 17, 'Duck'); // false
isDateValid({}); // false
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/is-date-valid.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you check whether a value (or set of arguments) produces a valid `Date`, and what "invalid" inputs does that check still accept?
back:
Construct the date and test whether its timestamp is `NaN`: an Invalid Date has `getTime()` / `valueOf()` of `NaN`. Spreading the arguments lets one helper accept a string, a number, or year/month/day parts.

```js
const isDateValid = (...val) => !Number.isNaN(new Date(...val).valueOf());

isDateValid('1995-12-17T03:24:00'); // true
isDateValid('Duck');                // false
isDateValid(1995, 11, 17);          // true
isDateValid(1995, 11, 17, 'Duck');  // false

// Still "valid", but probably not what the user meant:
isDateValid(2023, 1, 31);  // true — rolls over to Mar 3 2023
isDateValid(null);         // true — null becomes 0 (Jan 1 1970)
```

For form input, validate the format yourself (e.g. `/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/`) and check the parts round-trip (`d.getMonth() === month`). Non-ISO strings like `'December 17, 1995'` parse in browsers but the format is implementation-defined.

**Explain the approach**

Check if a year is a leap year in JavaScript

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
A [leap year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_year) is a year that is evenly divisible by 4, except for end-of-century years, which must be divisible by 400.

While detecting a leap year via code sounds like a lot of work, there's a method that **doesn't really involve any math** whatsoever. Using the `Date` object, you can easily check if a given year is a leap year.

All you have to do is use the `Date()` constructor to create an object for **February 29th of the given year**. If the month is February, then `Date.prototye.getMonth()` will return `1` (since months are zero-based in JavaScript), meaning it's a **leap year**. If the month is not February, the date will be set to March 1st, which means it's **not a leap year**.

```js
const isLeapYear = year => new Date(year, 1, 29).getMonth() === 1;

isLeapYear(2019); // false
isLeapYear(2020); // true
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/is-leap-year.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How can the `Date` constructor tell you whether a year is a leap year, without writing the divisible-by-4/100/400 rule?
back:
Create **February 29** of that year: `new Date(year, 1, 29)` (month 1 = February). In a leap year it stays in February; otherwise it rolls over to March 1. So check `getMonth() === 1`.

```js
const isLeapYear = year => new Date(year, 1, 29).getMonth() === 1;

isLeapYear(2019); // false
isLeapYear(2020); // true
isLeapYear(1900); // false (century, not divisible by 400)
isLeapYear(2000); // true
```

The explicit rule is `(y % 4 === 0 && y % 100 !== 0) || y % 400 === 0`. It relies on the same day-overflow behaviour that makes `setDate(getDate() + n)` work. Watch out: years 0–99 in the constructor are treated as 1900–1999.

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
JavaScript's built-in `Date.prototype.toISOString()` method converts a date to ISO string in **UTC time**.

```js
const toISOString = date => date.toISOString();

toISOString(
  new Date('2024-01-06T19:20:34+02:00')
); // '2024-01-06T17:20:34.000Z'
```

Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/js/s/iso-format-date-with-timezone.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `date.toISOString()` return, and what happens to a `Date` when you `JSON.stringify` it for an API request?
back:
`toISOString()` returns the instant in **UTC** in the fixed format `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ` (the `Z` means UTC). `JSON.stringify` calls `Date.prototype.toJSON()`, which uses `toISOString()`, so dates in a request body are sent as that string automatically.

```js
const d = new Date('2024-01-06T19:20:34+02:00');
d.toISOString();               // '2024-01-06T17:20:34.000Z'
JSON.stringify({ dueAt: d });  // '{"dueAt":"2024-01-06T17:20:34.000Z"}'
```

This is the right format for storing and transmitting instants. Two gotchas: `JSON.parse` does **not** turn the string back into a `Date` (call `new Date(str)` yourself), and `toISOString()` throws `RangeError: Invalid time value` on an Invalid Date.
