previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Evenly distributed children

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: In a flex row, what is the difference between `justify-content: space-between`, `space-around`, and `space-evenly`?
back:
`space-between` puts the first and last items flush against the edges and spreads the remaining space equally between items. `space-around` gives each item equal space on both sides, so the gaps between items are twice as wide as the gaps at the edges. `space-evenly` makes every gap, edges included, the same size.

```css
.toolbar {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;   /* logo left, actions right */
}
/*
space-between: |A    B    C|
space-around:  | A  B  C |   (edge = half of between)
space-evenly:  |  A  B  C  |  (all gaps equal)
*/
```

These distribute leftover space along the main axis, so in a `flex-direction: column` container they work vertically, but only if the container has spare height. If you just want a fixed gap between items, use `gap: 1rem` instead.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/evenly-distributed-children.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```css
justify-content: space-between;
```

`space-between` puts no space at the edges and splits the leftover space equally between items. `space-around` would add half-size gaps at the edges, and `space-evenly` would make all gaps (edges included) equal.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/evenly-distributed-children.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Flexbox Cheat Sheet — Items

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
- `flex-grow` determines how much the item can grow if necessary
  - Accepts a single positive number (unitless), default value is `0`
  - Specifies how much of the remaining space in the flex container should be assigned to the item
  - The remaining space is the size of the flex container minus the size of all flex items' sizes together
  - If all items have the same `flex-grow`, all items will receive an equal share of the remaining space
  - If not all items have the same `flex-grow`, the remaining space is distributed according to the ratio defined by these values
- `flex-shrink` determines how much the items can shrink if necessary
  - Accepts a single positive number (unitless), default value is `1`
  - If the size of all flex items is larger than the flex container, items shrink to fit according to `flex-shrink`
- `flex-basis` determines the initial size of a flex item before the remaining space is distributed
  - Can use any valid `width` value, intrinsic size values, `auto` (default) or `content`
  - `auto` means "look at my `width` or `height` property", whereas `content` is used for automatic sizing
- `flex`: shorthand combining `flex-grow`, `flex-shrink` and `flex-basis`
  - Formal syntax: `flex: none | [ <'flex-grow'> <'flex-shrink'>? || <'flex-basis'> ]`
- `align-self` allows the item to override the default `align-items` specified by the container
  - Valid values are the same as those of the `align-items` property in the container
- `order` determines the ordering of the item
  - Accepts an integer value
  - Items in a container are sorted by ascending `order` value and then by their source code order
  - Might cause accessibility issues if used incorrectly

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/flexbox-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What do `flex-grow`, `flex-shrink`, and `flex-basis` each control, and what do the shorthands `flex: 1`, `flex: auto`, and `flex: none` mean?
back:
`flex-basis` is the item's starting size before free space is shared out (`auto` means "use my width/height"). `flex-grow` is the item's share of any leftover space (default `0`, so items don't grow). `flex-shrink` is how much the item gives up when space is short (default `1`, so items shrink).

```css
.sidebar { flex: none; width: 240px; }  /* 0 0 auto: fixed size */
.main    { flex: 1; }                   /* 1 1 0%: take all remaining space */
.tag     { flex: auto; }                /* 1 1 auto: grow from content size */
```

Grow ratios apply only to the leftover space: with `flex-grow` 1 and 2, the second item gets twice as much of the extra space, not twice the total width. Other item properties: `align-self` overrides the container's `align-items` for one item, and `order` changes visual order only. Keyboard tab order and screen readers still follow the DOM, so avoid `order` when the reading order would become confusing.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/flexbox-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Fluid typography with CSS clamp

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Fluid typography is a technique that allows text to **scale according to the viewport width**. This is particularly useful for responsive designs, where you want the text to grow or shrink based on the available space.

> [!NOTE]
>
> While fluid typography is a cool technique, **hand-crafted typographic scales** can often look more polished. You may want to read more in the [typographic scale basics article](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/css/s/typographic-scale-basics).

In order to create fluid typography, you can use the `clamp()` CSS function to **clamp the value** of `font-size` between a minimum and maximum value. This ensures that the text size will never be smaller than the minimum value or larger than the maximum value.

It is advised to use `rem` units for the minimum and maximum values, as they are **relative to the root font size**. This allows you to set a base font size on the `html` element and have the text scale accordingly.

Finally, you should use a **formula to calculate the responsive value** for `font-size`. This formula should be based on the viewport width, so that the text size grows or shrinks as the viewport changes, thus you can use the `vw` unit.

In the example below, the `font-size` is clamped between `1rem` and `3rem`, and the formula `8vw - 2rem` is used to calculate the responsive value. This formula ensures that the text size will be `1rem` at `600px` viewport width and `3rem` at `1000px` viewport width.

```css
.fluid-type {
  font-size: clamp(1rem, 8vw - 2rem, 3rem);
}
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/fluid-typography.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: In the animated link underline (an `::after` bar scaled with `scaleX(0)` → `scaleX(1)`), what makes the underline grow from the left and shrink away to the right?

back:

front: Which kinds of CSS properties inherit from the parent by default, and which don't? Give examples of each.
back:
Text and typography properties inherit; box and layout properties don't. Inherited: `color`, `font` and all `font-*`, `line-height`, `letter-spacing`, `word-spacing`, `text-align`, `text-indent`, `text-transform`, `white-space`, `direction`, `visibility`, `cursor`, `list-style*`, `border-collapse`/`border-spacing`, `quotes`, and custom properties. Not inherited: `margin`, `padding`, `border`, `background`, `width`/`height`, `display`, `position`, `overflow`, `opacity`, and `text-decoration` (including `text-decoration-color`).

```css
.card { color: #333; font-family: system-ui; padding: 1rem; }
/* children get the color and font, not the padding */

.child { border: inherit; }   /* force inheritance for one property */
```

Gotcha: form controls (`input`, `button`, `select`, `textarea`) get their font from browser styles instead of inheriting it, so resets usually add `font: inherit` to them.

**Explain the approach**

Using the inset CSS property — Physical, not logical

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Although the `inset` property is defined in the [CSS Logical Properties and Values Module](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-logical-1/), it is a **physical property**, not a logical one. This means it always refers to the physical dimensions (`top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left`) of an element, regardless of the writing mode or text direction (e.g., left-to-right or right-to-left).

If you need logical positioning (e.g., `inline-start`, `block-end`), you'll need to use the logical properties instead.

[Further reading](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/css/s/logical-physical-properties-map)

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Using the inset CSS property — Positioned elements

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: You set `inset: 20px` on an element and nothing happens. What is the most likely cause?
back:
The element is not positioned. `inset` (like `top/right/bottom/left`) only applies when `position` is `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, or `sticky`. With the default `position: static`, it is ignored.

```css
.box {
  position: absolute;  /* required for inset to do anything */
  inset: 20px;         /* 20px from each edge of the containing block */
}
```

The effect depends on the position type. With `absolute`/`fixed`, the offsets are measured from the containing block's edges (with `absolute`, the nearest positioned ancestor). With `relative`, the element is shifted from its normal spot; if you set both `top` and `bottom`, `top` wins. In DevTools, the Computed pane shows `position: static` when this is the problem.

---

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: An "isometric" card uses `transform: rotateX(51deg) rotateZ(43deg)` and lifts on hover. Why does the hover rule have to repeat both rotations?

back:
One solution:

```css
transform: translate3d(0px, -16px, 0px) rotateX(51deg) rotateZ(43deg);
```

A new `transform` value replaces the whole list, so the rotations must be repeated after the translate. Keeping the same functions in the same order also lets the transition interpolate smoothly. `translate: 0 -16px;` also works, because the standalone property combines with the existing `transform`.

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
| Logical Property | Physical Property (LTR) |
|------------------|-------------------|
| `inline-size` | `width` |
| `min-inline-size` | `min-width` |
| `max-inline-size` | `max-width` |
| `block-size` | `height` |
| `min-block-size` | `min-height` |
| `max-block-size` | `max-height` |

front: What are the logical-property equivalents of `width`, `height`, `min-width`, and `max-height`?
back:
`width` → `inline-size`, `height` → `block-size`, `min-width` → `min-inline-size`, `max-height` → `max-block-size`. The same pattern gives `max-inline-size` and `min-block-size`.

| Logical | Physical (horizontal text) |
| --- | --- |
| `inline-size` | `width` |
| `min-inline-size` / `max-inline-size` | `min-width` / `max-width` |
| `block-size` | `height` |
| `min-block-size` / `max-block-size` | `min-height` / `max-height` |

Rule of thumb: inline = the direction text runs in a line; block = the direction lines and paragraphs stack. In normal horizontal writing, that's width and height; in vertical writing modes (some CJK layouts) they swap. Unlike left/right, these are the same in LTR and RTL.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/logical-physical-properties-map.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Logical and physical CSS properties equivalents — Position

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
| Logical Property | Physical Property (LTR) |
|------------------|-------------------|
| `inset-inline-start` | `left` |
| `inset-inline-end` | `right` |
| `inset-inline` | `left` & `right` |
| `inset-block-start` | `top` |
| `inset-block-end` | `bottom` |
| `inset-block` | `top` & `bottom` |

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/logical-physical-properties-map.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What are the logical equivalents of `left`, `right`, `top`, and `bottom` for positioned elements, and how do they behave in right-to-left text?
back:
`left` → `inset-inline-start`, `right` → `inset-inline-end`, `top` → `inset-block-start`, `bottom` → `inset-block-end`. The shorthands `inset-inline` and `inset-block` set both ends of an axis. In RTL, `inset-inline-start` becomes the right edge.

| Logical | Physical (LTR) |
| --- | --- |
| `inset-inline-start` / `inset-inline-end` | `left` / `right` |
| `inset-inline` | `left` & `right` |
| `inset-block-start` / `inset-block-end` | `top` / `bottom` |
| `inset-block` | `top` & `bottom` |

```css
.close-button {
  position: absolute;
  inset-block-start: 0.5rem;
  inset-inline-end: 0.5rem;   /* top-right in English, top-left in Arabic */
}
```

front: What are the logical equivalents of `border-left`, `border-top-color`, and `border-top-left-radius`, and what naming pattern do all logical border properties follow?
back:
`border-left` → `border-inline-start`; `border-top-color` → `border-block-start-color`; `border-top-left-radius` → `border-start-start-radius`. Pattern: swap the physical side for `block-start` (top), `block-end` (bottom), `inline-start` (left), or `inline-end` (right), and keep the suffix: `-color` maps to `-color`, `-style` to `-style`, `-width` to `-width`.

| Logical | Physical (LTR, horizontal) |
| --- | --- |
| `border-inline-start-width` | `border-left-width` |
| `border-inline-end-style` | `border-right-style` |
| `border-block-end-color` | `border-bottom-color` |
| `border-inline` / `border-block` | left & right / top & bottom |
| `border-start-start-radius` | `border-top-left-radius` |
| `border-start-end-radius` | `border-top-right-radius` |
| `border-end-start-radius` | `border-bottom-left-radius` |
| `border-end-end-radius` | `border-bottom-right-radius` |

Radius names are `border-<block side>-<inline side>-radius`: `start-end` = top (block start) and right (inline end) in LTR.

---

| Logical Value | Physical Value (LTR) |
|------------------|-------------------|
| `start` | `left` |
| `end` | `right` |
| `inline-start` | `left` |
| `inline-end` | `right` |
| `block-start` | `top` |
| `block-end` | `bottom` |

front: Which logical keyword values replace `left`/`right`/`top`/`bottom` in properties like `text-align` and `float`, and why use them?
back:
`start` / `end` (for `text-align`), `inline-start` / `inline-end` (for `float` and `clear`), and `block-start` / `block-end`. In LTR, start = left and end = right; in RTL they flip automatically, so the same stylesheet works for Arabic or Hebrew.

| Logical value | Physical value (LTR) |
| --- | --- |
| `start` / `end` | `left` / `right` |
| `inline-start` / `inline-end` | `left` / `right` |
| `block-start` / `block-end` | `top` / `bottom` |

```css
.form-hint { text-align: start; }            /* left in English, right in Hebrew */
.avatar    { float: inline-start; }          /* text wraps on the end side */
```

`text-align: start` is the initial value of `text-align`. Writing `left` explicitly is what breaks RTL layouts.

front: Why does the cursor-tracking gradient button wrap its label in a `` (``)?
back: The gradient is drawn on the button's absolutely positioned `::before`, and positioned boxes paint above the button's plain text. Wrapping the label in a `` with `position: relative` makes it positioned too; it comes after `::before` in the tree, so it paints on top and the text stays readable. ```html ``` ```css .gradient-button { position: relative; overflow: hidden; } .gradient-button::before { content: ""; position: absolute; inset: 0; /* gradient */ } .gradient-button span { position: relative; } /* paints above ::before */ ``` The same fix applies whenever a decorative pseudo-element covers text: position the text, or give the pseudo-element `z-index: -1` inside a parent that creates a stacking context. --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/mouse-cursor-gradient-tracking.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: A nav link's hover background is an `::before` with `z-index: -1`. Why does the link itself need `position: relative; z-index: 0`?

back:
One solution:

```css
transform: scale(0);
```

`scale(0)` shrinks the background to nothing around its center; the hover and focus rules transition it to `scale(1)`. Because the transition sits on the base rule, it also animates back when hover or focus ends.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Perfect nested border radius in CSS — The formula

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The border radius of the outer element should be equal to the sum of the border radius of the inner element and the distance between the two elements. This can be mathematically expressed as `innerRadius + distance = outerRadius` or more tersely `R1 + D = R2`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/nested-border-radius.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Nested rounded corners look uneven: the inner box's corners seem too round or too sharp. What formula relates the outer radius, inner radius, and the gap between them?
back:
outer radius = inner radius + gap, where the gap is the space between the two edges (usually the outer element's padding, plus its border width). Equivalently, inner = outer − gap. If both elements use the same radius, the curves aren't concentric and the gap looks thicker at the corners.

```css
.outer { border-radius: 24px; padding: 8px; }
.inner { border-radius: 16px; }   /* 24 − 8 */
```

If the inner radius comes out ≤ 0, use `0` (a square inner corner).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/nested-border-radius.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

```

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

The perfect duration for CSS transitions

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
We have all experienced a website interaction that feels sluggish or otherwise off on account of poor transition or animation duration and timing. However, there is a very simple "golden rule" to help you avoid this poor user experience, called **Doherty Threshold:**

> Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace (<400ms) that ensures that neither has to wait on the other.

The **magic number** of `0.4s` sounds like a very reasonable threshold, but take a look at any of your favorite websites and you'll notice that most `transition-duration` or `animation-duration` values are closer to `0.3s`. This might have something to do with our more recent expectation of what a fast interaction should feel like - after all the relevant research paper was published in 1982.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/perfect-transition-duration.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

What are CSS pseudo-classes? — Commonly used pseudo-classes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Below is a list of the top 5 most commonly used pseudo-classes and their usage. This list is by no means complete. You should always refer to relevant documentation from authoritative sources, such as [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Pseudo-classes) for more information.

- `:hover`, `:focus` and `:active` are used to provide feedback for user interaction (e.g. changing a button's color on hover)
- `:link` and `:visited` are useful for styling links based on navigation history (e.g. changing the color of visited links)
- `:first-child`, `:last-child`, `:nth-child()` and `:nth-last-child()` are useful when working with collections of elements
- `:not()` is used to match everything except the given selector and can be useful in styling hard to select elements
- `:lang()` allows you to apply special styles based on the language of the document and is useful for multilingual websites

**Explain the approach**

How can I create a custom responsive favicon for dark mode?

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How can a single SVG favicon switch colors when the user's system is in dark mode, and how do you link it with a PNG fallback?
back:
Put a `<style>` block inside the SVG with a `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` rule that changes the stroke or fill. The browser evaluates the media query inside the SVG, so the icon recolors itself. Link it with `type="image/svg+xml"`, next to a PNG or ICO fallback for browsers that don't support SVG favicons.

```html
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 24 24">
  <style>
    #icon { stroke: #000; stroke-width: 2; fill: none; }
    @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
      #icon { stroke: #fff; }
    }
  </style>
  <g id="icon"><path d="M6 2L3 6v14a2 2 0 0 0 2 2h14a2 2 0 0 0 2-2V6l-3-4z" /></g>
</svg>
```

```html
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.png" sizes="32x32" type="image/png">
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
```

Use one or two colors and a simple shape so the icon stays recognizable at 16px. The media query follows the OS/browser color scheme, not your site's own theme toggle.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/responsive-favicon-dark-mode.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```css
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
```

Media queries work inside an SVG's own `<style>`, so the favicon adapts by itself. Link it with `<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">`.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

What's the difference between :root and html in CSS? — Selector specificity

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: If a stylesheet sets `:root { background: red; }` and later `html { background: blue; }`, which color wins on an HTML page, and why?
back:
Red. `:root` is a pseudo-class, specificity (0,1,0), while `html` is a type selector, specificity (0,0,1). Both match the same element, and the higher specificity wins even though the `html` rule comes later.

```css
:root { background-color: red; }   /* 0,1,0 → wins */
html  { background-color: blue; }  /* 0,0,1 */
```

This is one reason global custom properties are conventionally declared on `:root`: they are hard to override by accident with a plain `html` rule.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/root-vs-html.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

What's the difference between :root and html in CSS? — Targeting the root element

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
CSS can be used to style other types of documents, apart from HTML. This is where the `:root` element comes in to play, allowing you to style the root element of a document. This can be especially important when styling SVG documents, where the `html` selector will not work.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/root-vs-html.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: `:root` and `html` select the same element in an HTML page, so why does `:root` exist at all?
back:
`:root` matches the root element of whatever document the CSS is applied to, not just HTML. In an SVG file (e.g. a standalone icon with its own `<style>`) or an XML document, the root element is `<svg>` or something else, so an `html` selector would match nothing, while `:root` still works.

```css
/* Works in HTML and in a standalone SVG's <style> */
:root { --icon-color: #333; }
```

In an HTML page they select the same `<html>` element; `:root` just has higher specificity (0,1,0 vs 0,0,1).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/root-vs-html.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Horizontal or vertical scroll snap in CSS — Scrollable containers that snap

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: What does `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory` do on a scroll container, and how does `mandatory` differ from `proximity`?
back:
It turns the element into a snap container on the horizontal axis. After the user scrolls, the browser settles at a snap point defined by the children's `scroll-snap-align`. With `mandatory`, it always comes to rest on a snap point. With `proximity`, the default if you give only an axis, it snaps only when it stops close to one.

```css
.carousel {
  overflow-x: auto;              /* must actually scroll */
  scroll-snap-type: x mandatory; /* x | y | both | inline | block */
}
.carousel > .slide { scroll-snap-align: start; }
```

Use `mandatory` for one-item-at-a-time carousels. Use `proximity` for long lists where users must be able to stop anywhere. With `mandatory`, items taller than the container are awkward: browsers let you scroll inside them, but snapping keeps pulling back. Nothing snaps unless the children have a `scroll-snap-align`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/scroll-snap.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Squiggle link hover effect — The SVG image

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How can an SVG used as a CSS `background-image` animate itself, as in an animated "squiggle" link underline?
back:
Put a `<style>` block with `@keyframes` inside the SVG itself. An SVG loaded as an image runs its own internal CSS animations, even though you can't script it or style it from the page. The squiggle is a wavy path longer than the viewBox, moved sideways by exactly one wave period (20 units) in an endless loop so the wave appears to flow without a jump.

```html
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 20 4">
  <style>
    .squiggle { animation: shift 0.3s linear infinite; }
    @keyframes shift { to { transform: translateX(-20px); } }
  </style>
  <path class="squiggle" fill="none" stroke="#0087ca" stroke-width="2"
    d="M0,3.5 c 5,0,5,-3,10,-3 s 5,3,10,3 c 5,0,5,-3,10,-3 s 5,3,10,3" />
</svg>
```

The page can't change colors inside an image SVG (no `currentColor`, no page CSS), so bake the color in or use `mask-image` instead. An endlessly moving underline is distracting; drop it under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/squiggle-link-hover-effect.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

One solution:

```css
animation: shift .3s linear infinite;
```

`linear` keeps the speed constant and `infinite` repeats forever. The loop is seamless because the shift (20px) equals one wave period of the path. The animation runs even when the SVG is used as a CSS `background-image`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/squiggle-link-hover-effect.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

Define a system font stack in CSS — Using a custom system font stack

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you want to **support older browsers** or are reluctant to use `system-ui`, you can simply build your own system font stack. In order to do so, you'll have to include the system fonts for all **major operating systems**, as well as a fallback. Here's a quick rundown of the most common system fonts: - `-apple-system` is San Francisco, used on iOS and macOS (not Chrome however). - `BlinkMacSystemFont` is San Francisco, used on macOS Chrome. - `'Segoe UI'` is used on Windows 10. - `Roboto` is used on Android. - `Oxygen-Sans` is used on Linux with KDE. - `Ubuntu` is used on Ubuntu (all variants). - `Cantarell` is used on Linux with GNOME Shell. - `'Helvetica Neue'` and `Helvetica` is used on macOS 10.10 and below. - `Arial` is a font widely supported by all operating systems. - `sans-serif` is the fallback sans serif font if none of the other fonts are supported. ```html

This text uses the system font.

``` ```css .system-font-stack { font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Oxygen-Sans, Ubuntu, Cantarell, 'Helvetica Neue', Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif; } ``` --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/system-font-stack.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What problem does a hand-written system font stack like `-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, …` solve, and why is it mostly unnecessary now?

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Define a system font stack in CSS — Using `system-ui`

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
<baseline-support featureId="font-family-system">
</baseline-support>

`system-ui` is a recently introduced generic font family that uses the **system's default UI font**. It's a great way to get a native feel across all operating systems and its browser support is quite impressive. Using `system-ui` with a **fallback** to `sans-serif` is the recommended way to define a system font stack.

```css
.system-font-stack {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Technically speaking, `system-ui` is still in **working draft status** and not yet a standard. However, it's already supported by all major browsers and doesn't seem like it's going anywhere.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/system-font-stack.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Are text-align and align-items the same when it comes to text alignment in CSS? — `text-align: center`

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: What exactly does `text-align: center` center, and why doesn't it center a fixed-width `<div>` inside its parent?
back:
`text-align` centers the inline content (text, inline elements, inline-block children) on each line inside the block that has the property. It doesn't move block-level children. A `<div>` with `width: 300px` stays on the left; center it with `margin-inline: auto`, or with flex/grid on the parent.

```css
p { text-align: center; }          /* centers each line of text */

.box {
  width: 300px;
  margin-inline: auto;             /* centers the block itself */
}
```

`text-align` is inherited, so setting it on a parent centers text in all its descendants unless they override it. Prefer `start`/`end` over `left`/`right` for right-to-left support.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/text-centering-line-block.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

Text truncation, using CSS — Truncate single line text

front: Which three declarations truncate a single line of text with an ellipsis ("…"), and why does it often fail inside a flex row?

back:
One solution:

```css
text-overflow: ellipsis;
```

`text-overflow` only takes effect when the text actually overflows a box with `overflow` other than `visible` and doesn't wrap. Inside a flex row, the item also needs `min-width: 0`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/text-truncation.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Text truncation, using CSS — Truncate multi line text

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
<baseline-support featureId="line-clamp">
</baseline-support>

For **multi-line text**, you'll still need to use `overflow: hidden` to **prevent the text from overflowing** its container. However, you can't use `text-overflow: ellipsis` to add an ellipsis at the end of the text.

Instead, you can use the `-webkit-line-clamp` property to **limit the number of lines** displayed. This property accepts an **integer value** that specifies the maximum number of lines to be displayed. You'll also need to use `display: -webkit-box` and `-webkit-box-orient: vertical` to ensure that `-webkit-line-clamp` is applied correctly.

> [!NOTE]
>
> At the time of writing, `-webkit-line-clamp` is still a **working draft**, but is supported across most modern browsers. Always check the [current browser support](https://caniuse.com/css-line-clamp) beforehand.

```css
.truncate-text-multiline {
  display: -webkit-box;
  -webkit-line-clamp: 3;
  -webkit-box-orient: vertical;
  overflow: hidden;
}
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/text-truncation.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you clamp a paragraph to 3 lines with an ellipsis at the end, e.g. for product descriptions in a card grid?

back:
One solution:

```css
-webkit-line-clamp: 3;
```

`-webkit-line-clamp` sets the number of visible lines. It only works together with `display: -webkit-box` and `-webkit-box-orient: vertical`, and it needs `overflow: hidden` to hide the rest. It works in all modern browsers despite the prefix.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/text-truncation.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

CSS units Cheat Sheet

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
- `px`: Absolute pixel value
- `rem`: Relative to the `font-size` of the root element
- `em`: Relative to the `font-size` of the element
- `%`: Relative to the parent element
- `vw`: Relative to the viewport's width, `1vw` = `1%` * viewport width
- `vh`: Relative to the viewport's height, `1vh` = `1%` * viewport height
- `vmin`: Relative to the viewport's smaller dimension, `1vmin` = min(`1vh`, `1vw`)
- `vmax`: Relative to the viewport's larger dimension, `vmax` = max(`1vh`, `1vw`)
- `ch`: Relative to the width of the glyph "0" of the element's font
- `in`: Inches `1in` = `2.54cm` = `96px`
- `pc`: Picas `1pc` = `1in` / `6` = `16px`
- `pt`: Points `1pt` = `1in` / `72` = `1.333px` (approximately)
- `cm`: Centimeters `1cm` = `96px` / `2.54` = `37.8px` (approximately)
- `mm`: Millimeters `1mm` = `1cm` / `10` = `3.78px` (approximately)

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/units-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What are the common CSS length units relative to (`px`, `rem`, `em`, `%`, `vw`/`vh`/`dvh`, `ch`), and which should you use for font sizes?
back:
`px`: a fixed CSS pixel. `rem`: the root (`html`) font size. `em`: the current element's font size (in `font-size` itself, the parent's). `%`: depends on the property: widths and padding use the containing block's width, `font-size` uses the parent's font size, `translate()` uses the element's own size. `vw`/`vh`: 1% of the viewport width/height; `dvh` accounts for mobile browser bars. `ch`: the width of the "0" glyph.

```css
html { font-size: 100%; }          /* respect the user's setting (usually 16px) */
body { font-size: 1rem; }
.prose { max-width: 65ch; }        /* readable line length */
.hero { min-height: 100dvh; }
.button { padding: 0.5em 1em; }    /* scales with the button's text */
```

Use `rem` for font sizes so text follows the user's browser font setting. `em` suits spacing that should scale with the element's own text. Container query units (`cqi`, `cqb`) are sized by a container instead of the viewport. Physical units (`in`, `cm`, `pt`) are mainly for print; `1in` = 96px.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/css/s/units-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

**Explain the approach**

8 tips for accessible websites — Design responsively

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Responsiveness is often thought in terms of screen size or mobile vs desktop, but there are many different devices where a user could browse your website. Try catering to any and all of them by providing ways to navigate and use your application via mouse, keyboard, thumb or any combination of the three.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/8-tips-for-accessible-websites.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: In accessibility terms, what does "design responsively" mean beyond adapting to screen size?
back:
Support every way people use the page: mouse, keyboard only, touch, screen readers, and zoom. Everything must work and stay usable at each.

- **Keyboard**: every control reachable with Tab and operable with Enter/Space, with a visible focus ring.
- **Touch**: tap targets big enough (WCAG 2.2 asks for at least 24×24 CSS px; about 44×44 is a comfortable goal).
- **Zoom/reflow**: content still works at 200% text size and at 320 px wide without horizontal scrolling.
- **No hover-only features**: a tooltip or menu that opens only on hover is unreachable on touch and for many keyboard users.

Quick test: unplug the mouse and complete your app's main CRUD flow (create, edit, delete) with the keyboard alone.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/8-tips-for-accessible-websites.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

8 tips for accessible websites — Use color correctly

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
[WCAG](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) specifies a minimum contrast ratio of `4.5:1` between text and background (viewable in Chrome Developer Tools), so you should always design with that in mind. Additionally, remember that color should be used meaningfully and sparsely to avoid confusion and information overload.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/8-tips-for-accessible-websites.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What minimum color contrast ratios does WCAG (level AA) require for text and UI controls?
back:
**4.5:1** for normal body text; **3:1** for large text (about 24 px regular or 18.66 px bold and up) and for UI components and meaningful graphics (input borders, icons, focus rings). Level AAA raises text to 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text).

Check it with the contrast info in the browser DevTools color picker or Lighthouse. Common failures are light-grey placeholder text, disabled-looking but active buttons, and pale input borders. Also use color sparingly and consistently (e.g. red always means error), so it carries meaning instead of noise.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/8-tips-for-accessible-websites.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:

However, icons and colors alone might not be accessible for everyone, so make sure to support them with the appropriate text literals, catering to all of your users in the process.

front: Why must a form error or status never be shown by color or an icon alone, and how do you fix it?
back:
Color-blind users, screen-reader users and people in bright sunlight can miss a red border or an icon, and WCAG forbids color as the only means of conveying information. Pair it with text, and give icon-only buttons an accessible name. ```html

⚠ Enter a valid email address

``` `aria-describedby` makes screen readers read the error text along with the field. `aria-invalid` announces the invalid state. --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/8-tips-for-accessible-websites.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

8 tips for accessible websites — Label your inputs

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Any kind of `<input>` element should be labelled appropriately, using either a `<label>` wrapper, the `for` attribute or an `aria-label` attribute. Do not rely on `placeholder` attributes to convey meaning about your `<input>` elements as this will cause problems for users on screenreaders.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/8-tips-for-accessible-websites.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How should you label a form `<input>` so it's accessible, and why isn't `placeholder` enough?
back:
Give every input a visible `<label>`: either linked with `for`/`id` or wrapping the input. Use `aria-label` only when a visible label truly isn't possible (e.g. a search box beside a search icon).

```html
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">

<label>Quantity <input type="number" name="qty"></label>
```

A `placeholder` disappears as soon as the user types, is often low-contrast, and isn't reliably announced as a label. A real `<label>` also makes clicking the text focus the input, which gives a bigger tap target on phones.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/8-tips-for-accessible-websites.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Recommended HTML head icon tags

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Over the years, I've seen many different and often conflicting guidelines about favicons and which tags are essential. Nowadays, I think you can get away with a very **minimal set of meta tags** and tailor them to your needs as you go. Here's my recommendation for the bare minimum you should include in your `<head>` element:

```html
<head>
  <link rel="icon" sizes="192x192" href="favicon.png">
  <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="favicon.png">
  <link rel="mask-icon" href="favicon.svg" color="#000000">
</head>
```

By creating a single 192x192 PNG asset, you can cover almost all modern devices and browsers, without too much hassle. If you want to go the extra mile, you can include a few more quite easily. Simply downscale the image and include more `rel="icon"` meta tags with different `sizes` attributes.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/head-icons.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What's a sensible minimal set of favicon/icon tags for a modern site's `<head>`?
back:
An ICO fallback, an SVG icon, an Apple touch icon, and a web app manifest (which lists 192 px and 512 px PNGs for Android/installed apps).

```html
<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="32x32">
<link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png"><!-- 180×180 -->
<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.webmanifest">
```

The SVG can adapt to dark mode with an internal `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` rule. `rel="mask-icon"` (Safari pinned tabs) is obsolete: current Safari uses the regular icons. Without any icon tag, browsers still request `/favicon.ico`, so a 404 appears in your logs if it's missing.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/head-icons.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Recommended HTML head links

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The `<head>` element of an HTML document is where you can include links to external resources such as CSS stylesheets and JavaScript files. Some `<link>` elements, however, are important for SEO and metadata purposes. Here's a list of a few really important ones I like to include:

```html
<head>
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://samplesite.com/page.html">
  <link rel="sitemap" type="application/xml" href="https://samplesite.com/sitemap.xml">
  <link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml" title="RSS" href="https://samplesite.com/rss.xml">
  <link rel="search" type="application/opensearchdescription+xml" title="Search" href="https://samplesite.com/search.xml">
</head>
```

- The `canonical` link element tells search engines which URL is the **canonical version** of the page. This helps prevent duplicate content issues and ensures that the correct page is indexed.
- The `sitemap` link element tells search engines where to find the **sitemap** for the website. Sitemaps are XML files that contain a list of all the pages on the website and their metadata. They are used by search engines to index the website and display it in search results.
- The `alternate` link element tells search engines where to find the **RSS feed** for the website. RSS feeds are XML files that contain a list of the most recent posts on the website. They are used by search engines to display the website's content in search results, as well as by RSS readers to display the website's content in a more convenient format.
- The `search` link element is used by browsers to display a **search box** in the browser's address bar. This allows users to search the website directly from the address bar, instead of having to navigate to the search page.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/head-links.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What do `<link rel="canonical">` and `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml">` tell search engines and browsers?
back:
`canonical` names the preferred URL for a page that's reachable at several URLs (e.g. with `?sort=` or tracking params), so search engines consolidate them. It's a strong hint, not a command. `alternate` with an RSS/Atom type advertises the site's feed, so feed readers and browser extensions can discover it.

```html
<link rel="canonical" href="https://shop.example.com/products/42">
<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml" title="Blog" href="/rss.xml">
<link rel="search" type="application/opensearchdescription+xml" title="Shop" href="/opensearch.xml">
```

`rel="search"` points to an OpenSearch file that some browsers use to offer your site as a search engine. There's no standard `rel="sitemap"`: search engines find sitemaps through a `Sitemap:` line in `robots.txt` or by submitting them in their webmaster tools.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/head-links.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

What is the purpose of the alt attribute on images? — What if the image is purely decorative?

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back: If an image is **purely decorative**, then it is best to leave the `alt` attribute **empty**. This will tell screen readers to skip over the image. ```html ``` Notice in this example that we still included the `alt` attribute, but we left it empty. This is different from not including the `alt` attribute at all. If you don't include the `alt` attribute, then screen readers will read the image's file name instead. --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/image-alt.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What's the difference between `` and an `` with no `alt` attribute at all?
back: `alt=""` explicitly marks the image as decorative, so screen readers skip it. With no `alt` at all, the image is treated as missing its description, and many screen readers announce the file name instead (e.g. "IMG_4821.jpg"). ```html ``` Use `alt=""` for purely visual flourishes, or for images whose meaning is already in nearby text (e.g. an avatar next to the user's name). Purely decorative images can also be CSS backgrounds. Validators and Lighthouse flag missing `alt`, not empty `alt`. --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/image-alt.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

What is the purpose of the alt attribute on images? — How to write good alt text

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back: The `alt` attribute should be used to describe the image in a way that makes sense to **someone who cannot see it**. Descriptions must be accurate and concise. Some screen readers are known to cut off descriptions after **125 characters**, so it is best to keep descriptions short. Let's look at an example. Imagine that you want to describe an image of a boat sailing on the ocean. You could use the following `alt` attribute: ```html ``` In this example, we've tried to describe the image as if we were describing to someone over the phone. Notice how we didn't use the word "picture" or "image" in the description. Additionally, we didn't simply say "boat" because that doesn't provide enough context. --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/image-alt.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you write good alt text for an informative image, e.g. a product photo or a chart?
back: Describe what the image *communicates in its context*, concisely, as you would to someone over the phone. Don't start with "image of" or "picture of", since screen readers already say it's an image. ```html ``` Keep it short (around 125 characters is a common guideline). For complex charts, put the full data in a nearby table or caption. For an image used as a link or button, describe the *action or destination*, not the picture. The same image may need different alt text on different pages. --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/image-alt.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Display the right type of keyboard for form inputs

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
A common issue with form inputs on **mobile devices** is that the wrong keyboard is displayed, making it harder for users to fill out the form. For example, a numeric keyboard should be shown for a phone number input, but a regular keyboard is displayed instead. This can be frustrating for users and can lead to incorrect input.

Luckily, HTML has a **built-in solution** for this, via the [`inputmode`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Global_attributes/inputmode) attribute. This attribute allows you to specify the **type of keyboard** that should be displayed for an input field. Here's how you can use it:

```html
<label>
  Phone number: <input type="tel" inputmode="tel" />
</label>
```

In this example, the `inputmode="tel"` attribute tells the browser to display a telephone keypad for the input field, making it easier for users to enter a phone number. Here's **all the possible values** for the `inputmode` attribute:

- `none`: No virtual keyboard is shown.
- `text`: A regular keyboard is shown.
- `url`: A URL keyboard is shown (includes keys like <kbd>.com</kbd> and <kbd>/</kbd>).
- `email`: An email keyboard is shown (includes keys like <kbd>@</kbd> and <kbd>.</kbd>).
- `tel`: A telephone keypad is shown.
- `search`: A search keyboard is shown (includes a <kbd>Go</kbd> button).
- `numeric`: A numeric keyboard is shown.
- `decimal`: A numeric keyboard with a decimal point is shown.

> [!WARNING]
>
> The `inputmode` attribute is not a replacement for the [`type`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/input#attr-type) attribute. The former acts as a hint to the browser about the type of keyboard to display, while the latter specifies the type of data expected in the input field.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/keyboard-type-using-inputmode.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you make phones show the right on-screen keyboard for a form field, and how does `inputmode` differ from `type`?
back:
Set `inputmode` to hint the virtual keyboard: `numeric`, `decimal`, `tel`, `email`, `url`, `search`, `text` or `none`. `type` defines the kind of data and its validation. `inputmode` only picks the keyboard, which matters most for `type="text"` fields holding digits.

```html
<label>Verification code
  <input type="text" inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code">
</label>
<label>Price
  <input type="text" inputmode="decimal" name="price">
</label>
<label>Phone <input type="tel" autocomplete="tel"></label>
```

`type="tel"`/`email`/`url` already choose a suitable keyboard, so there `inputmode` is redundant. `enterkeyhint="search"`/`"next"`/`"send"` sets the label on the Enter key. `inputmode` doesn't validate anything, so still validate the value.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/keyboard-type-using-inputmode.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Lazy load images in HTML

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back: In today's digital landscape, images play a pivotal role in capturing users' attention and conveying information. However, their impact on a webpage's **load time** can be significant, leading to suboptimal user experiences and lower search engine rankings. This makes **image optimization** a crucial part of any website's performance optimization strategy. The most common technique for optimizing images is that of **lazy loading**. This usually comes in the form of delaying loading images outside the initial viewport until they are close to being scrolled into view. By deferring the loading of images until they're about to be needed, lazy loading optimizes page performance and ensures a seamless browsing experience. Fortunately, the HTML standard already includes a built-in solution to effortlessly achieve lazy loading, the `loading` attribute. By simply adding `loading="lazy"` to the desired images, you unlock the power of lazy loading and allow browsers to optimize resource allocation and loading priorities. ```html ``` > [!NOTE] > > At the time of writing, the `loading` attribute is supported in most modern browsers, except for Safari, but not in legacy browsers, such as IE. On that note, lazy loading can be seen as a progressive enhancement for browsers that support it, so it's still worth adding for any users that can benefit from it. --- Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/lazy-loading-images.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

A user-friendly setup for number-only inputs with plain HTML

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Number-only inputs aren't as straightforward as you might expect. Most people would instinctively reach for the `type="number"` attribute, but it might not be enough. Sure, it shows a numeric keyboard on mobile, but allows users to enter non-numeric characters. Plus, the up and down arrows on desktop are not particularly useful for entering, say, a PIN code or a credit card number.

Instead, we can use `inputmode="numeric"`. This ensures that the **mobile keyboard is numeric-only**, not even including some symbols that were available. We should also add `pattern="[0-9]+"` to **constrain the input value**. And, as far as the `type` attribute is concerned, that's up to you. Either `type="text"` or `type="number"` will work just fine.

```html
<label>
  PIN code
  <input type="text" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]+"" />
</label>
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
>
> Most browsers don't bother validating that the input is numeric-only, even for `type="number"`. This, in combination with numeric inputs often accepting scientific notation (e.g. `1e3`), means that you'll need to write some validation logic yourself.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/number-only-input.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: For a digits-only field like a PIN or ZIP code, why use `type="text" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]+"` instead of `type="number"`?
back:
`type="number"` is for quantities, not digit strings. It drops leading zeros (`0123` becomes 123 as a number), shows spinner arrows, accepts `e`, `+`, `-` and `.`, and **ignores `pattern`**. A text input with `inputmode="numeric"` gets a digit keypad, keeps the exact string, and `pattern` validates it.

```html
<label>
  PIN code
  <input type="text" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]{4,6}"
         autocomplete="one-time-code" required>
</label>
```

`pattern` is matched against the whole value (it's implicitly anchored with `^...$`) and is checked on form submit (`:invalid` in CSS). Client-side validation is a UX nicety: validate again on the server.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/number-only-input.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

Simply adding a line to the `` of your HTML document will do the trick. ```html Example ``` > [!WARNING] > > There are some **security risks** involved with opening links in a new tab. back: It sets the default `target` for every link and form in the document, so all of them open in a new tab unless they set their own `target`. (`` similarly changes how every relative URL resolves.) ```html Opens in a new tab Also opens a new tab! ``` The catch is that it hits *everything*, including in-page `#anchor` links, internal navigation and form submissions. Unexpected new tabs also confuse screen-reader and keyboard users. previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Add autocomplete to an HTML password field

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The HTML `autocomplete` attribute provides a wide variety of options for `<input>` fields. One of these is the `new-password` value, which can be used when the user is asked to create a new password (e.g. signup or reset password forms). This value ensures that the browser will not accidentally fill in an existing password, while it also allows the browser to suggest a secure password:

```html
<form action="signup" method="post">
  <input type="text" autocomplete="username">
  <input type="password" autocomplete="new-password">
  <input type="submit" value="Sign up">
</form>
```

Additionally, if the form contains a second password field asking the user to retype the newly created password, `autocomplete="new-password"` should be used for both of the password fields.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/password-autocomplete-suggestion.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Which `autocomplete` values should a sign-up form's username and password fields use, and how does that differ from a login form?
back:
Sign-up/reset: `autocomplete="username"` plus `autocomplete="new-password"` on the password field (and on its "confirm password" field). Login: `autocomplete="current-password"`. `new-password` stops the browser filling in an existing password and lets it suggest a strong one; `current-password` tells password managers to fill the saved one.

```html
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <input name="email" type="email" autocomplete="username">
  <input name="password" type="password" autocomplete="new-password">
  <input name="confirm" type="password" autocomplete="new-password">
  <button>Sign up</button>
</form>
```

Avoid `autocomplete="off"` on password fields: browsers largely ignore it there, and it just makes password managers less helpful.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/password-autocomplete-suggestion.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Prefetching resources in the browser

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Resource prefetching is a great technique to improve perceived page speed on your website and provide a better user experience, without a lot of effort. Prefetching happens in the browser as soon as it is idle, meaning it will not slow down the initial load, but rather utilize idle time to fetch and cache resources that might be useful later on.

To prefetch a resource, you can add a `<link>` tag with the `rel="prefetch"` attribute inside your document's `<head>` or `<body>`:

```html
<link rel="prefetch" href="./cool_page/data.json">
```

What this does is hint the browser that we will need this resource, so it should download it when idle and store it in the cache. Bear in mind that prefetching is more of a hint rather to the browser than anything else, so there are situations where the browser might ignore it (due to other browser downloads, user settings, connection issues etc.).

Prefetching resources can increase the perceived load time of a page or resource that is often requested, while also providing major performance benefits for resources such as webfonts, as they will download after the browser downloads, parses and styles the DOM. Currently resource prefetching only supports `http://` and `https://` links, however the same-origin restriction does not apply to resource prefetching, so you can download external resources if necessary.

Similarly, you can preload assets using the `rel="preload"` attribute, which are not hints but rather directions that the browser must follow:

```html
<link rel="preload" href="./important_page/data.json">
```

The only downside to preloading resources compared to prefetching is that [browser support](https://caniuse.com/#search=preload) might be low depending on when you are reading this.

[Further reading](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/html/s/speculation-rules-api-first-look)

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/prefetching-resources.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What's the difference between `<link rel="prefetch">` and `<link rel="preload">`, and when would you use each?
back:
`preload` is a high-priority fetch of something **this page** will definitely need soon (e.g. a font or hero image found late by the parser). `prefetch` is a low-priority, idle-time hint for something a **future navigation** will probably need. The browser may ignore it.

```html
<!-- this page: must include `as` (plus crossorigin for fonts/fetch) -->
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
<!-- next page, probably -->
<link rel="prefetch" href="/checkout/data.json">
```

Pitfalls: `preload` without a correct `as` value gets the wrong priority and is fetched twice or not reused. Preloading something unused wastes bandwidth, and Chrome warns about it in the console. `preload` works in all modern browsers; Safari still doesn't act on `prefetch` (harmless, since it's only a hint). For whole pages, Chromium's Speculation Rules API is the newer tool.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/prefetching-resources.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Recommended minimum HTML head

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
An essential part of an HTML document is the `<head>` element, which contains metadata about the document. Some vital information, such as the document's title and character encoding are stored in the `<head>` element. It's also where you can include links to external resources such as CSS stylesheets and JavaScript files.

More often than not, this sort of metadata can grow in complexity with time. However, there are a few important things that should never be omitted. Here's a list of the bare minimum you should include in your `<head>` element:

```html
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Page Title</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Page description. No longer than 155 characters.">
</head>
```

- The `charset` meta tag tells the browser what **character encoding** to use when rendering the document.
- The `viewport` meta tag tells the browser how to render the page on **mobile devices**.
- The `title` element is used by search engines to display the page's **title** in search results.
- The `description` meta tag is used by search engines to display a **short description** of the page in search results.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/recommended-minimum-head.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Which tags belong in every HTML page's minimal `<head>`, and what does each do?
back:
`<meta charset="utf-8">`, the responsive viewport meta, a `<title>`, and a meta description, plus `<!doctype html>` and `<html lang="...">` around them.

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Orders – Acme Admin</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Search, filter and export your orders.">
</head>
```

- `charset`: text decoding. It must appear in the first 1024 bytes, so put it first.
- `viewport`: without it, phones render a ~980 px desktop layout zoomed out.
- `title`: the tab label, bookmark name, search result title, and the first thing screen readers announce.
- `description`: often shown as the search snippet (keep it around 155 characters).
- `lang`: correct screen-reader pronunciation and translation.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/recommended-minimum-head.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Resource Preloading Cheat Sheet

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Preloading content is one of many ways to improve web performance. The `rel` attribute of the `link` element can be used to instruct the browser how to handle different resources. Here's a handy cheatsheet to help you remember the different values and their effects.

- `rel="preload"`: Download the resource as soon as possible. Used when you're going to need a resource in a few seconds, on the same page.
- `rel="prefetch"`: Suggest that the resource is fetched in advance. Used when you're going to need a resource for the next page.
- `rel="preconnect"`: Establish a connection to the linked website, to speed up fetching resources from it later. Used when you're going to need a resource, but you don't know its full URL yet.
- `rel="dns-prefetch"`: Resolve the DNS for the linked website, to speed up fetching resources from it later. Used when you're going to need a resource, but you don't know its full URL yet (mainly for older browsers).
- `rel="prerender"`: Preload the resource and render it in the background, speeding up page load in the future. Used when users are likely to navigate to a specific page.
- `rel="modulepreload"`: Preload a JavaScript module script. Used when you're going to need an ES module script soon.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/resource-preloading-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Which `<link rel>` resource hint fits each case: a font this page needs, a page the user will likely open next, a third-party API origin you'll call soon, and an ES module needed shortly?
back:
- Font for this page → `rel="preload"` (with `as="font" crossorigin`): fetch now, high priority.
- Likely next page's assets → `rel="prefetch"`: low-priority idle fetch for a future navigation.
- Third-party origin → `rel="preconnect"`: do DNS + TCP + TLS early, when you know the origin but not the exact URL. `rel="dns-prefetch"` is the cheaper DNS-only fallback.
- ES module → `rel="modulepreload"`: fetch and parse a module (and it can be reused by `import`).

```html
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://api.payments.example" crossorigin>
<link rel="modulepreload" href="/js/editor.mjs">
```

`rel="prerender"` is obsolete: prerendering whole pages is now done with the Speculation Rules API (Chromium). Keep hints few: each one costs bandwidth or sockets.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/resource-preloading-cheatsheet.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

A first look at the Speculation Rules API — The Speculation Rules API

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
<baseline-support featureId="speculation-rules">
</baseline-support>

Prefetching individual links, however, is often tedious, even without the hassle of deciding which links needs prefetching. This is where the currently experimental [**Speculation Rules API**](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Speculation_Rules_API) comes in.

> [!WARNING]
>
> This API is, as stated, **currently experimental**. This means it's very likely to change before it becomes stable and any **information provided here may become outdated**. Always refer to the official documentation for more information.
>
> At the time of writing, the [Chrome team's blog post on the topic](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/prerender-pages#impact_on_extensions) is the source of most of the information presented in this article.

What this API does is pretty straightforward. Instead of prefetching individual links, it allows developers to **define rules for when and how resources should be prefetched**, making the process more efficient and adaptive to the user's behavior.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/speculation-rules-api-first-look.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does the Speculation Rules API add over individual `<link rel="prefetch">` tags, and which browsers support it?
back:
It lets you declare *rules* in a JSON `<script type="speculationrules">` block: which URLs or link patterns may be prefetched or prerendered, and how eagerly. The browser then speculates based on user behaviour (hover, pointer down), instead of you hand-picking URLs.

```html
<script type="speculationrules">
{
  "prefetch": [{
    "where": { "href_matches": "/products/*" },
    "eagerness": "moderate"
  }]
}
</script>
```

Support is Chromium-first (Chrome, Edge, Opera); other engines have lagged, so check caniuse. Browsers without support ignore the script type, so it's a safe progressive enhancement. Prerendering is limited to same-origin pages by default, and speculations are listed in DevTools' Application panel under Speculative loads.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/speculation-rules-api-first-look.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

A first look at the Speculation Rules API — Rules and patterns

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
<baseline-support featureId="urlpattern">
</baseline-support>

As we've already seen, you can use the [URL Pattern API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URL_Pattern_API) to match **specific URL patterns** in your speculation rules. This API is quite extensive and can help you create more sophisticated matching logic.

```html
<script type="speculationrules">
{
  "prefetch": [{
    "where": {
      "and": [
        { "href_matches": "/*" },
        { "not": {"href_matches": "/wp-admin"}},
        { "not": {"href_matches": "/*\\?*(^|&)add-to-cart=*"}},
        { "not": {"selector_matches": "[rel~=nofollow]"}}
      ]
    }
  }]
}
</script>
```

In this example, we are using a combination of `"href_matches"` and `"not"` conditions, wrapped in an `"and"` condition to create a set of rules for when to prefetch a page. The rules specify that any local page should be considered for prefetching, except for the ones **explicitly excluded**.

Apart from rules, you can also specify **exact URL matches** for prefetching:

```html
<script type="speculationrules">
{
  "prefetch": [
    {
      "urls": ["/home", "/about", "/contact"]
    }
  ]
}
</script>
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/html/s/speculation-rules-api-first-look.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: In a Speculation Rules "document rule", how do you prefetch all same-site links except ones that must not be fetched early (like logout or add-to-cart links)?

back:
One solution:

```html
      { "not": { "href_matches": "/logout" } },
```

`"not"` wraps any condition to exclude matches. `href_matches` uses URL Pattern syntax, and `selector_matches` uses CSS selectors. Prefetching is a real GET request, so any link whose GET has side effects (logout, add-to-cart, delete) must be excluded, or better, changed to a POST.
