However, there are cases where you might want to **disable fast-forward merging** by default. For example, you might want to **preserve the history** of the branches you're merging, or you might want to **enforce a merge commit** to capture the merge operation.

In order to disable the default fast-forward merging behavior in Git, you can use the `merge.ff` configuration option. By using `git config --add merge.ff false`, you can disable fast-forward merging for all branches, even if it is possible. You can also use the `--global` flag to **configure this option globally**.

```shell
# Usage: git config [--global] --add merge.ff false

git config --global --add merge.ff false
# Globally disables fast-forward merging by default

git checkout master
git merge my-branch
# Will never fast forward even if it's possible
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/disable-fast-forward.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front:
Globally stop `git merge` from fast-forwarding, so every merge creates a merge commit.

```shell
____

git switch main
git merge my-branch   # always creates a merge commit now
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git config --global merge.ff false
```

Equivalent to always passing `--no-ff`. It also applies to the merge inside `git pull`, so pair it with `git config --global pull.ff only` to avoid "Merge branch 'main' of …" commits on every pull.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/disable-fast-forward.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Discard uncommitted or untracked changes in Git — Discard uncommitted changes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you have made changes to your files but haven't committed them yet, you can discard them using the `git reset --hard HEAD` command. This command will **reset your working directory to match the latest commit on the current branch**, discarding all uncommitted changes.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Be careful when using `git reset --hard HEAD`, as it is a **potentially destructive action**. Make sure you don't have any changes you want to keep before running this command.

```shell
# Usage: git reset --hard HEAD

git reset --hard HEAD
# Discards all uncommitted changes
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/discard-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you throw away all uncommitted changes to tracked files and go back to the last commit — and what does that NOT remove?
back:
`git reset --hard HEAD` resets both the staging area and your tracked files to the last commit. The modern equivalent is `git restore --staged --worktree .`. Untracked (never-added) files are left alone; `git clean` removes those.

```shell
git status                 # see what you're about to lose
git reset --hard HEAD      # discard staged + unstaged edits to tracked files

git restore --staged --worktree .   # same effect, newer command
```

Changes that were never committed or stashed can't be recovered afterwards, not even from the reflog. If you're unsure, `git stash` first: it clears the working tree the same way but keeps a copy.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/discard-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Discard uncommitted or untracked changes in Git — Discard untracked changes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Similarly, if you have untracked files in your working directory that you want to discard, you can use the `git clean -f -d` command. This command will **remove all untracked files and directories from your working directory**.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Be careful when using `git clean -f -d`, as it is a **potentially destructive action**. Make sure you don't have any changes you want to keep before running this command.

```shell
# Usage: git clean -f -d

git clean -f -d
# Discards all untracked changes
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/discard-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you delete untracked files and folders (e.g. leftover generated files) from your working tree, and how do you check what will go first?
back:
`git clean -fd` deletes untracked files (`-f`, required as a safety catch) and untracked directories (`-d`). Run it with `-n` first for a dry run that only lists what would be deleted.

```shell
git clean -nd     # Would remove tmp/
                  # Would remove src/debug-notes.txt
git clean -fd     # actually delete them
```

Ignored files (e.g. `node_modules`, `.env`) are kept unless you add `-x`, which is usually not what you want. Deleted untracked files aren't in Git, so they can't be recovered.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/discard-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Edit the Git configuration file

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Using `git config` a dozen times to set up your Git configuration can be a bit tedious. Instead, you can open the **Git configuration file** in the Git text editor and make the changes directly.

> [!TIP]
>
> You may want to [configure Git's default text editor](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/configure-default-text-editor) before using this command, to ensure you're comfortable with the text editor that opens the configuration file.

Using `git config -e`, you can open the Git configuration file in the **default Git text editor**. This allows you to make changes to the configuration file directly, without having to remember the specific commands for each setting.

You can add the `--global` flag to edit the **global Git configuration file**, or omit it to edit the local repository configuration file.

```shell
# Usage: git config [--global] -e

git config --global -e
# Opens the global git configuration file in the default git text editor

git config -e
# Opens the local repository git configuration file in the text editor
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/edit-config.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you open Git's config file in an editor instead of running many `git config` commands, and which file do you get with and without `--global`?
back:
`git config --global --edit` (short: `-e`) opens your user-wide `~/.gitconfig` in Git's editor; without `--global` it opens the current repo's `.git/config`, whose settings override the global ones for that repo.

```shell
git config --global --edit    # ~/.gitconfig: name, email, aliases...
git config --edit             # .git/config of this repo: remotes, branches

git config --list --show-origin   # every setting + the file it came from
```

`--show-origin` is the quickest way to answer "why is Git using this value?".

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/edit-config.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

How does Git's fast-forward mode work? — Non fast-forward merge

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
GitHub, on the other hand, uses non fast-forward merge by default. It will create a merge commit at the tip of the branch you're merging into, optionally referencing the branch being merged in the commit message. This has the advantage of **keeping track of branches** more explicitly than fast-forward merge. If you want to get the same behavior in a Git terminal, you can use the `--no-ff` flag.

As a side note, you can configure the default Git merge behavior, using `git config`. To learn how to do so, you can take a look at the [relevant article](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/disable-fast-forward).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/fast-forward-merge.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does a non-fast-forward merge (`git merge --no-ff`) add to history compared with a fast-forward, and which does GitHub's default "Merge pull request" button do?
back:
It always creates a merge commit with two parents, even when Git could have just moved the branch pointer forward. The branch's commits stay visibly grouped, and the whole feature can be undone by reverting that one merge commit. GitHub's default "Create a merge commit" option behaves like `--no-ff`.

```shell
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature-login
git log --oneline --graph -4
# *   9f2c1ab Merge branch 'feature-login'
# |\
# | * 41d0e2c Add login form
# |/
# * 3050fc0 Previous main commit

git revert -m 1 9f2c1ab   # undo the whole feature
```

A fast-forward leaves no trace that a branch existed. GitHub also offers "Squash and merge" and "Rebase and merge".

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/fast-forward-merge.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Fetch latest Git changes from the remote repository

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Keeping in sync with the latest changes from the remote repository is essential when working with Git. The `git fetch` command allows you to **retrieve the latest changes** from the remote repository without applying them to your local repository. This can be useful when you want to see what changes have been made before merging them into your local branch.

```shell
# Syntax: git fetch

git fetch
# Fetches the latest updates from the remote
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/fetch-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git fetch` change in your repository, and what does it leave alone?
back:
It downloads new commits from the remote and updates your **remote-tracking branches** (`origin/main`, `origin/fix-login`, …). It never touches your local branches or working files, so it's always safe to run.

```shell
git fetch            # or: git fetch --prune (also drop deleted remote branches)
git log --oneline main..origin/main   # commits you don't have yet
git merge origin/main                 # or rebase, when you're ready
```

`git pull` is `git fetch` followed by a merge (or rebase) into your current branch. Fetching first lets you see what's coming before it lands in your code.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/fetch-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Find the Git commit that introduced a bug — Automatically find the commit with a bug

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If all of that seems like too much work, thankfully you can automate the process using `git bisect run`. This command will **run a given script on each subsequent commit** to find which commit introduced the bug.

Apart from that the startup of the process is the same, you need to use `git bisect start` and mark a commit as "good" and another as "bad". After that, you can use `git bisect run <command>` to run the given command on each subsequent commit and wait for the bad commit to be printed.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git bisect start
#  git bisect good <commit>
#  git bisect bad <commit>
#  git bisect run <command>
#  git bisect reset [<commit>]

git bisect start

git bisect good 3050fc0de
git bisect bad c191f90c7

git bisect run npm test # Run `npm test` for each commit

# ... some time later the bad commit will be printed
git bisect reset # Goes to the original branch
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-commit-with-bug.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How can `git bisect run` find the commit that broke your tests automatically, and how must the test command report its result?
back:
Start a bisect, mark one bad and one good commit, then `git bisect run <cmd>`: Git checks out commits in a binary search and runs the command on each. Exit code **0 means good**, **125 means skip** (can't test this commit), and any other code from 1 to 127 means bad.

```shell
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # current commit is broken
git bisect good v1.4.0         # last known-good tag or hash
git bisect run npm test -- src/cart.test.ts
# ... "a1b2c3d is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset               # back to where you started
```

The test must exist in the old commits too; otherwise point `run` at a script stored outside the repo.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-commit-with-bug.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Find the Git commit that introduced a bug — Manually find the commit with a bug

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In order to start the process, you need to use `git bisect start`. You need to first **mark a commit as "good"**, indicating it is known to be bug-free, and **another commit as "bad"**, indicating it has the bug. You can do so using `git bisect good <commit>` and `git bisect bad <commit>`.

Having performed these steps, the binary search algorithm will **stop at each commit** and you'll have to use `git bisect (good | bad)` to mark each commit as "good" or "bad" depending on whether it has the bug or not.

After running through the commits, the algorithm will **print the commit that introduced the bug**. Finally, you can reset to the original branch using `git bisect reset`. You can optionally specify a commit to reset to.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git bisect start
#  git bisect good <commit>
#  git bisect bad <commit>
#  git bisect (good | bad)
#  git bisect reset [<commit>]

git bisect start

git bisect good 3050fc0de
git bisect bad c191f90c7

git bisect good  # Current commit is good
git bisect bad   # Current commit is buggy

# ... some time later the bad commit will be printed
git bisect reset # Goes to the original branch
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-commit-with-bug.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How does `git bisect` help you find the commit that introduced a bug, and what do you do at each step?
back:
It binary-searches the history between a known-good and a known-bad commit. At each step Git checks out a commit halfway between; you test it and answer `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`, halving the range until Git names the first bad commit. 1,000 commits take about 10 steps.

```shell
git bisect start
git bisect bad              # current commit has the bug
git bisect good v1.4.0      # this release didn't
# Git checks out a middle commit -> test it
git bisect good             # or: git bisect bad
# ... repeat until "abc1234 is the first bad commit"
git bisect reset            # return to your branch
```

Use `git bisect skip` for a commit you can't test (e.g. it doesn't build).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-commit-with-bug.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Find lost files using Git

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you've **lost files or commits** in your Git repository, you can use the `git fsck` command to find them. This command is useful for recovering lost data or understanding the state of your repository.

Simply running `git fsck --lost-found` will print a list of all **dangling objects** (lost files and commits) in your repository. These objects will be extracted into the `.git/lost-found` directory for further inspection.

```shell
# Syntax: git fsck --lost-found

git fsck --lost-found
# dangling commit 3050fc0de
# dangling blob 807e3fa41
# dangling commit 59ff8481d
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-lost-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: A dropped stash or lost commit isn't in `git reflog`. How can `git fsck --lost-found` help you recover it?
back:
It lists **dangling** objects — commits and file contents (blobs) that no branch, tag, or reflog entry points to — and copies them into `.git/lost-found/commit/` and `.git/lost-found/other/`. Inspect a candidate with `git show`, then give it a branch name to keep it.

```shell
git fsck --lost-found
# dangling commit d49248cfaf38...
# dangling blob 807e3fa41...

git show d49248c            # is this my stash / commit?
git branch rescued d49248c  # keep it
```

Try `git reflog` first — it's easier. Dangling objects are only kept until garbage collection prunes them (by default after about two weeks).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-lost-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Use Git to find matching files — Limit to a specific file extension

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you want to search only in files with a **specific extension**, you can use `git grep <pattern> -- <pathspec>`. This will limit the search to files with the specified extension.

```shell
# Syntax: git grep <pattern> -- <pathspec>

git grep "TODO" -- "*.js"
# Returns all files with a `.js` extension that contain the word "TODO"

git grep "TODO" -- "*.[jt]s"
# Returns all files with a `.js` or `.ts` extension that contain the word "TODO"
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-matching-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you limit a `git grep` search to certain file types, e.g. only `.js` and `.ts` files?
back:
Add pathspecs after `--`: `git grep "FIXME" -- '*.js' '*.ts'`, or one glob such as `'*.[jt]s'`. Quote them so Git, not your shell, expands the glob — then it matches in every subfolder.

```shell
git grep "FIXME" -- '*.js'
git grep "FIXME" -- '*.[jt]s'
# src/cart.js:  // FIXME rounding
# src/api.ts:   // FIXME retry
```

`git grep` prints each matching line prefixed by its file, and only searches files Git tracks, so `node_modules` and other ignored files are skipped automatically.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-matching-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front:
Search only `.js` files for the word `FIXME` with `git grep`.

```shell
# Syntax: git grep <pattern> -- <pathspec>
____
# prints matching lines from .js files in any folder

git grep "FIXME" -- '*.[jt]s'   # .js and .ts files
```

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Use Git to find matching files — Multi-pattern search

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
You can search for **multiple patterns** combining them using the `--or` or `--and` flags. The `--or` flag will return files that match any of the patterns, while the `--and` flag will return files that match all of the patterns.

```shell
# Syntax: git grep <pattern1> --or <pattern2>

git grep "TODO" --or "FIXME"
# Returns all files that contain either the word "TODO" or "FIXME"

# Syntax: git grep <pattern1> --and <pattern2>

git grep "TODO" --and "FIXME"
# Returns all files that contain both the word "TODO" and "FIXME"
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-matching-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you make `git grep` match lines containing either of two patterns, or both patterns on the same line?
back:
Give each pattern with `-e` and combine them: several `-e` patterns (or `--or`) match lines containing **either**; `--and` matches lines containing **both**. Results are lines, not whole files.

```shell
git grep -e "FIXME" -e "console.log"         # either (OR is the default)
git grep -e "FIXME" --or -e "console.log"    # same, explicit

git grep -e "FIXME" --and -e "console"       # both on the same line
```

Without `-e`, `git grep FIXME --or ...` fails with "option '--or' must come before non-option arguments". To find *files* containing both words on any lines, use `--all-match` with `-l`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-matching-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Use Git to find matching files — Show the number of matches

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you want to know how many matches there are in each file, you can use the `-c` flag to show the **count of matches** for each file.

```shell
# Syntax: git grep -c <pattern>

git grep -c "TODO"
# Returns the count of matches for the word "TODO" in each file
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-matching-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you get the number of matching lines per file from `git grep`?
back:
Add `-c`: each file with matches is printed as `path:count`.

```shell
git grep -c "FIXME"
# src/cart.js:2
# src/api.ts:1
# vendors/chart.js:1
```

The count is of matching **lines**: a line containing `FIXME` twice counts once. Combine with a pathspec (`-- src/`) to focus on your own code.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-matching-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Use Git to find matching files — Limit results

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
By default, `git grep` will return all files that match the pattern. If you want to limit the results, there are various ways to do so.

---

front: What are the main ways to narrow down `git grep` results?
back:
Restrict **where** it looks with pathspecs after `--` (a folder, a glob, or `:^path` to exclude), **what snapshot** by naming a branch/tag/commit, and **how** it matches with flags like `-i` (ignore case) and `-w` (whole word only).

```shell
git grep -w "user" -- src/ ':^src/generated/'
git grep -i "fixme" main -- '*.ts'
git grep -l "fetchUser"          # just file names
```

Pathspecs always go last, after `--`, so Git never mistakes them for branch names.

Use Git to find matching files — Case-insensitive search

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
By default, `git grep` is case-sensitive. If you want to search for **case-insensitive** patterns, you can use the `-i` flag.

```shell

# Returns all files that contain the word "TODO" in any case
```

front: How do you search case-insensitively with `git grep`, so `fixme`, `FixMe`, and `FIXME` all match?
back:
Add `-i` (`--ignore-case`).

```shell
git grep -i "fixme"
# src/cart.js:// FIXME rounding
# src/api.ts:// fixme: retry on 503
```

`git grep` is case-sensitive by default. Pair `-i` with `-w` to match whole words only, so `-iw "id"` finds `id` and `ID` but not `userId` or `hidden`.

**Explain the approach**

Use Git to find matching files — Limit to a specific directory

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Similarly, you can use `git grep <pattern> -- <pathspec>` to search only in a **specific directory**. You can also use `:^` to **exclude** files from a specific directory.

```shell
# Syntax: git grep <pattern> -- <pathspec>

git grep "TODO" -- src/
# Returns all files in the `src/` directory that contain the word "TODO"

git grep "TODO" -- :^vendors/
# Returns all files that contain the word "TODO", excluding files in the `vendors/` directory
```

front: How do you make `git grep` search only one folder, or skip a folder like `vendors/`?
back:
Put the folder as a pathspec after `--`; to exclude one, prefix it with `:^` (or `:!`), and quote it.

```shell
git grep "FIXME" -- src/                 # only under src/
git grep "FIXME" -- ':^vendors/'         # everything except vendors/
git grep "FIXME" -- src/ ':^src/legacy/' # src/ minus a subfolder
```

The quotes matter: in many shells a bare `!` or `^` is special. An exclusion-only pathspec means "everything except".

front: How do you search the files as they are on another branch (say `main`) with `git grep`, without switching to it?
back:
Pass the branch (or any tag/commit) after the pattern: `git grep "FIXME" main`. Git searches that snapshot straight from the repository; your working tree isn't touched.

```shell
git grep "FIXME" main
# main:src/cart.js:// FIXME rounding

git grep "FIXME" origin/release-1.4 -- src/
```

Each line is prefixed with the revision name. Handy for checking whether a fix or a leftover `console.log` exists on a branch you don't have checked out.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Use Git to find matching files — Find files matching a pattern

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Using `git grep <pattern>` you can search for files in your repository that match a specific pattern. **Regular expressions** are supported, so you can use all the power of regex to find exactly what you're looking for.

```shell
# Syntax: git grep <pattern>

git grep "TODO"
# Returns all files that contain the word "TODO"

git grep "TODO.*"
# Returns all files that contain the word "TODO" followed by any characters
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-matching-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Does `git grep` accept regular expressions, and which flag do you need for `|` alternation like `console\.(log|debug)`?
back:
Yes. Patterns are **basic** regular expressions by default, where `(`, `|` and `+` are literal characters; add `-E` for extended regex syntax (similar to JavaScript's).

```shell
git grep -E "console\.(log|debug)"
# src/cart.js:console.log(total)
# src/api.ts:console.debug(res)

git grep "console\.(log|debug)"   # no -E: finds nothing
```

`-F` does the opposite: treats the pattern as a fixed string, so dots and brackets need no escaping.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

How can I find the merge commit given a Git commit?

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Oftentimes, we know the commit hash of a specific Git commit and want to find the **merge commit** where the changes from that commit were merged into a branch.

This can be especially useful if your team uses GitHub and you want to find the **pull request** that introduced a specific change. It's also pretty helpful when you need to understand the **context** of a commit and how it fits into the project's history or when you're looking for **files related to a change**.

While there are a few different solutions that might work under different circumstances, after trial and error and a whole lot of Googling, I found a method that works pretty well. [Adding the following alias](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/aliases) to your **Git configuration** will allow you to use `git find-merge <commit>` to find the merge commit for a given commit hash.

```properties title="~/.gitconfig"
[alias]
  find-merge = "!sh -c 'commit=$0 && branch=${1:-HEAD} && (git rev-list $commit..$branch --ancestry-path | cat -n; git rev-list $commit..$branch --first-parent | cat -n) | sort -k2 -s | uniq -f1 -d | sort -n | tail -1 | cut -f2'"
```

```shell
# Syntax: git find-merge <commit>

git find-merge 3050fc0
# c2ec1385b47a4b9024bdde77c0978a34359480ac
```

Using `git rev-list`, the command lists all the **commits between the given commit and the branch**, first following the full ancestry path and then following only the first parent. The output of these two commands is then concatenated, sorted, and filtered to find the **merge commit** where the two paths converge. Finally, the resulting **commit hash** is returned.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-merge-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Given a commit hash, how can you find the merge commit (e.g. the merged pull request) that brought it into `main`?
back:
Find the first merge on `main`'s own line (first-parent) that has the commit as an ancestor. This alias intersects the two histories and prints that merge's hash:

```ini
[alias]
  find-merge = "!sh -c 'commit=$0 && branch=${1:-HEAD} && (git rev-list $commit..$branch --ancestry-path | cat -n; git rev-list $commit..$branch --first-parent | cat -n) | sort -k2 -s | uniq -f1 -d | sort -n | tail -1 | cut -f2'"
```

```shell
git switch main
git find-merge 3050fc0
# c2ec1385b47a4b9024bdde77c0978a34359480ac
git show --no-patch c2ec138      # "Merge pull request #142 from ..."
```

`--ancestry-path` lists commits that descend from the given one; `--first-parent` lists only `main`'s direct line. The oldest commit in both is the merge. A plain `git log --merges --ancestry-path` can instead return a "merge main into feature" commit from inside the branch.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/find-merge-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

A better alternative to force pushing

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
I've been using `git push --force` for quite a few years now, and while it can be pretty handy, I've never quite managed to shake the feeling I'm going to break something. Thankfully, `git reflog` has saved me in those rare cases when I've messed up, but I've always been on the lookout for a **better alternative**.

```shell
git push --force
# Force push changes to the remote branch, overwriting any conflicting changes
```

[You may also like](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/view-undo-history)

Turns out, there has been a solution all along: `git push --force-with-lease`! This command works similarly to `git push --force`, but with an **added layer of safety**. It checks **if the remote branch has been updated since your last fetch** before allowing the force push. If someone else has pushed changes to the remote branch, **the force push will be rejected**, preventing you from accidentally overwriting their work.

```shell
git push --force-with-lease
# Force push changes to the remote branch only if it hasn't been updated since the last fetch
```

Now, obviously, this might not be the silver bullet you were looking for, but **it will prevent the most common issue on shared branches**. It also comes with its own pitfalls, such as `git fetch` tricking it into thinking your branch is up to date when it isn't. But overall, it's a much safer alternative to `git push --force`, and I highly recommend giving it a try. So much so that I've completely replace my `git push --force` usage with it!

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/force-push-better-alternative.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Why prefer `git push --force-with-lease` over `git push --force`, and what can still defeat its safety check?
back:
`--force-with-lease` only overwrites the remote branch if it still points where your last fetch saw it (your `origin/<branch>`). If a teammate pushed since then, the push is rejected instead of silently deleting their commits. Plain `--force` overwrites unconditionally.

```shell
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease
# ! [rejected] ... (stale info)  <- someone pushed; fetch and look first
```

Pitfall: a background `git fetch` (many editors do this) updates `origin/<branch>` without you looking, so the lease passes anyway. Adding `--force-if-includes` (Git 2.30+, or `git config --global push.useForceIfIncludes true`) also requires that you've actually integrated the remote commits.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/force-push-better-alternative.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

How can I update a remote branch after rewriting Git history?

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
When you rewrite the Git history locally, the remote branch will not be updated automatically. This can lead to a **divergence between the local and remote branches**. In that case, the remote will refuse to accept the changes, as the history doesn't match. In such as scenario, you need to force update the remote branch.

> [!WARNING]
>
> Rewriting history is a **potentially destructive operation**. Make sure you understand the implications before proceeding, especially if you are force updating a **shared branch**.

Using `git push -f` is the solution to this problem. The `-f` flag **forces the update of the remote branch**, overwriting it with the local branch's changes. This operation is necessary anytime your local and remote repository diverge.

```shell
# Usage: git push -f

git checkout patch-1
git pull
git rebase master
# Local `patch-1` branch has been rebased onto `master`, thus diverging
# from the remote `patch-1` branch

git push -f
# Force update the remote `patch-1` branch
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Force updating a remote branch **may not be allowed** for all users or all branches. Make sure you have the necessary permissions before proceeding.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/force-update-remote-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: After rebasing or amending commits you already pushed, why does `git push` get rejected, and how do you update the remote branch safely?
back:
The rewritten commits have new hashes, so your branch no longer contains the remote's commits and Git rejects the push as a non-fast-forward. Replace the remote branch with `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime.

```shell
git switch patch-1
git fetch
git rebase origin/main
git push
# ! [rejected] patch-1 -> patch-1 (non-fast-forward)
git push --force-with-lease
```

Only do this on a branch that is yours. Anyone who pulled the old commits now has diverged history. Protected branches like `main` usually block force-pushes entirely — and should.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/force-update-remote-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

How to add multiple authors to a commit — Notes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
- To correctly attribute a commit to a co-author, you must use the email associated with their GitHub account.
- If a person's email is private, you can use their GitHub-provided `no-reply` email.
- Leave one or preferably two empty lines before any `Co-authored-by` trailers.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/github-co-authors.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What must a `Co-authored-by:` trailer look like for GitHub to credit a co-author on a commit?
back:
Put it at the very end of the commit message, after one blank line, one line per person: `Co-authored-by: Name <email>`. The email must be one linked to their GitHub account (their `ID+username@users.noreply.github.com` address works if they keep theirs private).

```shell
git commit -m "Add login form" \
  --trailer "Co-authored-by: Ana Ruiz <ana@example.com>"
# Add login form
#
# Co-authored-by: Ana Ruiz <ana@example.com>
```

`--trailer` (Git 2.32+) adds the blank line for you. If the email doesn't match an account, GitHub shows the trailer text but credits nobody.

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Perform an interactive rebase in Git — Perform an interactive rebase

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Simply using `git rebase -i <commit>` will **open an editor** with a list of commits and actions to perform for each one. You can reorder the commits, squash them together, edit commit messages, and more.

> [!TIP]
>
> If you want to learn how to [configure Git's default text editor](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/configure-default-text-editor) before using this command, check the linked article.

If you encounter **merge conflicts** or need to stop the rebase to make changes, you can continue the rebase when ready using `git rebase --continue` or abort it using `git rebase --abort`.

Similarly, if you want to **edit the list of commits** after stopping the rebase, you can use `git rebase -i --edit-todo` to open the list in the editor again. This can be particularly useful, if the rebase stops due to some error or conflict.

Additionally, you can use the `--autosquash` option to **automatically squash fixup commits** into the commits they are fixing.

> [!NOTE]
>
> You can read more about **fixup commits** in the [relevant article](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/create-fixup-commit).

```shell
# Syntax: git rebase -i [--autosquash] <commit>

git rebase -i 3050fc0de
# Performs an interactive rebase starting from `3050fc0de`

git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~5
# Performs an interactive rebase of the last 5 commits,
# automatically squashing fixup commits
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/interactive-rebase.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What can you do to commits in `git rebase -i`, and how do you continue, abort, or re-edit the todo list mid-rebase?
back:
`git rebase -i <base>` opens a todo list of the commits after `<base>`. Change each line's word to `pick` (keep), `reword` (edit message), `edit` (stop to change it), `squash`/`fixup` (merge into the previous one) or `drop`, or reorder lines. Save and close to run it.

```shell
git rebase -i HEAD~5                 # last 5 commits
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main   # fixup! commits pre-arranged

git rebase --continue      # after fixing a conflict (git add first)
git rebase --abort         # give up, back to how it was
git rebase --edit-todo     # change the remaining plan
```

Every rewritten commit gets a new hash, so only rebase commits that aren't on a shared branch, and push with `--force-with-lease`.

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Configure Git's line endings

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you're working with a team that uses **different operating systems**, you might run into issues with **line endings**. Windows uses a different line ending (`\r\n`) compared to UNIX systems (`\n`). This can cause problems when sharing files between different systems.

Luckily, Git provides a way to configure line endings for a repository. By setting the `core.eol` configuration, you can specify whether to use UNIX (`\n`) or DOS (`\r\n`) line endings in your repository.

You can simply run `git config core.eol [lf | crlf]` to configure the line endings for your repository. `lf` stands for **UNIX line endings**, while `crlf` stands for **DOS line endings**.

```shell
# Usage: git config core.eol [lf | crlf]

git config core.eol lf
# Configures to use UNIX line endings

git config core.eol crlf
# Configures to use DOS line endings
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/line-endings.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: A team mixes Windows and macOS and diffs show every line changed because of line endings. Why isn't `git config core.eol lf` a reliable fix, and what is?
back:
`core.eol` is a per-machine setting that only affects files Git already treats as text, and it's ignored when `core.autocrlf` is `true` or `input` (the Windows installer's default is `true`). Commit a `.gitattributes` file instead, so the rule travels with the repo and applies to everyone.

```text
# .gitattributes
* text=auto eol=lf
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.png binary
```

```shell
git add .gitattributes
git add --renormalize .    # re-save existing files with the new rule
git commit -m "Normalize line endings"
```

`text=auto` lets Git detect text files; `eol=lf` checks them out with LF (`\n`) instead of Windows CRLF (`\r\n`).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/line-endings.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

List all Git aliases

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Setting up Git aliases can be a great way to save time and make your workflow more efficient. However, if you've set up a lot of aliases, it can be hard to remember what they all are. Luckily, you can easily list them using the `git config` command.

> [!TIP]
>
> I've compiled a list of [the most useful Git aliases](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/aliases), as well as a guide on **how to set them up**, which might come in handy.

In order to print all your aliases, you'll first have to use `git config -l` to **list all variables** set in the configuration file. In order to filter the output and only keep aliases, you can **pipe** the output (`|`) to `grep alias`. Finally, you can use `sed 's/^alias\.//g'` to remove the `alias.` part from each alias.

```shell
# Syntax: git config -l | grep alias | sed 's/^alias\.//g'

# Examples
git config -l | grep alias | sed 's/^alias\.//g'
# st=status
# co=checkout
# rb=rebase
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/list-aliases.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you list all your Git aliases and what they expand to?
back:
`git config --get-regexp '^alias\.'` prints every setting whose name starts with `alias.`, one per line as `name value`.

```shell
git config --get-regexp '^alias\.'
# alias.st status -sb
# alias.sw switch

git config --get-regexp '^alias\.' | sed 's/^alias\.//'
# st status -sb
# sw switch
```

The older `git config -l | grep alias` also catches unrelated settings whose value contains the word "alias". You can make this an alias itself: `git config --global alias.aliases "config --get-regexp ^alias\."`.

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Merge a branch in Git — Creating a merge commit

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If, instead, you want to **create a merge commit**, you can use the `--no-ff` flag when merging. This will create a merge commit at the tip of the target branch, optionally referencing the source branch in the commit message. The rest of the process remains the same.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git checkout <target-branch>
#  git merge --no-ff -m <message> <source-branch>

git checkout master
git merge --no-ff -m "Merge patch-1" patch-1
# Merges the `patch-1` branch into `master` and creates a commit
# with the message "Merge patch-1"
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/merge-branch-merge-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you merge `patch-1` into `main` so that a merge commit is always created, with your own message?
back:
Switch to `main`, then run `git merge --no-ff -m "<message>" patch-1`. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward was possible.

```shell
git switch main
git merge --no-ff -m "Merge patch-1: validate signup email" patch-1
```

The merge commit groups the branch's work under one commit, so it's easy to see in `git log --graph` and to undo as a unit with `git revert -m 1 <merge-hash>`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/merge-branch-merge-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Merge a branch in Git — Merging a branch

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In order to merge a branch, you want to **switch to the target branch** first, using `git checkout`. Then, you can use `git merge` to **merge the source branch into the target branch**.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git checkout <target-branch>
#  git merge <source-branch>

git checkout master
git merge patch-1 # Merges the `patch-1` branch into `master`
```

By default, Git will use [fast-forward merge](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/fast-forward-merge) to merge the branch. This means that it will create a **linear history**, by placing the commits from the source branch at the tip of the target branch.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/merge-branch-merge-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: To merge `patch-1` into `main`, which branch must you be on, and when does Git fast-forward instead of creating a merge commit?
back:
Be on the **target** (`main`) and name the source: `git merge patch-1`. Git fast-forwards — just moves `main` up to `patch-1` — only when `main` has no new commits since `patch-1` branched off. If both moved, it creates a merge commit with two parents.

```shell
git switch main
git pull
git merge patch-1
# "Fast-forward"  or  "Merge made by the 'ort' strategy."
```

On conflicts, Git stops: fix the marked files, `git add` them, then `git merge --continue` — or `git merge --abort` to back out completely.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/merge-branch-merge-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Optimize the local Git repository

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Is your Git repository getting bloated? Maybe you've seen a significant increase in the repository size, or you're experiencing performance issues. One way to address this is by **optimizing the local repository**.

Using `git gc --prune=now --aggressive`, you can **garbage collect loose objects** in the repository. This command will optimize the repository by removing unnecessary objects and compressing the repository data.

```shell
# Usage: git gc --prune=now --aggressive

git gc --prune=now --aggressive
# Optimizes the local repository
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> The command might take a minute to run, so hang back and let Git do its magic. Once it's done, you should see an optimized repository with improved performance.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/optimize-repository.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git gc --prune=now --aggressive` do, and why do you rarely need it?
back:
`git gc` packs loose objects into compressed packfiles and deletes unreachable ones. `--prune=now` deletes unreachable objects immediately instead of keeping them about two weeks, and `--aggressive` recompresses everything much harder (slow). Git already runs a lighter `git gc --auto` for you.

```shell
git count-objects -vH           # check size first
git gc --prune=now --aggressive
```

Cost: `--prune=now` throws away dangling commits you might still want to recover, like a stash you dropped yesterday. And it won't shrink a repo whose history still contains a huge file; that needs a history rewrite (e.g. `git filter-repo`).

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Pick changes from one or more Git commits

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Oftentimes, working on one feature or bug fix might unveil a solution or refactor that could be a standalone set of changes. In such cases, you might want to isolate the relevant commits and apply them in a **different branch**. Alternatively, you might want to use work from another branch in your current branch. This is where `git cherry-pick` comes in handy.

Using `git cherry-pick <commit>`, you can **pick changes from a single commit** and apply them on top of your current branch. If you have **multiple commits** you want to pick, you can specify them space-separated or as a range, using `git cherry-pick <commit-1> <commit-2>...`.

Similarly, if you want to pick changes from a **range of commits**, you can use `git cherry-pick <first-commit>..<last-commit>`. As this range is not inclusive of the `first-commit`, you can use `git cherry-pick <first-commit>^..<last-commit>` to include it.

```shell
# Usage: git cherry-pick (<commit>... | <first-commit>..<last-commit>)

git cherry-pick 3050fc0de
# Picks changes from the commit `3050fc0de`

git cherry-pick 3050fc0de c191f90c7
# Picks changes from the commits `3050fc0de`, `c191f90c7` and `0b552a6d4`

git cherry-pick 3050fc0de..c191f90c7
# Picks changes from the commits in the range:
#  `3050fc0de` (not inclusive) - `c191f90c7` (inclusive)

git cherry-pick 3050fc0de^..c191f90c7
# Picks changes from the commits in the range:
#  `3050fc0de` - `c191f90c7` (both inclusive)
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/pick-commits.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you copy one commit, several commits, or a range of commits onto your current branch with `git cherry-pick`, and does `A..B` include `A`?
back:
Pass hashes (`git cherry-pick <c1> <c2>`) or a range. `A..B` means "after A up to and including B", so **A is excluded**; write `A^..B` to include it. Each picked commit becomes a new commit (new hash) on your branch.

```shell
git switch release-1.5
git cherry-pick 3050fc0                # one commit
git cherry-pick 3050fc0 c191f90        # these two
git cherry-pick 3050fc0..c191f90       # after 3050fc0 .. c191f90
git cherry-pick 3050fc0^..c191f90      # 3050fc0 .. c191f90, inclusive
```

On a conflict: fix, `git add`, `git cherry-pick --continue` (or `--abort`). Add `-x` to note the original hash in the message, useful for backports.

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Git Basics - Push and pull changes between local and remote — Pull changes from remote

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Similar to pushing changes to a remote repository, you'll have to set up a remote tracking branch before you can pull changes from it. Luckily, `git checkout` is smart enough to do this for you, provided there is no local branch with the same name as the remote one. Then, you can use `git pull` to fetch and apply the latest changes from the remote.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git checkout <branch>
#  git pull

git checkout patch-1
git pull
# The local `patch-1` branch is now up to date with the remote branch `patch-1`
```

In case you have a local branch with the same name as the remote one and don't want to overwrite it, things are a bit more complicated. You'll have to use `git checkout` with the `-b` flag to specify the local branch's name and the `--track` flag to specify the remote branch's name. Then, you can use `git pull` as usual.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git checkout -b <local-branch> --track <remote>/<branch>
#  git pull

git checkout -b patch-one --track origin/patch-1
git pull
# The local `patch-one` branch is now up to date with the remote branch `patch-1`
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/push-pull-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you get a local copy of a teammate's remote branch and keep it up to date, and what if you want a different local name?
back:
`git switch patch-1`: if no local `patch-1` exists but `origin/patch-1` does, Git creates a local branch that tracks it. After that, `git pull` fetches and merges new commits. For a different local name, create it with `--track`.

```shell
git fetch
git switch patch-1        # local patch-1 tracking origin/patch-1
git pull                  # later: bring in their new commits

git switch -c patch-one --track origin/patch-1   # custom local name
```

`git checkout patch-1` does the same auto-tracking. `git pull` is `git fetch` plus a merge (or a rebase with `--rebase` / `pull.rebase true`) into your current branch.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/push-pull-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Git Basics - Push and pull changes between local and remote — Push changes to remote

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In order to push changes to the remote repository, you'll first have to set up a remote tracking branch. This is often done by using `git branch` with the `-u` flag. Then, you can use `git push` to push the latest changes from the local branch to the remote.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git branch -u <remote>/<branch>
#  git push

git branch -u origin/patch-1
git push
# The remote `patch-1` branch is now up to date with the local branch
```

Alternatively, you can use the `--set-upstream` flag with `git push` to set up a remote tracking branch and push the latest changes in one go. This is only possible if the remote branch doesn't exist yet.

```shell
# Syntax: git push --set-upstream <remote> <branch>

git push --set-upstream origin patch-1
# The remote `patch-1` branch is now up to date with the local branch
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/push-pull-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you push a new local branch and link it to its remote counterpart, so later `git push` and `git pull` need no arguments?
back:
`git push -u origin <branch>` (`-u` = `--set-upstream`): it creates the remote branch if needed and records it as your branch's upstream.

```shell
git switch -c patch-1
git commit -am "Fix cart total rounding"
git push -u origin patch-1
git push            # from now on, no arguments needed
```

`git branch -u origin/patch-1` only *links* to a remote branch that already exists — on a brand-new branch it fails with "the requested upstream branch 'origin/patch-1' does not exist". Set `push.autoSetupRemote true` to skip `-u` entirely.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/push-pull-changes.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Rebase onto another Git branch

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you've ever worked on a large project, you might have come across the need to get your branch up-to-date with another branch. Git provides a way to do this using the `git rebase` command.

In order to perform a rebase, you'll first have to use `git checkout` to **switch to the branch you want to rebase**. Then, you can use `git rebase` to **rebase the current branch onto the target branch**.

If you have **merge conflicts** or stop to make changes, you can continue the rebase when ready using `git rebase --continue` or abort it using `git rebase --abort`.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git checkout <branch>
#  git rebase <base-branch>

git checkout patch-1
git rebase master
# `patch-1` is rebased onto `master`

git checkout patch-2
git fetch origin
# Fetch latest remote branches
git rebase origin/master
# `patch-2` is rebased onto the latest remote `master`
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rebase-onto-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git rebase origin/main` do to your feature branch's commits, and how do you handle a conflict partway through?
back:
It sets your branch's commits aside, moves the branch to the tip of `origin/main`, and re-applies your commits one by one on top — as new commits with new hashes. The result reads as if you'd started your work from the latest `main`.

```shell
git switch patch-2
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# CONFLICT in src/cart.js
#   fix the file, then:
git add src/cart.js
git rebase --continue      # or: git rebase --abort
```

A conflict can stop the rebase once per commit being replayed. If the branch was already pushed, update it with `git push --force-with-lease`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rebase-onto-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Remove a file from the last Git commit

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Have you ever made a commit only to realize that a file should not have been included? This is a common problem, yet it's fairly easy to fix. All you have to do is **remove the file** and then **amend the last commit**.

Simply, using `git rm --cached <file>` removes the specified `<file>` from the index, and `git commit --amend` updates the contents of the last commit without changing its message.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git rm --cached <file>
#  git commit --amend

git rm --cached "30-seconds.txt"
git commit --amend
# Removes `30-seconds.txt` from the last commit
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> If you have **already pushed your changes** to a remote repository, you might be better off creating a new commit that removes the file, unless you're not on a shared branch and can **rewrite history**. In that case, you can use `git push --force` to update the remote branch.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/remove-file-from-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: You committed `.env` by mistake (not pushed yet). How do you take it out of the last commit while keeping the file on disk?
back:
`git rm --cached .env` removes it from the index (not from disk), then `git commit --amend --no-edit` rewrites the last commit without it. Add it to `.gitignore` so it doesn't come back.

```shell
git rm --cached .env
echo ".env" >> .gitignore
git add .gitignore
git commit --amend --no-edit
```

If the commit was already pushed, amending means `git push --force-with-lease` (only on your own branch). Any secret that reached the remote must be rotated — it's in history and may already be copied.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/remove-file-from-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Rename a local or remote Git branch — Rename remote branch

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In order to rename a remote branch, you have to use `git push origin --delete <old-name>` to **delete the old remote branch**. Then, you can use `git push origin -u <new-name>` to set `<new-name>` as the remote branch for the renamed branch.

```shell
# Usage:
#  git push origin --delete <old-name>
#  git push origin -u <new-name>

git checkout patch-1
git push origin --delete patch-1
git push origin -u patch-2
# Renames the remote branch `patch-1` to `patch-2`
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rename-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you rename a branch that has already been pushed, so the remote gets the new name too?
back:
Git can't rename a remote branch directly: rename it locally, push the new name with `-u`, then delete the old name on the remote.

```shell
git branch -m patch-1 patch-2          # rename locally
git push -u origin patch-2             # create + track the new one
git push origin --delete patch-1       # remove the old one
```

Teammates with the old branch must switch to the new one. On GitHub, deleting the old branch closes its open pull requests; renaming via the web UI ("Rename branch") keeps them.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rename-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Rename a local or remote Git branch — Rename local branch

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you want to rename a local branch, you can use the `git branch -m <old-name> <new-name>` command. This command renames the branch `<old-name>` to `<new-name>`.

```shell
# Usage: git branch -m <old-name> <new-name>

git checkout master
git branch -m patch-1 patch-2
# Renames `patch-1` to `patch-2`
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rename-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you rename a local Git branch — both the one you're on and a different one?
back:
`git branch -m <new-name>` renames the current branch; `git branch -m <old-name> <new-name>` renames any branch.

```shell
git switch fix-lgoin
git branch -m fix-login              # rename current branch

git branch -m patch-1 cart-rounding  # rename another branch
```

`-m` refuses if the new name already exists; `-M` overwrites it. This only renames locally — a pushed branch also needs the new name pushed and the old one deleted.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rename-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Reset your local master branch to match remote

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you've ever worked with Git, chances are you've encountered a situation where your local `master` branch is **out of sync with the remote**. This can happen if you've made some local changes to the `master` branch and want to reset it to match the one on the remote.

The first step to fix this is to make sure you have the **latest updates** from the remote. You can do this by using `git fetch origin`. After that, you can **switch** to the `master` branch using `git checkout master` and **reset** it to match the one on the remote using `git reset --hard origin/master`.

```shell
# Syntax
#  git fetch origin
#  git checkout master
#  git reset --hard origin/master

git fetch origin
git checkout master
git reset --hard origin/master
# Local `master` branch is now up to date with remote `master`
```

> [!TIP]
>
> You can follow this process for **any branch**, not just `master`. Simply replace `master` with the name of the branch you want to reset.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/reset-master.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Your local `main` has stray commits and you want it to exactly match `origin/main`. Which commands do that, and what do they destroy?
back:
Fetch, switch to `main`, and hard-reset it to the remote-tracking branch. This throws away `main`'s local-only commits and any uncommitted changes to tracked files; untracked files stay.

```shell
git fetch origin
git switch main
git branch backup-main          # optional safety net
git reset --hard origin/main
```

Works for any branch. Commits you reset away are recoverable for a while through `git reflog`, but uncommitted edits are not. If those stray commits are real work, move them to a new branch first (the `backup-main` line does exactly that).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/reset-master.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Restore deleted files in a Git commit

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Have you accidentally deleted a file? Or maybe you need to restore a file that was deleted? Luckily, Git provides a way to **restore files** that were deleted in a **specific commit**.

All you need is `git checkout <commit>^ -- <pathspec>`. This command will restore the specified `<file>` that was deleted in the specified `<commit>`. As the latter part of the command accepts a **filename or fileglob**, you can even restore multiple files.

```shell
# Syntax: git checkout <commit>^ -- <pathspec>

# "30seconds.txt" was deleted in the commit `3050fc0de`
git checkout 3050fc0de^ -- "30seconds.txt"
# Restores the 30seconds.txt file

# "src/*.json" was deleted in the commit `3050fc0de`
git checkout 3050fc0de^ -- "src/*.json"
# Restores all JSON files in the src/ directory
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/restore-deleted-file.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: A file was deleted in commit `3050fc0`. How do you bring it back, and why do you need the `^` in `3050fc0^`?
back:
Restore it from the commit *before* the deletion: `git restore --source=3050fc0^ -- <path>` (older: `git checkout 3050fc0^ -- <path>`). `^` means "parent of"; in `3050fc0` itself the file no longer exists.

```shell
git log --oneline --diff-filter=D -- src/api/client.js
# 3050fc0 Remove old API client

git restore --source=3050fc0^ -- src/api/client.js
git restore --source=3050fc0^ -- 'src/*.json'   # globs work, but also overwrite
                                                # json files that still exist
```

The file comes back as a new, uncommitted file; `git add` and commit it. `--diff-filter=D` shows only commits that deleted the path.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/restore-deleted-file.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Rewind back to a specific commit in Git — Rewind back n commits

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
You can also use `git reset` to rewind back a **given number of commits**. To do so, you can use the `HEAD~<n>` syntax, where `<n>` is the number of commits you want to rewind back.

```shell
# Syntax: git reset [--hard] HEAD~<n>

git reset HEAD~5
# Rewinds back 5 commits but keeps changes in the working directory

git reset --hard HEAD~3
# Rewinds back 3 commits and deletes changes
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rewind-to-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `HEAD~3` refer to, and how do you use it to undo your last three commits but keep their changes?
back:
`HEAD~3` is the commit three steps back along the current branch (`HEAD~1` = the previous commit). `git reset HEAD~3` moves the branch there and leaves the undone commits' changes in your files as unstaged edits.

```shell
git reset HEAD~3           # undo 3 commits, keep the changes
git reset --soft HEAD~3    # same, but keep them staged (easy re-commit)
git reset --hard HEAD~3    # undo 3 commits AND discard their changes
```

A common use is squashing messy local commits: `git reset --soft HEAD~3` then one clean `git commit`. Only do this to commits you haven't pushed to a shared branch.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rewind-to-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Rewind back to a specific commit in Git — Rewind to a commit

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
To rewind back to a specific commit, you can use `git reset`. This command will **uncommit and unstage changes**, but leave them in the working directory. You can use the `--hard` flag to **uncommit, unstage and delete** changes instead.

```shell
# Syntax: git reset [--hard] <commit>

git reset 3050fc0
# Rewinds back to `3050fc0` but keeps changes in the working directory

git reset --hard c0d30f3
# Rewinds back to `c0d30f3` and deletes changes
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rewind-to-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: When you `git reset <commit>` to move your branch back, what happens to the undone changes with `--soft`, the default (`--mixed`), and `--hard`?
back:
All three move the branch to `<commit>`. `--soft` keeps the undone changes **staged**, the default `--mixed` keeps them as **unstaged edits**, and `--hard` **deletes** them from the staging area and your files.

```shell
git reset --soft 3050fc0    # changes staged, ready to re-commit
git reset 3050fc0           # changes kept, unstaged
git reset --hard 3050fc0    # changes gone
```

If `--hard` went wrong, `git reflog` still shows the old commit so you can `git reset --hard <old-hash>` back — but uncommitted edits it wiped are lost for good.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rewind-to-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Rewind back to a specific commit in Git — Notes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The `--hard` flag is considered a destructive action, which means you should be extra careful when using it. If things go wrong, you might be able to recover your changes by [viewing the reference log](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/view-undo-history).

In case you've already pushed some changes to a remote repository, you might not want to rewrite history, especially if other people have already pulled your changes. In that case, you can use `git revert` to [undo a commit without rewriting history](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/undo-commit-without-rewriting-history).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/rewind-to-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Before you run `git reset --hard <commit>` to rewind a branch, what can it destroy, how can you recover rewound commits, and when should you use `git revert` instead?
back:
`git reset --hard <commit>` moves the current branch to `<commit>` and overwrites the staging area and working tree to match, so uncommitted changes are lost for good. The commits you rewound past are only orphaned: `git reflog` still lists them for weeks, so you can get them back. If those commits are already pushed to a shared branch, use `git revert` instead, which adds undo commits rather than rewriting history.

```shell
git status                  # anything uncommitted? stash or commit it first
git reset --hard a1b2c3d    # branch now points at a1b2c3d
git reflog                  # changed your mind? find where you were
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}   # jump back to the pre-reset position
```

Resetting a pushed branch means you must force-push, and anyone who already pulled the old commits ends up with a diverged history. Keep `reset --hard` for your own local, unpushed work.

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Set the default push branch name in Git

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Manually specifying the **remote branch name** when pushing can be a hassle. Git provides a way to automate this process by setting the default push branch name to the **current branch name**.

Using `git config push.default current` will configure Git to use the name of the current branch as the **default** remote branch name. This setting is particularly useful when local branches are expected to have the same name as their remote counterparts.

Using the `--global` flag will set this configuration globally on your machine.

```shell
# Syntax: git config [--global] push.default current

git config --global push.default current

git checkout -b my-branch
git push -u
# Pushes to origin/my-branch
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/set-default-push-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git config --global push.default current` change about a bare `git push` on a new branch, and which newer setting also sets up tracking automatically?
back:
With `push.default current`, a bare `git push` pushes the current branch to a same-named branch on the remote, creating it if needed, so you don't have to type `git push origin my-branch`. Since Git 2.37, `push.autoSetupRemote true` goes further: the first plain `git push` of a new branch also records the upstream, as if you had typed `-u`.

```shell
git config --global push.autoSetupRemote true

git switch -c fix-login-form
git push     # creates origin/fix-login-form and tracks it
```

The default, `simple`, pushes only to the branch's configured upstream (with the same name) and errors with "has no upstream branch" otherwise. With `current` alone, add `-u` on the first push if you want `git pull` and `git status` to know the upstream. Both settings assume local and remote branch names match, which is the normal team setup.

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Create a commit by a different author in Git — Create a commit by a different author

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
As long as you have the author's information, you can create a commit by them. Using the `--author` option for `git commit` will allow you to **create a new commit by a different author**.

```shell
# Syntax: git commit --author="<name> <email>"

# Make some changes to files
git add .
git commit -m "Fix the network bug" --author="Duck Quackers <cool.duck@qua.ck>"
# Creates a commit by `Duck Quackers`
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/set-or-amend-commit-author.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: You're committing a fix a teammate wrote on your machine. Which `git commit` option records them as the author, and who is recorded as the committer?
back:
Use `--author="Name <email>"`: Git records that person as the author, while you (from your `user.name`/`user.email`) stay recorded as the committer. Every commit stores both.

```shell
git add src/api/users.js
git commit -m "Fix null email in signup" --author="Ana Lopez <ana@example.com>"
git log -1 --format='%an | %cn'
# Ana Lopez | Dev
```

Use an email the hosting site (e.g. GitHub) links to their account, or the commit won't show on their profile. If you both worked on it, keep yourself as author and add a `Co-authored-by: Name <email>` line at the end of the message instead; `--author` takes only one person.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/set-or-amend-commit-author.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).
