previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Create a commit by a different author in Git — Caveats

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Changing the author of a commit will also change its **SHA-1 checksum**. If you've already pushed the commit to a remote repository, you will need to force push the updated commit to the remote.

Additionally, if your remote repository is configured to only accept **signed commits**, you might be unable to sign the commit unless you have the original author's GPG key.

Finally, you can't use `--author` to add **multiple authors** to a commit. If you want to do so, you can find more information in [the relevant article](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/github-co-authors).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/set-or-amend-commit-author.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: You need to change the author of a commit you already made. How do you do it, and why does it cause trouble if that commit was already pushed?
back:
Amend it: `git commit --amend --no-edit --author="Name <email>"`. The author is part of the commit's content, so Git creates a replacement commit with a new hash. If the old commit was pushed, the remote no longer matches your branch and you must force-push, which rewrites history for anyone who already pulled it.

```shell
git commit --amend --no-edit --author="Ana Lopez <ana@example.com>"
git push --force-with-lease    # only on a branch nobody else uses
```

`--force-with-lease` refuses to overwrite the remote if someone pushed there since you last fetched, unlike plain `--force`. Never rewrite shared branches such as `main`. For an older commit, use `git rebase -i`, mark it `edit`, then run the same amend. `--author` takes one person only; credit a pair with a `Co-authored-by:` trailer.

---

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View Git branches sorted by date

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Have you ever wanted to see a list of all your **local Git branches** sorted by date? There's a very easy way to do so, using the `git branch` command with the `--sort` option.

In order to sort branches by date, you usually want to use the `committerdate` field, which represents the **date of the commit** on the branch. In order to sort branches in descending order (**most recent first**), you can use the `-` sign before the field name.

Putting it all together, using `git branch --sort=-committerdate` will display a list of all local branches sorted by the date of their last commit.  You can use the **arrow keys** to navigate through the list and press <kbd>Q</kbd> to **exit**.

```shell
# Syntax: git branch --sort=-committerdate

git branch --sort=-committerdate
# master
# patch-1
# patch-2
```

If, instead, you want to sort branches in ascending order (**oldest first**), you can drop the `-` sign, and use `git branch --sort=committerdate`.

```shell
# Syntax: git branch --sort=committerdate

git branch --sort=committerdate
# patch-2
# patch-1
# master
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Depending on your environment and team, you might want to use `authordate` instead of `committerdate`. These fields often have identical values, but they **can differ** in certain situations, such as when a commit is cherry-picked or rebased. The `authordate` field represents the date of the **original commit**, while the `committerdate` field represents the date of the **commit in the current branch**.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/sort-branches-by-date.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Which command lists your local branches with the most recently committed-to branch first, and what does the `-` in the sort key do?
back:
`git branch --sort=-committerdate`. It sorts branches by the date of their latest commit; the leading `-` reverses the order so the newest comes first (without it, the oldest is first).

```shell
git branch --sort=-committerdate
# * fix-login-form
#   main
#   old-experiment

git config --global branch.sort -committerdate   # make it the default
```

`committerdate` is when the commit was last written; rebase, amend and cherry-pick update it. `authordate` is when the change was originally made. For "which branch did I touch last", `committerdate` is usually what you want.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/sort-branches-by-date.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Split a Git commit into multiple commits

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
I've often found myself, especially when working on larger feature branches, in a situation where I've made a commit that should have been split into multiple smaller commits. This can happen for various reasons, such as including unrelated changes in a single commit or realizing that a commit should have been broken down into smaller, more focused commits.

While it might sound a little intimidating, it's a fairly straightforward process so long as you're familiar with [Git's interactive rebase](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/interactive-rebase) feature. All you need to do is **find the commit** you want to split and then mark it with `edit` to stop the rebase process. Once you've done that, you can use `git reset HEAD^` to **unstage your changes** and then **commit them separately**. Let's take a look at an example.

```shell
# 1. Use git rebase -i <commit>
git rebase -i HEAD~2
```

```shell title="git-rebase-todo"
# 2. Mark the commit you want to split with `edit`
edit 3050fc0de Fix network bug
pick 7b1e3f2a2 Update README
# 3. Save and close the editor to start the rebase
```

```shell
# Stopped at 3050fc0...  Fix network bug
# You can amend the commit now, with
#
#   git commit --amend
#
# Once you are satisfied with your changes, run
#
#   git rebase --continue

# 4. Use `git reset HEAD^` to unstage the changes
git reset HEAD^
# Unstaged changes after reset:
# M       src/sever/network.js
# M       src/public/index.html
# M       package.json

# 5. Commit the changes separately
git add src/server/network.js
git commit -m 'Fix network bug'
# [detached HEAD 1f3e4d5] Fix network bug
#  1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)

git add src/public/index.html
git commit -m 'Update documentation'
# [detached HEAD 9a8b7c6] Update documentation
#  1 file changed, 62 insertions(+)

git add package.json
git commit -m 'Update dependencies'
# [detached HEAD 6d5c4b3] Update dependencies
#  2 files changed, 737 insertions(+), 802 deletions(-)

# 6. Continue the rebase
git rebase --continue
# Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/network-bug.

# Check the log to confirm the changes
git log --oneline --decorate -4
# 1f3e4d5 (HEAD -> network-bug) Fix network bug
# 9a8b7c6 Update documentation
# 6d5c4b3 Update dependencies
# 7b1e3f2 Update README
```

And there you have it! Without too much hassle, you've successfully **split a commit into multiple smaller commits**. This process can be easily adapted to suit your needs and it can also be repeated as much as you like. Just remember to be careful when **rewriting Git history**, especially if you're working on a shared branch.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/split-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: One commit on your feature branch mixes a bug fix, a docs change and a dependency bump. How do you split it into three commits with interactive rebase?
back:
Start `git rebase -i` from before that commit, mark it `edit`, and when the rebase stops there run `git reset HEAD^`: this undoes the commit but keeps its changes in your working tree. Then stage and commit each part separately, and finish with `git rebase --continue`.

```shell
git rebase -i HEAD~2
# In the todo list, change `pick` to `edit`:
#   edit 3050fc0 Fix network bug
#   pick 7b1e3f2 Update README

git reset HEAD^                     # undo the commit, keep the changes
git add src/server/network.js && git commit -m "Fix network bug"
git add docs/api.md && git commit -m "Update API docs"
git add package.json package-lock.json && git commit -m "Update dependencies"
git rebase --continue

git log --oneline -4
# 9c1d2e3 (HEAD -> network-bug) Update README
# 6d5c4b3 Update dependencies
# 9a8b7c6 Update API docs
# 1f3e4d5 Fix network bug
```

Every commit from the split point onward gets a new hash (even "Update README"), so this rewrites history. Do it on your own branch; if it was already pushed, push with `--force-with-lease` and only when nobody else builds on it. To split changes inside a single file, stage parts of it with `git add -p`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/split-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Add or remove files from the Git staging area — Stage files

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Adding changes to the staging area is as simple as using the `git add <pathspec>` command, with an appropriate **filename or fileglob**. That way, you can add individual files, files with a specific extension, or all changes in the working directory.

```shell
# Usage: git add <pathspec>

git add "30seconds.txt"
# Add the file `30seconds.txt` to the staging area

git add src/*.json
# Add all files with a `.json` extension in the `src` directory

git add .
# Adds all changes to the staging area
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stage-unstage-files.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you stage a single file, all files matching a pattern, or everything with `git add`, and what exactly does `git add .` cover?
back:
`git add <pathspec>` stages the current content of whatever matches: a file, a glob, or a directory. `git add .` stages every change (new, modified and deleted files) under the current directory; `git add -A` does the same for the whole repository, wherever you are in it.

```shell
git add src/components/LoginForm.jsx   # one file
git add 'src/*.json'                    # quoted: Git expands the glob
git add .                               # everything under this folder
git add -p                              # pick changes hunk by hunk
```

Quote globs so Git, not your shell, expands them; Git's pathspec `*` also matches files in subfolders and deleted files. Check `git status` before committing so you don't stage `.env` or build output, and list those in `.gitignore`.

---

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Subsequently, you can remove files from the staging area using the `git restore --staged <pathspec>` command. This command allows you to unstage individual files, files with a specific extension, or all changes in the staging area.

```shell
# Usage: git restore --staged <pathspec>

# Remove all changes from the staging area
```

front: You ran `git add .` and accidentally staged `.env`. Which command unstages it without losing your edits to the file?
back:
`git restore --staged .env`. It resets the file's entry in the staging area to match the last commit and leaves your working-tree file untouched. It takes any pathspec, so `git restore --staged .` unstages everything.

```shell
git restore --staged .env     # unstage one file
git restore --staged .        # unstage everything
echo ".env" >> .gitignore     # stop it happening again
```

Don't confuse it with `git restore .env` (no `--staged`), which discards your working-tree changes. Older tutorials use `git reset HEAD <file>` for the same unstage. If `.env` was already committed, `git rm --cached .env` stops tracking it, but the secret stays in history, so rotate it.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

A guide to Git stashing — Stashing changes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In order to stash your changes, you can use the `git stash push` command. This command saves the **current state** of the working directory and index into a new stash. You can optionally provide a message for the stash, and include **untracked files** using the `-u` option.

```shell
# Usage: git stash push [-u] [<message>]

git stash push
# Creates a new stash

git stash push -u
# Creates a new stash, including untracked files

git stash push "Bugfix WIP"
# Creates a new stash with the message "Bugfix WIP"
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> You can **omit** the `push` subcommand when using `git stash`. Additionally, you might have seen `git stash save` being used in **older versions** of Git. This command is now **deprecated** in favor of `git stash push`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: You're mid-change and need to switch branches for an urgent fix. How do you stash your work with a label, including brand-new files?
back:
`git stash push -u -m "label"`. `push` saves your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) as a new stash and resets the working tree to the last commit. `-u` also stashes untracked (new) files, and `-m` sets the message.

```shell
git stash push -u -m "WIP: signup validation"
git switch main          # clean tree: do the hotfix
git switch -             # back to your branch
git stash pop
```

The message needs `-m`: `git stash push "WIP"` treats the text as a file path and fails with "pathspec did not match". Plain `git stash` is short for `git stash push`, and `git stash save` is deprecated. Ignored files such as `node_modules` are never stashed unless you use `-a`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

A guide to Git stashing — Viewing stash changes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
To view the changes stored in a stash, you can use the `git stash show` command. This command displays the changes introduced by the stash relative to the parent commit. You can provide the **stash reference** to view a specific stash, or omit it to view the latest stash.

```shell
# Usage: git stash show [<stash>]

git stash show
# Displays the changes in the latest stash

git stash show stash@{1}
# Displays the changes in the stash with the reference stash@{1}
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you see exactly what's inside a stash before applying it, and why does plain `git stash show` look so short?
back:
`git stash show -p stash@{1}` prints the stash's full diff. Without `-p`, `git stash show` prints only a diffstat (changed files with +/- counts). Leave out the name to use the latest stash, `stash@{0}`.

```shell
git stash list
git stash show               # diffstat of the latest stash
git stash show -p            # full diff of the latest stash
git stash show -p stash@{1}  # full diff of an older one
```

Untracked files stashed with `-u` are not shown by default; add `--include-untracked` (Git 2.32+). In PowerShell, quote the ref (`'stash@{1}'`), because braces are special there.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

A guide to Git stashing — Deleting stashes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
You can **delete stashes** using the `git stash drop` command. This command removes the specified stash from the stash list.

```shell
# Usage: git stash drop <stash>

git stash drop
# Deletes the latest stash

git stash drop stash@{1}
# Deletes the stash with the reference stash@{1}
```

Moreover, you can **delete all stashes** using the `git stash clear` command.

```shell
# Usage: git stash clear

git stash clear
# Deletes all stashes
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you delete one stash versus all of them, and can a dropped stash be recovered?
back:
`git stash drop [<stash>]` deletes one stash (the latest if you name none); `git stash clear` deletes them all. A dropped stash can be recovered while you still have the hash Git printed.

```shell
git stash drop stash@{1}
# Dropped stash@{1} (4f2a9c1e...)
git stash apply 4f2a9c1e     # undo the drop: re-apply by hash

git stash clear              # remove every stash
```

Stashes removed with `clear` have no printed hashes and are hard to find (you'd need `git fsck`), so treat `clear` as permanent. After a drop the remaining stashes renumber, so check `git stash list` before dropping another by number.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

A guide to Git stashing — Applying a stash

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
To apply a specific stash, you can use the `git stash apply` command. This command applies the changes from the specified stash to the working directory. You can provide the **stash reference** to apply a specific stash, or omit it to apply the **latest stash**.

```shell
# Usage: git stash apply [<stash>]

git stash apply
# Applies the latest stash

git stash apply stash@{1}
# Applies the stash with the reference stash@{1}
```

Similarly, you can use the `git stash pop` command to apply the changes from the specified stash and **remove it from the stash list**.

```shell
# Usage: git stash pop [<stash>]

git stash pop
# Applies the latest stash and removes it from the stash list

git stash pop stash@{1}
# Applies the stash with the reference stash@{1} and
#  removes it from the stash list
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What's the difference between `git stash apply` and `git stash pop`, and what happens to the stash if `pop` hits a merge conflict?
back:
Both re-apply a stash's changes to your working tree (the latest stash by default). `apply` keeps the stash in the list; `pop` removes it once it applies cleanly. If `pop` hits a conflict, Git keeps the stash so nothing is lost: resolve the conflict, then run `git stash drop` yourself.

```shell
git stash apply            # keep a copy, e.g. to apply on two branches
git stash pop              # apply the latest and remove it
git stash pop stash@{1}    # apply an older one and remove it
```

A stash isn't tied to its branch: you can apply it on a different branch, which is handy when you started work on the wrong one.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

A guide to Git stashing — Listing stashes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Stashes are stored as a **stack**, with the most recent stash at the top. You can view a list of all stashes using the `git stash list` command. This command displays the stash reference, the branch or commit the stash was created on, and the message associated with the stash.

```shell
# Usage: git stash list

git stash list
# stash@{0}: WIP on patch-1: ee52eda Fix network bug
# stash@{1}: WIP on master: 2b1e8a7 Add new feature
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git stash list` show, and which stash is `stash@{0}`?
back:
It lists every stash, newest first: `stash@{0}` is the most recent, and each older stash's number is one higher. Each line shows the stash ref, the branch it was made on, and its message.

```shell
git stash list
# stash@{0}: On fix-login: WIP: signup validation
# stash@{1}: WIP on main: 2b1e8a7 Add users table
```

`On <branch>: <message>` means the stash was made with `-m`; `WIP on <branch>: <commit>` is the automatic message naming the commit you were on. Numbers shift whenever you push or drop a stash, so label stashes with `-m` and re-check the list before popping one by number.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/stashing.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

An introductory guide to Git submodules — Delete a submodule

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Deleting a submodule is a little more complicated. You'll first have to use `git submodule deinit -f -- <submodule>` to **unregister the submodule**. Then, you need to remove the `.git/modules/<submodule>` directory, using `rm -rf .git/modules/<submodule>`. Finally, you can **remove the working tree** of the submodule using `git rm -f <submodule>`.

```shell
# Syntax:
#  git submodule deinit -f -- <submodule>
#  rm -rf .git/modules/<submodule>
#  git rm -f <submodule>

git submodule deinit -f -- 30code
rm -rf .git/modules/30code
git rm -f 30code
# Removes the `30code` submodule
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/submodules.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you completely remove a Git submodule from a repository, including the copy Git keeps inside `.git/`?
back:
Three steps, then commit: `git submodule deinit -f -- <path>` unregisters the submodule and empties its folder; `git rm -f <path>` deletes the folder, removes its `.gitmodules` entry and stages both; `rm -rf .git/modules/<name>` deletes the submodule's stored repository, which nothing else cleans up.

```shell
git submodule deinit -f -- vendor/ui-kit
git rm -f vendor/ui-kit
rm -rf .git/modules/vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Remove ui-kit submodule"
```

`<name>` is the name in `.gitmodules` (`[submodule "name"]`), usually the original path; it can differ from the current path after a `git mv`. Skipping the last step leaves a stale copy that gets in the way if you re-add a submodule at that path. In PowerShell, use `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force` instead of `rm -rf`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/submodules.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

An introductory guide to Git submodules — Initialize submodules

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
After adding a submodule to your repository, you will need to **initialize and update** the submodule to fetch its contents. You can do this by running `git submodule update --init --recursive`.

While the `--recursive` flag isn't strictly necessary, it ensures that any **nested submodules** are also updated. This is useful if the submodule itself contains submodules, as it will ensure that all submodules are initialized and updated.

```shell
# Syntax: git submodule update --init --recursive

git submodule update --init --recursive
# Clones missing submodules and checks out commits
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/submodules.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: You cloned a repo and its submodule folders are empty. Which command fetches and checks them out, and how could you have avoided this at clone time?
back:
`git submodule update --init --recursive`. `--init` registers the submodules listed in `.gitmodules`, `update` clones them and checks out the exact commit the parent repo recorded, and `--recursive` does the same for submodules nested inside them.

```shell
git submodule update --init --recursive

# or, at clone time:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/acme/shop.git
```

Submodules are checked out on a detached HEAD at the pinned commit, not on a branch. If you plan to commit inside one, switch it to a branch first (e.g. `git switch main`, if that is the submodule's branch). `git config --global submodule.recurse true` makes `pull` and `switch` keep submodules in sync automatically.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/submodules.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

An introductory guide to Git submodules — Update submodules

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
When you clone a repository that contains submodules, the submodules will be **checked out at a specific commit**. When you want to **update the contents** of the submodules to the latest version, you can use `git submodule update --recursive --remote`. Again, the `--recursive` flag ensures that any submodules within the submodule are also updated.

```shell
# Syntax: git submodule update --recursive --remote

git submodule update --recursive --remote
# Pulls all submodules from their respective remotes
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/submodules.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git submodule update --remote` do differently from plain `git submodule update`, and what must you do afterwards?
back:
Plain `update` checks out the commit your repo has recorded for each submodule. `--remote` instead fetches each submodule and checks out the latest commit of its remote branch (the remote's default branch unless `.gitmodules` sets `branch`). That changes the recorded commit, so afterwards you commit the new pointer in the parent repo.

```shell
git submodule update --remote --recursive
git status            # modified: vendor/ui-kit (new commits)
git add vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Bump ui-kit submodule"
```

Until you commit and push that pointer, teammates still get the old version. Test before committing: `--remote` pulls in whatever changed upstream.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/submodules.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

An introductory guide to Git submodules — Add a submodule

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
To add a submodule to your repository, you can use `git submodule add <upstream-path> <local-path>`. The first argument is the **URL of the repository** you want to add as a submodule, and the second argument is the **path** where you want the submodule to be located within your repository.

```shell
# Syntax: git submodule add <upstream-path> <local-path>

git submodule add https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code ./30code
# Creates the directory `30code` containing the submodule from
# "https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code"
```

Adding a submodule will create a **new directory** in your repository that contains the contents of the submodule repository. The submodule directory will contain a `.git` directory that points to the submodule repository, allowing you to **track changes** to the submodule independently of your main repository.

Additionally, a `.gitmodules` file will be created in the root of your repository that contains information about the submodule, such as the URL of the submodule repository and the path where the submodule is located.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/submodules.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git submodule add <url> <path>` create in your repo, and what actually gets committed?
back:
It clones the other repository into `<path>` and stages two things: a `.gitmodules` entry (URL and path) and a special entry for `<path>` that records one exact commit of the submodule. Your repo stores that pointer, not the submodule's files.

```shell
git submodule add https://github.com/acme/ui-kit.git vendor/ui-kit
git status -s
# A  .gitmodules
# A  vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Add ui-kit submodule"
```

Inside `vendor/ui-kit`, `.git` is a small file (`gitdir: ../../.git/modules/vendor/ui-kit`) pointing to where the submodule's history lives. It's a separate repo: new commits in it don't change what the parent records until you `git add vendor/ui-kit` in the parent and commit.

---

front:
Add the repository `https://github.com/acme/ui-kit.git` as a submodule in the folder `vendor/ui-kit`.

```shell
____
git status -s
# A  .gitmodules
# A  vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Add ui-kit submodule"
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git submodule add https://github.com/acme/ui-kit.git vendor/ui-kit
```

The first argument is the repository URL, the second the path inside your repo. Git clones it there and stages a `.gitmodules` entry plus a pointer to the submodule's current commit; committing records both.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

An introductory guide to Git submodules — Rename a submodule

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Luckily, renaming a submodule is just as easy as renaming a directory. Using `git mv <old-submodule> <new-submodule>` will **rename the directory** containing the submodule. This will also **update the submodule's path** in the `.gitmodules` file.

```shell
# Syntax: git mv <old-submodule> <new-submodule>

git mv 30code 30-seconds-of-code
# Renames the `30code` submodule to `30-seconds-of-code`
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/submodules.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you move or rename a submodule's folder so that `.gitmodules` stays correct?
back:
Use `git mv <old-path> <new-path>`. Git moves the folder, updates the submodule's `path` in `.gitmodules`, and stages both; then commit.

```shell
git mv vendor/lib vendor/ui-kit
git commit -m "Move ui-kit submodule"
```

Moving the folder with your file manager or plain `mv` does not update `.gitmodules`, so the submodule breaks. The submodule's name (`[submodule "vendor/lib"]`) stays the same; only its `path` changes.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/submodules.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Switch to a Git branch — Switch to an existing branch

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
In order to switch to an **existing branch**, you can use `git checkout <branch>`. If you're using a newer version of Git, you can also use `git switch <branch>`.

```shell
# Syntax: git checkout <branch>
#     or: git switch <branch>

git checkout patch-1
# Switches to the branch named `patch-1`

git switch patch-1
# Switches to the branch named `patch-1`
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/switch-to-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Which modern command switches to an existing branch, and why is it safer than `git checkout` for this?
back:
`git switch <branch>` (Git 2.23+). It only switches branches, while `git checkout` also restores files: if no branch matches the name, `git checkout <name>` can treat it as a file and silently discard your uncommitted edits to it.

```shell
git switch fix-login        # existing branch
git switch -c fix-login     # create it and switch
git switch -                # back to the previous branch
```

If switching would overwrite uncommitted changes, Git refuses; commit or stash first. If `fix-login` exists only on the remote, `git switch fix-login` creates a local branch tracking `origin/fix-login`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/switch-to-branch.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Undo a commit in Git — Revert a commit

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
As you might have guessed, `git revert` is the command you're looking for. Using this command, you can **revert a commit**, creating a new commit with the inverse of the commit's changes.

```shell
# Syntax: git revert <commit>

git revert 3050fc0
# Reverts the commit `3050fc0` and creates a new commit
# with the inverse of its changes
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/undo-commit-without-rewriting-history.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: A bad commit is already on the shared `main` branch. How do you undo it without rewriting history?
back:
`git revert <commit>` creates a new commit that applies the exact inverse of that commit's changes. History only grows, so teammates who already pulled are unaffected and you push normally.

```shell
git revert 3050fc0
# [main 8e1f2a4] Revert "Add discount column"
git push
```

To revert a merge commit, add `-m 1` to say which parent is the mainline. If later commits changed the same lines, the revert can conflict: resolve it, then run `git revert --continue`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/undo-commit-without-rewriting-history.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Undo a commit in Git — Revert the last commit

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
The **latest commit** can be references using the `HEAD` pointer. So, to revert the last commit, you can simply use `git revert HEAD`.

```shell
# Syntax: git revert HEAD

git revert HEAD
# Reverts the last commit and creates a new commit
# with the inverse of its changes
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/undo-commit-without-rewriting-history.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What's the quickest way to undo your most recent commit when it's already pushed, and what does it leave in the history?
back:
`git revert HEAD`. `HEAD` is the commit you're on (the latest on your branch), and revert adds a new commit that reverses it, so both the original and the "Revert …" commit stay in the log.

```shell
git revert HEAD
git log --oneline -2
# 8e1f2a4 Revert "Add discount column"
# 3050fc0 Add discount column
```

If the commit is not pushed yet, `git reset --soft HEAD~1` is often cleaner: it removes the commit but keeps its changes staged so you can fix them and commit again.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/undo-commit-without-rewriting-history.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Change the last commit's message or contents in Git — Change the last commit's message

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you only want to change the last commit's message, you can use `--amend` and simply add the `-m` option followed by the new message. This will replace the last commit's message with the new one.

```shell
# Syntax: git commit --amend -m <message>

git add .
git commit -m "Fix the network bug"
# Creates the commit: 3050fc0 Fix network bug

git commit --amend -m "Fix the network bug"
# The last commit's message is now "Fix the network bug"
# This also changes its SHA-1 checksum
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/update-commit-message-or-contents.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: You just committed with a typo in the message and haven't pushed yet. How do you fix only the message?
back:
`git commit --amend -m "New message"`. It replaces the last commit with a new one that has the same changes and the corrected message. Anything currently staged is added too, so check `git status` first.

```shell
git commit -m "Fix netwrok bug"
git commit --amend -m "Fix network bug"
```

Amending creates a new commit hash. That's harmless before pushing; after pushing you would need `git push --force-with-lease`, so only do it on a branch nobody else uses. Without `-m`, `--amend` opens your editor with the old message.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/update-commit-message-or-contents.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

Change the last commit's message or contents in Git — Change the last commit's contents

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you want to change the last commit's contents, you can use `--amend` after staging the changes you want to add to the last commit. This will add any staged changes to the last commit, without changing its message.

If you want to keep the same commit message and only add the staged changes, you can use `--no-edit` to prevent Git from opening the default editor to change the commit message.

```shell
# Syntax: git commit --amend --no-edit

git add .
git commit -m "Fix the network bug"
# Creates the commit: 3050fc0 Fix network bug

# Edit or add files
git add .
git commit --amend --no-edit
# The last commit includes the edited/added files
# This also changes its SHA-1 checksum
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/update-commit-message-or-contents.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: You committed but forgot to include one file. How do you add it to that last commit without changing the message?
back:
Stage the file, then run `git commit --amend --no-edit`. The last commit is replaced by one that includes everything now staged, and `--no-edit` keeps the existing message instead of opening the editor.

```shell
git commit -m "Add signup form"
git add src/validation.js      # the forgotten file
git commit --amend --no-edit
```

The result is a new commit with a new hash. Fine before pushing; if the commit is already pushed, it needs `git push --force-with-lease` and shouldn't be done on shared branches (make a new commit there instead).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/update-commit-message-or-contents.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View all Git branches — View all remote branches

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Similarly, you can use `git branch -r` to display a list of all **remote branches**. You can use the same navigation keys and exit key as before.

```shell
# Syntax: git branch -r

git branch -r
# origin/master
# origin/patch-1
# origin/patch-2
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-all-branches.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you list the branches that exist on the remote, and why might that list be out of date?
back:
`git branch -r` lists your remote-tracking branches, such as `origin/main`. They are local snapshots of the remote, updated only when you fetch or pull, so run `git fetch --prune` first to add new branches and drop deleted ones.

```shell
git fetch --prune
git branch -r
#   origin/HEAD -> origin/main
#   origin/fix-login
#   origin/main
```

`git branch -a` shows local and remote-tracking branches together. `git ls-remote --heads origin` asks the server directly without updating anything locally.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-all-branches.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View all Git branches — View all local branches

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
You can use `git branch` to display a list of all **local branches**. As usual, you can use the arrow keys to navigate the list and press <kbd>Q</kbd> to exit.

```shell
# Syntax: git branch

git branch
# master
# patch-1
# patch-2
```

Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-all-branches.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does plain `git branch` show, and how can you tell which branch you're on?
back:
It lists your local branches and marks the current one with `*`.

```shell
git branch
#   fix-login
# * main
#   old-experiment

git branch -vv          # plus last commit, upstream, ahead/behind
git branch --show-current
# main
```

It doesn't show remote branches (use `-r` or `-a`), and `git branch <name>` creates a branch instead of listing. `git status` also names the current branch on its first line.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View or change the remote URL of a Git repository — View the remote URL

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
You can use `git config --get remote.origin.url` to display the URL of the remote repository. The `origin` is the **default name of the remote repository**, but you can replace it with the name of your remote repository.

```shell
# Syntax: git config --get remote.origin.url

git config --get remote.origin.url
# https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-change-remote-url.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you check which URL your `origin` remote points to?
back:
`git remote get-url origin` prints it. `git remote -v` lists every remote with its fetch and push URLs, and `git config --get remote.origin.url` reads the same value straight from the config.

```shell
git remote get-url origin
# https://github.com/acme/shop.git

git remote -v
# origin  https://github.com/acme/shop.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/acme/shop.git (push)
```

`origin` is just the default name `git clone` gives the remote you cloned from; in a fork workflow you often add a second remote called `upstream` for the original project.

---

View or change the remote URL of a Git repository — Change the remote URL

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Similarly, you can use `git remote set-url origin <url>` to change the URL of the remote repository to `<url>`. Again, replace `origin` with the name of your remote repository if it's different.

```shell
# Syntax: git remote set-url origin <url>
```

front: Your repo moved, or you're switching from HTTPS to SSH. Which command points the existing `origin` remote at the new URL?
back:
`git remote set-url origin <new-url>`. It changes the URL of the existing remote in place, so your branches and their tracking setup keep working.

```shell
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:acme/shop.git
git remote -v    # confirm the fetch and push URLs

```

Don't `git remote remove` and re-add it for this: removing a remote also deletes its remote-tracking branches and the upstream settings of your local branches.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View a summary of changes between two Git commits

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Have you ever wanted to see the **changes between two commits** in a Git repository without having to go through the entire commit history? A summary of changes can help you understand the differences between two commits quickly. So how can you do that?

Using `git shortlog <commit>..<other-commit>`, you can view a summary of changes between two given commits. Note that the two commits **don't have to be consecutive**, and you can use any valid commit references, such as **commit hashes**, **branch names**, or **tags**. This allows you to compare any two points in the repository's history.

As usual, you can navigate through the summary using the arrow keys and exit by pressing <kbd>Q</kbd>.

```shell
# Syntax: git shortlog <commit>..<other-commit>

git shortlog 3050fc0de..HEAD
# Duck Quacking (2):
#      Fix network bug
#      Update documentation

git shortlog v1.0..v2.0
# Duck Quacking (2):
#      Add new feature
#      Update dependencies

git shortlog master..feature-branch
# Duck Quacking (2):
#      Add new feature
#      Update documentation
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-changes-summary.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git shortlog main..feature` show, and which commits does `main..feature` select?
back:
It lists the commits on `feature` that are not on `main`, grouped by author with a count, showing each commit's subject line. It summarizes who did what, not the code changes. `A..B` means "commits reachable from B but not from A", so the order matters.

```shell
git shortlog main..feature
# Ana Lopez (2):
#       Add signup form
#       Validate email format
#
# Sam Kim (1):
#       Fix password hint

git shortlog -sn v1.0..v2.0     # only commit counts per author
```

Any refs work: hashes, branches, tags. To see file changes between two points use `git diff --stat A B`; for plain release notes use `git log --oneline A..B`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-changes-summary.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

**Explain the approach**

View a visual graph of the Git repository

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
If you're more of a visual person, you can view a **graph of all commits and branches** in the repository using a single Git command.

Running `git log --pretty=oneline --graph --decorate --all` prints a visual graph of the whole repository's history. This command displays a **visual representation** of all commits and branches in the repository. You can then use the arrow keys to navigate, or press <kbd>Q</kbd> to exit.

```shell
# Syntax: git log --pretty=oneline --graph --decorate --all

git log --pretty=oneline --graph --decorate --all
# * 3050fc0de Fix network bug
# * c191f90c7 Initial commit
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-commit-graph.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Which `git log` command draws a text graph of all branches and merges, with one line per commit?
back:
`git log --oneline --graph --all`. `--graph` draws branch and merge lines on the left, `--all` includes every branch instead of just the current one, and `--oneline` keeps each commit to a short hash plus subject. In a terminal, branch and tag names are shown next to commits by default (older guides add `--decorate` to force this).

```shell
git log --oneline --graph --all
# *   665318e (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'fix-login'
# |\
# | * 4af79a5 (fix-login) Fix login redirect
# * | 9ededda Update README
# |/
# * d82f06d Add login form
```

Save it as an alias with `git config --global alias.graph "log --oneline --graph --all"`, then run `git graph`.

View Git commits by a certain author or committer — View commits by a specific author

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
When you're looking for commits made by a **specific author**, you can use `git log --author=<author>` to filter the commit history. Replace `<author>` with the name of the author you're interested in.

```shell
# Syntax: git log --author=<author>

git log --author="Duck Quacking"
# commit c191f90c7766ee6d5f24e90b552a6d446f0d02e4
# Author: 30 seconds of code
# Date: Tue Apr 6 11:11:08 2021 +0300
# [...]
```

---

front: How do you list only the commits written by a particular person, and what does `git log --author` actually match against?
back:
`git log --author=<pattern>`. The pattern is a regular expression matched against the author's `Name <email>`, so part of a name or an email address both work. Matching is case-sensitive unless you add `-i`.

```shell
git log --author="Ana" --oneline
git log --author="@acme.com" --oneline      # anyone with a company email
git log --author="Ana" --author="Sam"       # either person
```

Repeating `--author` means "any of these". It filters on who wrote the change; to filter on who created the commit object (e.g. after a rebase or a web-UI merge) use `--committer`.

---

front: In Git, what's the difference between a commit's author and its committer, and how do you filter `git log` by committer?
back:
The author wrote the change; the committer created that commit object, for example by rebasing, cherry-picking, amending, or merging a pull request in a web UI. Filter with `git log --committer=<pattern>`, which matches `Name <email>` just like `--author`.

```shell
git log --committer="GitHub" --oneline   # commits created by GitHub's web UI
git log -1 --format='%an <%ae> | %cn <%ce>'
# Ana Lopez <ana@acme.com> | GitHub <noreply@github.com>
```

Usually author and committer are the same person. They differ when someone or something else applies your change, which is why `--author` is the right filter for "who wrote this".

**Explain the approach**

View Git commits that manipulated a specific string

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Finding all commits that **manipulated a specific string** in a Git repository sounds like a pretty tricky task, if you don't know how to do it. Fortunately, Git provides a straightforward way to search for commits that manipulated a given string.

Using `git log -S<string>`, you can find all commits that manipulated the specified `<string>`. The `-S` flag is used to look for differences that change the **number of occurrences** of the specified string.

You can additionally apply any other valid filters to the `git log` command to further narrow down the search results (e.g. by date range).

```shell
# Syntax: git log -S<string>

git log -S<string>
# commit c191f90c7766ee6d5f24e90b552a6d446f0d02e4
# Author: 30 seconds of code
# Date: Tue Apr 6 11:11:08 2021 +0300
# [...]
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-commits-by-string.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: A function called `calculateTax` vanished from the codebase. Which `git log` option finds the commits that added or removed that string?
back:
`git log -S"calculateTax"` (the "pickaxe"). It lists commits that changed the number of occurrences of the string, meaning it was added or removed, not every commit that merely edited a line containing it.

```shell
git log -S"calculateTax" --oneline
# 81ea5bc Remove legacy tax helper
# 4b2c7d1 Add calculateTax

git log -S"calculateTax" -p -- src/billing/   # show diffs, only in that folder
```

Use `-G<regex>` instead to find commits whose added or removed lines match a regex, which also catches edits to a line that still contains the text. Combine with other filters such as `--since` or `--author`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-commits-by-string.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: How do you list only the commits from the last two weeks, and what date formats does `git log --since` accept?
back:
`git log --since="2 weeks ago"`. `--since` (alias `--after`) keeps commits newer than the given date and accepts ISO dates such as `2025-04-01 09:00` or relative phrases like `yesterday`, `3 days ago` or `last monday`.

```shell
git log --since="2 weeks ago" --oneline
git log --since="last monday" --author="Ana" --oneline   # standup notes
```

It filters by committer date, while `git log` displays the author date by default, so a rebased or cherry-picked commit can show an older date than the filter suggests.

front: What does `git log --until=<date>` do, and how would you find the last commit on `main` before a release date?
back:
`--until` (alias `--before`) keeps only commits older than the given date. Add `-1` to get just the newest of those.

```shell
git log --until="2025-03-31 23:59" --oneline
git log --until="2025-03-31 23:59" -1 --format=%h main
# 6d5c4b3
git switch --detach 6d5c4b3     # look at the code as it was
```

Like `--since`, it compares committer dates. A date without a time (`2025-03-31`) means that day at the current time of day, so add a time when the cut-off matters. `git switch main` takes you back.

previous.back:

```shell
# Syntax: git log [--since=<date-from>] [--until=<date-to>]

git log --since='Apr 1 2021' --until='Apr 4 2021'
# commit c191f90c7766ee6d5f24e90b552a6d446f0d02e4
# Author: 30 seconds of code
# Date: Tue Apr 6 11:11:08 2021 +0300
# [...]
```

front: How do you list the commits made from April 1 through April 4, 2025, and why should you include times of day?
back:
Combine both limits: `git log --since="2025-04-01 00:00" --until="2025-04-04 23:59"`. A bare date like `2025-04-01` is read as that day at the current time of day, so without explicit times you can miss commits at either end of the range.

```shell
git log --since="2025-04-01 00:00" --until="2025-04-04 23:59" --oneline
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Add login form
```

Relative forms also work (`yesterday`, `3 days ago`, `last monday`). Prefer ISO `YYYY-MM-DD` over `04/01/2025`, which readers can take as either April 1 or January 4.

previous.back:
One solution:

```shell
git log --since='Apr 1 2021' --until='Apr 4 2021'
```

Using `git log --since=<date-from> --until=<date-to>`, you can view all commits **between** `<date-from>` and `<date-to>`. The dates can be specified in a variety of formats, such as `YYYY-MM-DD`, `MM/DD/YYYY`, or even relative terms like `yesterday`, `2 weeks ago`, etc.

```shell
# Syntax: git log [--since=<date-from>] [--until=<date-to>]

git log --since='Apr 1 2021' --until='Apr 4 2021'
# commit c191f90c7766ee6d5f24e90b552a6d446f0d02e4
# Author: 30 seconds of code
# Date: Tue Apr 6 11:11:08 2021 +0300
# [...]
```

front:
List, one line each, the commits made from April 1 through April 4, 2025 (whole days).

```shell
____
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Add login form
```
back:
One solution:

```shell
git log --since="2025-04-01 00:00" --until="2025-04-04 23:59" --oneline
```

`--since` and `--until` can be combined to bound both ends. Explicit times matter: a bare date means that day at the current time of day.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View a short summary of Git commits — Short summary of commits without merges

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Other options can be used in conjunction with `--oneline` to further customize the output. For example, you can use `--no-merges` to exclude merge commits from the output.

```shell
git log --oneline --no-merges
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Initial commit
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-commits-summary.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Your `git log --oneline` is cluttered with "Merge pull request" commits. How do you hide them?
back:
Add `--no-merges`: it drops every commit with more than one parent, leaving only the commits that made actual changes.

```shell
git log --oneline --no-merges
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Initial commit

git log --oneline --merges        # the opposite: only merge commits
```

Handy for release notes, e.g. `git log --oneline --no-merges v1.0..main`. Teams that squash-merge or rebase-merge have no merge commits to hide in the first place.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-commits-summary.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View a short summary of Git commits — Short summary of all commits

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
One of these is `--oneline`, which is actually a shorthand for `--pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit`. It prints a short summary of all commits, with each commit being printed on a single line.

```shell
git log --oneline
# d540ba1 Merge network bug fix
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Initial commit
```

Notice the short, 7-character commit identifiers. This is because of the `--abbrev-commit` option, which abbreviates the commit SHA-1 checksum to 7 characters. This shorter string is enough to uniquely identify a commit.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-commits-summary.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git log --oneline` print for each commit, and how long are the hashes it shows?
back:
One line per commit: an abbreviated hash plus the subject (first line) of the message. It is shorthand for `--pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit`.

```shell
git log --oneline -3
# d540ba1 (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'fix-network'
# 3050fc0 Fix network bug
# c191f90 Initial commit
```

Hashes are shortened to at least 7 characters; in large repositories Git automatically uses more (often 10 to 12) so each short hash stays unique. You can pass a short hash to other commands, e.g. `git show 3050fc0`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-commits-summary.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View differences in Git changes

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
When working with Git, you'll often need to view the **differences between your changes and the last commit**. This can help you understand what you've modified, what you're about to commit, and what changes you've made since the last commit.

Git provides the `git diff` command to help you with this, allowing you to compare your changes with the last commit. The result will show you the differences between your **unstaged** changes, by default, but you can view the differences between your **staged** changes and the last commit instead, using the `--staged` option.

```shell
# Syntax: git diff [--staged]

git diff
# Displays the differences between unstaged changes and the last commit

git diff --staged
# Displays the differences between staged changes and the last commit
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-differences.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What do `git diff`, `git diff --staged` and `git diff HEAD` each compare?
back:
`git diff` compares your working tree with the staging area (index), so it shows only changes you have not staged yet. `git diff --staged` (same as `--cached`) compares the staging area with the last commit: exactly what `git commit` would record. `git diff HEAD` compares the working tree with the last commit, showing staged and unstaged changes together.

```shell
# after editing src/api.js and src/app.js:
git add src/api.js
git diff --name-only            # src/app.js  (unstaged)
git diff --staged --name-only   # src/api.js  (staged)
git diff HEAD --name-only       # both files
```

A common surprise: right after `git add`, plain `git diff` prints nothing, because the change is now staged. Review with `git diff --staged` before committing.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-differences.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View the last Git commit

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Checking the contents of the last Git commit can sometimes be useful to orient yourself in the repository's history. The `git log` command can help you with this by displaying the last commit in the repository.

Using `git log -1`, you can view the last commit in the repository. This command will show you the **commit hash**, **author**, **date**, and **commit message** of the last commit. You can navigate through the commit history using the arrow keys and exit by pressing <kbd>Q</kbd>.

```shell
# Syntax: git log -1

git log -1
# commit c191f90c7766ee6d5f24e90b552a6d446f0d02e4
# Author: 30 seconds of code
# Date: Tue Apr 6 11:11:08 2021 +0300
# [...]
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-last-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Which command shows the most recent commit's hash, author, date and message, and which one also shows its code changes?
back:
`git log -1` shows the latest commit's hash, author, date and message; `git show` shows the same plus its full diff. Both default to `HEAD` and accept any other commit or branch.

```shell
git log -1
# commit c191f90c7766ee6d5f24e90b552a6d446f0d02e4 (HEAD -> main)
# Author: Ana Lopez <ana@acme.com>
# Date:   Tue Apr 6 11:11:08 2021 +0300
#
#     Fix network bug

git show --stat        # latest commit + list of changed files
git log -1 --oneline   # c191f90 (HEAD -> main) Fix network bug
```

`-1` (or `-n 1`) limits any `git log` to that many commits, e.g. `git log -3 main`.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-last-commit.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View all merged Git branches

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Looking for a way to list all **merged branches** in your Git repository? This can be useful in a variety of scenarios, including cleaning up your repository or identifying branches that are ready to be deleted.

> [!TIP]
>
> You can easily [delete merged branches](https://www.30secondsofcode.org/git/s/delete-branch#delete-merged-branches), using a single command. Check out the linked article for more information.

Using `git branch -a --merged` allows you to view a list of all merged local branches. This command displays branches that have been **merged into the current branch**, making it easy to identify branches that are no longer needed. Use the arrow keys to navigate the list and press <kbd>Q</kbd> to exit.

```shell
# Syntax: git branch -a --merged

git checkout master
git branch -a --merged
# patch-1
# patch-2
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-merged-branches.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: Before deleting old branches, how do you list the ones already merged into `main`, and what does adding `-a` change?
back:
Run `git branch --merged main` (or switch to `main` and run `git branch --merged`). It lists branches whose tip commit is already contained in `main`, so deleting them loses nothing. Adding `-a` also lists remote-tracking branches such as `remotes/origin/fix-login`.

```shell
git switch main
git pull
git branch --merged
#   fix-login
# * main
git branch -a --merged      # local + remote-tracking
git branch -d fix-login     # -d refuses if the branch isn't merged
```

Pitfall: branches merged with a squash or rebase merge (common on GitHub) usually don't appear, because their original commits never entered `main`. The list also includes `main` itself; don't delete that.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-merged-branches.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View the current Git status

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Git provides a command to view the **current status of the working tree**. The `git status` command shows you which files are staged, unstaged, and untracked, as well as the current branch you're on.

If you want a more concise output, you can use the `-sb` flag to view the **short form of the status**. This is useful when you want to quickly check the status of the working tree without the additional details.

```shell
# Usage: git status [-sb]

git status
# On branch patch-1
# Your branch is up to date with 'origin/patch-1'.
#
# Untracked files:
#  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
#  30-seconds.txt
#
# nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

git status -sb
# ## patch-1...origin/patch-1
# ?? 30-seconds.txt
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-status.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: What does `git status -sb` show, and how do you read the `M`, `A` and `??` codes in its output?
back:
It's the short status (`-s`) plus a branch line (`-b`): first your branch, its upstream and ahead/behind counts, then one line per changed file with a two-letter code. The left letter is the staging area, the right letter the working tree.

```shell
git status -sb
# ## fix-login...origin/fix-login [ahead 1]
# M  src/api.js         <- modified, staged
#  M src/app.js         <- modified, not staged
# A  src/validate.js    <- new file, staged
# ?? notes.txt          <- untracked
```

`MM` means staged, then edited again. Plain `git status` gives the same information in long form, with hints for the next command to run.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-status.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

View Git "undo" history

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
Sometimes, `git log` doesn't cut it, especially for commands that don't show up in your commit history. Fortunately, there's a way to view your **"undo" history**. `git reflog` is basically your safety net after running "scary" commands like `git rebase`. It allows you to see not only the commits you made, but each of the actions that led you there.

To view you "undo" history, you can use `git reflog`, which displays the git reference log:

```shell
git reflog
# b6a4f9d6ff9 (HEAD -> patch-1, origin/patch-1) HEAD@{0}: Update docs
# 3050fc0de HEAD@{1}: rebase -i (finish): returning to refs/heads/patch-1
# 3050fc0de HEAD@{2}: rebase -i (pick): Fix network bug
# 93df3f495 (origin/patch-2) HEAD@{3}: rebase -i (start): checkout origin/master
# 69beaeabb HEAD@{4}: rebase -i (finish): returning to refs/heads/patch-1
```

After you've found the commit you want, you can use `git reset` to go back to it.

```shell
git reset --hard 3050fc0de # Go back to the commit with the given hash
```

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-undo-history.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: A bad `git rebase` or `git reset` "lost" some of your commits. How does `git reflog` help you get them back?
back:
`git reflog` lists every position `HEAD` has had in your local repo (commits, checkouts, resets, rebase steps), newest first, including commits no branch points to anymore. Find the entry from before the mistake and point a branch at it.

```shell
git reflog
# 3ddf121 HEAD@{0}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/fix-login
# 5049dbb HEAD@{1}: rebase (pick): Fix network bug
# 4410b18 HEAD@{2}: rebase (start): checkout main
# b6a4f9d HEAD@{3}: commit: Add signup form

git branch rescue b6a4f9d    # safest: keep it on a new branch
git reset --hard b6a4f9d     # or move this branch back (discards uncommitted work)
```

The reflog is local only (never pushed or cloned) and entries expire, by default after 90 days, or 30 for commits no longer on any branch. Uncommitted changes never enter it, so it can't bring those back.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/git/s/view-undo-history.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

Advanced React state hooks — `useToggler` hook

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How would you write a `useToggler` custom hook that returns a boolean plus a `toggle` function whose identity stays the same on every render?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
const toggleValue = useCallback(() => setValue(prev => !prev), []);
```

The functional updater `prev => !prev` reads the latest state from React, so the callback depends on nothing and `useCallback(..., [])` can return the same function forever. `setValue` itself is guaranteed stable, so it does not need to be a dependency either.

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: A counter increments inside `setTimeout`, and quick repeated clicks lose updates because each timeout captured an old `count`. How does a `useGetSet` hook (a ref plus a forced re-render) fix that, and what is the simpler built-in fix?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
const [, update] = useReducer(x => x + 1, 0);
```

Writing to a ref never re-renders, so the hook needs a dispatch function that changes some state. A reducer that returns a new value each time (a counter, or `() => ({})`) always differs under `Object.is`, so every `update()` triggers a render that shows the new `state.current`.

**Explain the approach**

Automatic text linking in React

How would you do this, and what makes it work?

front: How can a React component turn URLs inside a plain-text comment into clickable links without using `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`?

back:
One solution:

```jsx
i % 2 === 1
```

When the separator regex contains a capturing group, `split` puts each captured match between the surrounding text pieces, so the matches always land at odd indices, even when the text starts with a URL (index 0 is then `''`):

```js
'https://a.io and x'.split(/(https?:\/\/[^\s<]+)/g);
// → ['', 'https://a.io', ' and x']
```

An alternative is `URL_RE.test(part)`, but a `/g` regex keeps `lastIndex` between `test` calls and can give wrong answers, so the index check is simpler and safer.

**Explain the approach**

Writing readable reducers in Redux — Identifying the problems

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
While the code in the example is not that complicated right now, complexity can increase very fast as more action types need to be handled by our application. This is due to the fact that each `action.type`'s logic is nested inside the `reducer` function, thus adding more code and complexity with each new action.

Another issue we can identify is that each `action` has a different structure, which increases cognitive load for future maintainers, as they have to remember what keys their `action` needs to have. There's also the added issue of running into a case where `action.type` might be needed to pass actual data to the state (i.e. `state.type` could exist).

Finally, our `action.type` values are hardcoded inside the `reducer` function, making it hard to remember and sync across other files and components. This might seem like the least of our problems, but it's probably the easiest one to fix, so let's start there.

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

React rendering — Rendering behavior

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
React's default behavior is to **recursively render all child components inside of it when a parent component is rendered**. This means that it does not care if a component's `props` have changed - as long as the parent component rendered, its children will render unconditionally.

To put this another way, calling `setState()` in the root component without any other changes, will cause React to re-render every single component in the component tree. Most likely, most of the components will return the exact same render output as the last render, meaning React will not have to make any changes to the DOM, but the rendering and diffing calculations will be performed regardless, taking time and effort.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/react/s/rendering.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

front: When a parent component re-renders, which of its child components re-render by default, and does that mean the DOM is updated?

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

React rendering — React-Redux

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
React-Redux provides bindings for **Redux**, a state container for JavaScript applications, and works a little differently from React's Context API. One of the key differences is that React-Redux only re-renders components that need to render, due to the fact that components subscribed to the Redux store read the latest store state, diff the values and force re-render only if the relevant data has changed, while React is not involved at all in the subscription callback process.

While this most likely means that fewer components will have to re-render compared to using a context, React-Redux always executes its `mapStateToProps` and `useSelector` functions for every connected component in the tree whenever the store state is updated. These calculations are usually less expensive than React's rendering, but if there are costly calculations performed or new references returned when they shouldn't, it might become problematic.

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/react/s/rendering.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).

previous.front:
**Explain the approach**

React rendering — Context API

How would you do this, and what makes it work?
previous.back:
React's **Context API** provides a way to pass data through the component tree without using `props`, but should not be used for state management as it requires manual updating. Any component inside a context's `Provider` can access the data in the context instance using a `Consumer` component or, for function components only, the `useContext()` hook.

When a new reference is passed to a context `Provider` it will cause any connected components to update. React will look for any components consuming the context in the component tree and update them to reflect the change in the context's value. Passing a new object to a context `Provider` is essentially a new reference, as the context holds a single value (in this case an object).

---
Adapted from [30 seconds of code](https://github.com/30-seconds/30-seconds-of-code/blob/f1b2d5a65c32432a877de94a749be40a396ebed2/content/snippets/react/s/rendering.md) · [CC BY 4.0](/licenses/30-seconds.txt).
